div.head: rob
div.p: rob

The rate of expenditure, which had been reduced during the previous Quinquennium, has been reduced Six per cent. in the Ordinary Branch and Seven per cent in the Industrial Branch during this Quinquennium. There is every reason to believe that the reduction in the Industrial Branch will be continued. In the Ordinary Branch the Annual Premium Income has Increased from £83,245 to £142,732. aud the Assurance Fund from .2473,862 to £744,583. In the Industrial Branch the increase in the Annual Premium Income has been from £980,575 to £2,051,024, and the Assur- ance Fund from £373,492 to £1,721,492. The Directors would draw attention to the Report made by Mr. A. H. BAILEY on the results of the Valuation, and to his approval of the methods adopted by the Company's Actuaries. It is gratifying to know that these results have been secured after fully providing for every liability, and after adding a considerable amount to the Contingency Fund, and carrying forward a large balance in each Branch.

div.head: EXTRACT FROM MR. A. H. BAILEY'S REPORT.
div.p: EXTRACT FROM MR. A. H. BAILEY'S REPORT.

I have carefully examined the several papers which you have placed in my hands containing the results of the Valuation of the Liabilities of your Company to the 31st December, 1881. During the progress of the work, which has occupied several months, and on which more than 600 persons have been en- gaged, I have had opportunities of inspecting the various pro- cesses that have been employed, and of satisfying myself of the care and pains that have been taken to insure accuracy throughput. Your business is derived mainly from the large classes of the community whose means will admit of their effecting Life Assurance for small or very moderate sums only, and whom the greater number of the ,xisting Life Assurance Societies have been unable or unwilling to reach. In furtherance of this object the business of the Company is divided into two Branches, for each Of which separate accounts are kept and separate investments made. (1). The Ordinary Branch, in which the Premiums are pay- able ,in most cases annually, but sometimes half-yearly or quarterly. (2). The Industrial Branch, in which all the Premiums without exception are payable weekly. ORDINARY BhaNclr.—For the Policies on single lives for the whole term with profits, which constitute the bulk of the risks, the average amount assured by each p,licy is nearly £137, the average Annual Premium £4 Bs. 6d., or at the rate of 2.3 4s. 9d. per cent, on the sum assured. From Mr. Hughes' report it will be observed that the num- ber of policies in force (exclusive of annuities) is 31,616, the Premium Income being £142,642. The business of this Branch alone is therefore of considerable magnitude and im- portance. The Valuation of the Liabilities has been made upon a basis the effect of which is to require a larger Reserve than most Life Assurance Companies retain or think necessary. •

INDUSTRIAL BrtAwar.—ln this Branch the average amount assured by each Policy is £9 4s. 10d., the average weekly pre- inium almost exactly 2d., being at the rate of £4 12s. Id. per cent, per annum on the sum assured. The number of policies In force is £8,822,519, so that the lives assured comorise about one-eighth of the entire population of Great Britain and Ireland. The annual premium income is £2,051,024, Experience has shown that for business of this character two conditions are indispensable; the premiums must be payable weekly and agents must be employed to call regularly for their collection. These two conditions occasion ,heavy expense, and as a necessary consequence the rates of premium are and must be higher than the Ordinary Branch. But offering as you do both systems of assurance to the public, you find that the majority are willing to pay the higher rates for the convenience of the weekly recoipt and collection of the premiums. Careful consideration has been given to the principles moon which these liabilities should be valued, comprehending risks from infancy to extreme old age. By the requirements of the Act of Parliament returns have to be made to the Board of Trade of the sums assured and premiums payable at every age of life, and calculations have been made of the present value of these quantities for all the policies in force. But of the recently effected policies, a large proportion are on the lives of children with whom the risk of death diminishes, instead of increasing as they become older; again, a large number of these recently effected policies are allowed to lapse after they have been a short time only in force. To such policies, therefore, it seems to me that the usual methods of Valuation are not properly ap- plicable. It was therefore decided, as explained in Mr. Dewey's report, that for Whole Life Policies exceeding £5O, all Endowment and Joint Life Assurances, and all other policies which had been five years in force, and where the lives assured were above ten years of age, a reserve should be made on the same principles as in the Ordinary Branch, except that the Tables of Mortality employed should be the English Life Tables. The other policies of which although the number is large the liability under them is very small, have been regarded as short term risks. It is in the highest degree satisfactory to find that after sub- jecting the liabilities to the stringent tests that have been described your resources have been found to be so ample to meet all your engagements; and the general results of this searching investigation cannot but be most gratifying to all who are Interested in the prosperity of the Company. EXTRA.CT FROM THE REPORT OF MR. W. HUGHES,

div.head: ACT 61THE ORDINARY -BRANCH.
div.p: ACT 61THE ORDINARY -BRANCH.

There were in force at the date of the Valuation 31,616 Life Assurance Policies, assuring with Bonus £4,242,449, and pro- ducing an Annual Premium Income of £142,642. The Imme- diate Annuities are 186 in number, and involve a charge of £4,202 per annum. The Table of Mortality employed for the valuation of the Life Assurance Policies is the Institute of Actuaries Hirt Table, and for the Immediate Annuities Mr, Finlalson's Government Annuity Tables, being the same that were used at the last valuation. The rate of interest assumed in the calculations for both kinds of contract is 3 per cent. _ .

The whole of the loading, or difference between the premiums actually receivable and the pure premiums, has been reserved. This loading amounts to £31,377 per annum, and is available to meet future expenses and provide for future profits.
EXTRACT FROM THE REPORT OF MR. T. C. DEWEY, ACTUARY OF THE INDUSTRIAL BRANCH.

The policies in existence were 4,822,519 in number, assuring the sum of £44.558,814, and producing a weeidy income from premiums of £39,442 Ifs., and an Annual Premium Income of £2,051,024. The special tables for Endowment Assurance, issued after the last valuation, have been very successful, the amount of busi- ness now in existence producing an Annual Premium Income of £32,700. The facilities offered in this Branch for Assurances on the lives of the middle classes, have resulted in a large accession of income, the Premium Income derived from Assurances of £5O and upwards being now £115,489 per annum,

During the Quinquennium the mortality of this Branch of the Company's business has been carefully recorded week by week. The results nearly correspond with Dr. Farr's English Life Table (No. 3), and, as directed by you, I have taken that Table as the basis of the valuation for every description of risk. As at previous investigations I have assumed that the interest realized will, for the future, be £3 per cent. per annum. Male and Female lives have been kept separate throughout the valuation, the number of each sex assured is in nearly similar proportion to that shown by the population of the country. Each year's business has been valued separately, and as the oldest policies have been 30 years in existence sixty separate valuations have consequently been necessary. A pure Premium Valuation has been made for all policies, upon lives exceeding ten years of age, which have been in existence five years, and for a)l policies issued under the Endow- ment Assurance, the Middle Class, and the Joint Life Tables, however short their duration.

For Infantile Assurances and all other policies under £-0 in amount and of less than five years' duration, a method has been adopted which produces a liability on every policy and reserves a sum sufficient to meet thepermanent expenses of the Branch it follows, therefore, that all negative values have been excluded. _ BEAUTIFUL BEA.

Beautiful sea ;:1-riCse facile bosom waves In unison with Neptune's fickleheart,— That here in anger yawns a my; iad graves, And there but bursts In smiles it's lips apart. It's temper infantile in moods—at rest One hour, asleep an I unconcerned; The next, destroys it's peace, disturbs it's breast, To nocent spleen it's sweetness turned. See now it gazes at the azure sky, Where interlaciog clouds unnumbered pass, As some fair maiden in her vanity Might peer into the tell-tale looking glass How grand it is! how lovable it's mien! Reflecting from you sun-illumined arch, ( Whose ether depths define an empyrean screen), The tinted clouds that oft beneath it march. Ah ! well may poets consecrate ale sea To rhapsody and finely-measured praise! So be they lured by liquid melody, Enraptured by the ocean's sweetest ways.

For Natu4rouses4nore than Art excites Of joy-assuring love of perfect things. And tempts the nnnd to scale msthetic heig'nts, Whence Poesy ker inspiration brings Warrington, March 21st, 1382. BENI. BAT.-DON.

-------- The three things most difficult are to keep a secret, to ferget an injury, and make good 'use of leisure. Duty does not consist in suffering everything, but in suf- lering everything for duty. Sometimes, indeed, it is our *duty not to suffer.—Dr. rind. Just in proportion as a man becomes good, divine, Christ- like, he passes ott of the relixion of theorising, of system. building, and hireling service into the religion of beneficent activities. It is well to think well; it is divine to act vrell. —Horace Mann. The frozen rill running its course will somewhere find a break in its icy vesture to laugh back the glint of the sun- shine. So of those natures reserved even unto iciness; somewhere the sunshine of love will find a break in their chilly enfoldment, and love -will answer love with glinting kisses. Curran and a friend were walking in the streets of Dublin one day, when they heard a passer-by use the word cur'osity " for "curiosity." Said Curran's friend, "How that fellow murders the King's English !" "Not so bad as 'that," observed the wit ; "it is not murder quite; he has only knocked an eye (i) out." Dr. Vaneittart, an eminent lawyer, was pleading a cause asainst Serjeant Bearcrott. Said Bearcroft to the Court, '" As long names will be tiresome, I beg leave to call the counsel on the opposite side Mr. Van." "I have no objec- tion," said Vansittart, " and I will return the compliment, and will name the learned gentleman by the appropriate title of Mr. Bear 1" The Academy says that a good anecdote is reported of -Victor Hugo in connection with his bust just completed by Villain. He was, with difficulty, persuaded by his friends to allow it to be crowned with laurel, but it happens -that David d'Angers made a bust of him when he was yet young, and so crowned it. "After all," said the great poet, -C' you are right perhaps; since David d'Angers crowned me with laurels, I must not, now I am old, seem to have lost them en route." Josst BILLINGS'S PHILOSOPHY.—All ov natur's works an a part ov a perfckshnn ov a plan. She makes no mistakes, creates no vacancys, and guesses at nothing. Laffter proves nothing. Wize men laff, and idiots grin all the time. Gravity iz becuming to a plaool at all times, but only to a wizs man on state ockashune. Heroism iz simple, and yet it iz rare. Every one who duz the best they kin iz a hero. Good breeding iz the only thing that kan make a % phool endurable. There iz great art in knowing how to give mahout creating an obligashun. SERPENT WORSHIP.—One of the earliest forms of idolatry was serpent worship, which was closely allied with sun wor- ship, and became well-nigh universal. We find its traces I amongst different races, and in many lands; in general curiously mingled with traditions of the temptation aid fall In Eden. The story reappears in one form or other in al- most every mythology of Europe and Asia, and even in the more isolated lands of North and South America. The es- teem and reverence in which the serpent was held in all ancient lands can only be traced to its being regarded as the embodiment of wisdom, in some dim association with the traditions of Eden. It would seem as if this idea was in some degree kept up by our Lotcl's own words, when He recommends His disciples to be " wise as serpents," as well as "harmless as doves." But this probably refers to the well-known great sagacity of the serpent in taking care of itself, or *avoiding danger. What was Satan's tempting promise to Eve? That she should be wise as God Himself, knowing good from evil. What became of the faith which God Himeelf revealed to Adam, and which was his support in the agony of expulsion from his beautiful home? How came it that, in the course of two or three centuries, the very imtrument of his egradation and misery became to his descendants an object of reverence and worship ?—The

Quiver. A Clemons Lzrrens—Mr. Wesley wrote the following letter to Mr. S—, at Armagh, in Ireland, April 24,1709 :- 4. Be active, be diligent, avoid all sloth, laziness, indolence. Fly from every appearance of it, else you will never be more than half a Christian. Be cleanly. In this let the Metho- dists take pattern by the Quakers. Avoid all nastiness, dirt, slovenliness, both in your person, clothes, and house. Be always sweet above ground; uncleanliness is a bad fruit of laziness; use all dilligence to be clean, as one says— Let thy mind's sweetness have its operation Upon thy person, clothes, and habitation. Whatever clothes you have, let them be whole; no rents, no tatters, no rags. These are a scandal to either man or woman, being another fruit of vile laziness. Mend your clothes, or I shall never expect you to mend your lives. Let none ever see a ragged Methodist. It is an uncleanly and unwholesome self-iedulgence ; and the more customary it is the more resolutely should you break off from every degree of that evil custom. Use no snuff unless prescribed by a Physician. I suppose no other nation in Europe is in such bondage to this silly, nasty, dirty custom, as the Irish are. . . . Touch no dram. It is liquid fire. It is a sure ' though slow poison. It saps the very springs of life. In Ireland, avove all countries in the world, I would sacredly abstain from this, because the evil is so general; and to this, and snuff, and smoky cabins, I impute the blindness which is so common throughout the nation. THE ELEPHANT IN THE MIDDLE AGES.—Matthew Paris mentions that the Soldan of Babylon, Matek el.Kamel, sent an elephant as a rare present to the Emperor Frederic IL, in the year A.D. 1229 (Sir Frederick Madden's edition of the " Historia Minor," vol. ii., p. 314). Bat it was not until the year 1255 that the first elephant was seen in Eng- land. This was presented ty the King of France to our King Henry 111. The chi-older, John of Oxenedee, chronicles the arrival of this animal at London, and declares that it was believed that none had ever been brought to England before. Of the elephant Matthew Paris made a very' good drawing, the original of which is still extant among the Cottonian manuscripts in the British Museum (Nero, D. I.) ; and an equally good, but smaller, drawing is given by John de Walingford, in another Cottonian manu- script (Julius, D. VII.). The beast arrived at Sandwich, and was conveyed to the Tower of London, where the sheriffs had been directed by royal precept to build a house for it 401 t. in length, and 201 t. in breadth, taking care to let the building have sufficient strength to be fit for any other pur- pose. The animal itself was 101 t. in height from the top of the back to the ground, and was 10 years old. It lived on to the 41st year of Henry 111., AD., 1257, in which year it appears from the "Chancellor's Roll" that for the main- tenance of the elephant and its keeper, from Michaelmas to St. Valentine's Day, immediately before the animal died, at the age of 12 years only, the charge amounted to £l6 13s. id. The name of the keeper is recorded to have been John Gooch. Many chroniclers mention this elephant—e.g., Matthew Paris, iii., 334; annals of Barton, i., 329. 'the '44 Majora " of Matthew Paris states (vol. v., p. 489) that no •elephant had ever before been seen on this side of the Alps, but that statement will hardly agree with the record of the elephant presented to the German Emperor in A.D. 1229, as already mentioned. Crowds of people went to see the king's elephant, according to this author, and we may well believe it. The drawings seem to indicate an Indian rather than an African elephant, but it is difficult to determine the question. Tine Foneszs oreFasurou.—The follies of conventional costume, with its unequal distribution of clothing and irra- tional compression of parts of the body—especially parts that ought to be free, such as the waist—have been fre- quently exposed, and their injurious tendencies completely demonstrated. There is, however, no tyranny so oppresive as that of the mode. A woman might as well be dead as out of the fashion. It is the aim of her existence to dress for the admiration of the opposite sex; and in carrying out this, her natural passion, she is not content to be guided as in- stinct instructs her, but feels and acts as the subject of an unseen authority which dominates society, and renders even sensible and in other respects reasoning and reasonable women slaves. There is something mysterious in this admission, be- cause it is perfectly well-known that the rulers of fashion are not its leaders. Those who determine to cut, colour, and general contrivance of feminine costume are not the wearers of the dress they design, but the manufacturers. "Women of fashion" are so only in name; they are, in fact, nothing more than the show figures on which tradesmen and tradeswomen display their wares. If the facts were fully and plainly stated, the fashionable intelligence would not announce that at a particular assembly Lady Little Waist wore gorgeous apparrel of such or such a material and made in such and such a style; but that Messieurs or Mesdames Snip and Stitch exhibited a costume on the person of Lady L. W. This is not a travesty of the truth as to the transaction, but a simple statement of the facts. It is notorious that mothers recognise the evils and the anomalies of the mode, and yet train up their daughters to walk in their footsteps as the slaves of fashion. Dress can never be thoroughly reformed or fashion rendered less foolish until women begin to assert their individuality and clothe them- selves in costumes which are understood to be of their own choosing, E 0 that the wearer of the indelicate or graceless attire re 'le -*and confessed as personally responsible for the transgression of the rules of reason and modesty. It is under the cover of the mode women dress, or rather undress, themselves, to the verge of flagrant impropriety, that they distort their figures and strangle their waists. They would not dare to do these deeds of folly or offence, nor would their husbands and fathers allow them to be done in their families, but that the responsibility is supposed to rest with the makers of fashion. Women of fashion protest that they are "in the hands of their dressmaker," and hence they can, and do, go madly astray.—Lancet.

SCIENTIFIC NOTES. Jerusalem is the latest addition to the field of journalistic enterorie,e. The Gamete de Jerusalem is to appear in Eng- lish, French, and GE-man. The excavation e san the plains of Cheronea have resulted in the discovery nf a qeadrangular wall, inside of which were found the remains of 185 Thebans ia clay. All bore traces of the wounds received 4th August, 338 B.C. in fight- ing against the Macedonians. A rich discovery cf Laucestrine relics has been made at Steckherne, on Lake Constance. They consist of flint and bone implements, pottery, bones of animals now extinct, and a quantity o: wheat and oats. The relics have been placed in the Franenfield Museum. The Illustrkle Zeitung reports the discovery of marble pillars and a wrecked war ship in Greece. Some divers for sponges at Ga.ugaliana first discovered the marble pillars, and then the wrecked ship. On the ship were three bronze cannons of ancient make, having a peculiar mechanism for breach-loading. One of the cannons had the number 1073 on it, and the inscription' Al bel zetto." Some interesting particulars have lately reached Khar- toum respecting Dr. Janker's recent proceedings, the most important item being the announcement that he had suc- ceeded in penetrating six days' journey to the eonth-west of Scheeeinfurth'e river Welle. It may therefore be ex- pected that he has at lest solved one of the great problems of African hydrography, and fall details of his explorations will b 3 eagerly looked'for. Accounts of additional cures of snake-bites come from Brazil. The Monitor Campista reports the cure cf a boy, bitten by the deadly pregnicosa, at S. Joao da Barra, with permanganate of potash injected into the wound; and from Minas Geraes comes the account of the successful treatment of a bite on the ankle with hydrate of chloral syrup. In eels latter case the man was bitten by a rattlesnake, and the care was effected by the administration of four spoonfuls of the syrup with an interval of half-an-hour between each. The American papers report the discovery in some marl. pits near Marlborough, New Jersey, of the fossil remains of two remarkable reptiles, of a species hitherto unknown. ' Adopting the almost universal practice of applying the term "sea-serpent" to any mysterious aquatic creature, says the Colonies and India, the remains are described as an antediluvian "sea-serpent," though the details furnished by Professor Lockwood, after a careful examination of the bones, show that the creature was more formidable than the most terrible sea-serpent ever yet seen or imagined. METEORITES IN TRANSYLVANIA.—On February 3,e1 a re markable fall of meteorites occurred in Transylvania. At Klausenberg an intense light suddenly flashed into view at 3 45 p.m. on that day, the sky being perfectly cloudless. The meteor was seen in the north-east part of the sky, and when it disappeared a white cloud was seen in its stead, which spread into a thin streak stretching from west to east. Soon afterwards a loud report was heard. The next day the news arrived that near Moos, about twenty-five miles to the east of Klausenhurg, some meteorites had fallen; one of these weighs 35 kilogrammes, and penetrated 68 centimetres deep into the ground. Two other places were found near Olah Gyeres, and five others near Vajcla Kamaras. Prof. Koch collected no less than sixty pieces of smaller dimen- sions near Gyulatelke, Visa, and Bare, to the north of Mocs. The direction of the meteor was from nortimvest to south- east, to judge from the position of the fragments; the latter were scattered over a line of about 15 miles in length. THE METAL CSltrM.—The discovery of caesium and rubidium by Bunsen and Kirchhoff was it is known, one of the first fruits of spectrum analysis. These are the most elect° positive of all known elements, and have a remark- able affinity for oxygen—so great in the case of csesium, that it has heretofore been found impossible to isolate the metal. The problem, however, has now been solved by Herr Setterberg by electrolysis of a fused mixture of cyanide lof mei= and cyanide of barium (large quantities of these costly substances having been placed at his disposal). ICfesiuna is like the other alkali matters; it is silver white, and very soft and extensible. Its melting point is about 126dege5 C.; and its specific gravity 1.88. In the air it Ignites spontaneously, and when thrown on water behaves quite like* sodium, potassium, and rubidium. Herr Setter- jeerg has anew proved in his experiments that it is quite impossible to obtain cm3ium by the method adopted for rubidium and potassium, distilling the carbonate with char- coal at a white heat. STRANGE ELECTRICAL PHENOZFENON.—Mr. James Moir, of Savoch, Ellon, Aberdeenshire, writes to 11Tature :—On February 18th this part of Scotland was visited by a furious gale of wind, rain, sleet, and hail. The gale subsided con- siderably about five o'clock in the afternoon. At eight o'clock the sky was fairly clear, when a black cloud sprang up in the north, and the night became suddenly intensely dark. With the darkness came a tremendous shower of hail. All at once I was startled by a vivid flash of lightning close at hand, but without thunder. At the same instant Ifound myself enveloped in a sheet of pale, flickering, white light. It seemed to proceed from every part of my clothes, es- pecially on the side least exposed to the hail, and more par- ticularly and brightly from My arm, shoulder, and head. Though I turned about pretty smartly, and shifted my posi- tion, I found it impossible to shake off the flickering flames. When I walked on they continued with me for two cr three minute 3, disappearing only when the violence of the blast was somewhat diminished. I felt no unusual sensation be- yond the stinging of the bail, and no sound except that of the storm. Then and since I have puzzled myself to account for the strange phenomenon, and can only-imagine it to have been a peculiar manifestation of St. Elmo's Fire, so well known to sailors during thunderstorms within the tropics. THE DAILY SWELLING AND CONTRACTION OF PLANTS. —With delicate means of measurement Herr Kraus has recently proved the existence of a phenomenon in all plant organs, which is connected with their variable water con- tent, and consists in a periodical swelling and contraction in the 24 hours. Leaves, dec., decrease in thickness from the early morning till the afternoon, when they begin to swell again, attaining a greater size by night than by day (this is well seen in agave, aloe, and the like). Similarly with buds, flowers, green cones, fruits, ct.c.; and with sterns and branches. Herr Kaiser bad before proved such a period in trunks of trees, and Herr Kraus shows that both wood and bark share in it, independently or unitedly. The various experiments of Herr Kraus—removal of foliage, watering, shutting out light, kc., lead to explanation of the phe- nomena by the varying reciprocal action of those factors which bring water into the plant, and those which carry it away. By night only the water-absorbing activity of the parts below ground operates, by day the water-consuming activity of the parts above ground besides. The water- consuming activity depends mainly on the foliage and on light (removal of leaves or of light stops the contraction) and consists essentially in transpiration. Herr Kraus states that when a plant is watered these things occur: —ln a short time, less than an hour, the stem begins to swell; both wood and bark take part in this, the wood always first. The swelling progresses at a pretty;quick rate, upwards of several metres per second. After some time, perhaps an hour, con- traction gradually recurs. The contraction began at the upper part of an acacia after 10 minutes, whereas the swel- ling at the lower part continued 50 minutes. This shows that the contraction is due to the activity of the foliage, and is gradually extended downwards. 6ELF-LxGHTING ELECTRIC BUOYS AND SELF-ACTING FOGHORNS.—A novel application of the motive power sup- plied by the waves of the sea has been designed by an American inventor, Mr. Bigler, of Newbury, in the utilisa- tion of the movements of the water for the purpose of illu- minating an electric lamp attached to buoys placed to mark sunken rocks or other dangers to navigation. Experiments recently made at New York seem to prove the practicability of the scheme. A small dynamo-electric machine is fixed to the buoy connected with a mechanical contrivance so ar- ranged that the movements of the buoy as it is tossed about by the waves set it in motion and so generate a current of e:ectricity, which is conveyed to an Edison incandescent lamp fixed outside the buoy. The intermittent action of the waves conveys a corresponding intermittent action to the machine, and causes a similar alternate illumination and extinction of the little lamp. Consequently, when the sea is rough, the lamp is instantaneously lighted, and remains alight during the passage of one wave over the side of the buoy, and then remains extinguished till the next wave sets I the machinery in action. This ingenious contrivance is an adaptation of an existing method of causing buoys to be- come self-acting foghorns. The buoy is fitted with an ap- paratus so placed that the pressure of a wave confines a cer- tain amount of air in the receiver from which it can only escape through a whistle or horn. By this means a warning sound is emitted at short intervals, more or less intense,and of longer or shorter duration, according as the sea is rough or smooth. During a calm, when the buoy is easily seen or avoided, both foghorn and warning light are not in action ; but they both come into activity when the violence of the sea increases the necessity for the signals which they afford.

Of a person noted for a certain useless over-pity, Douglas Jerrold said, " He was so benevolent a man that, in his mis- taken compassion, he would have held an umbrella Over a duck in a shower of rain." Do rest awhile. You are wearing out the vital forces faster than there is need, an in this way subtracting years Isom the sum total of yonr life. This rush and worry day by day, this restless anxiety after something you have not got, is like pebble stones in machinery—they grate and grind the life out of you. IGNORANCE.—ProbabIy there is no quality more efficient in dispelling ignorance than the courage which dares to con- fess it. The child learns fast, chiefly because he has no self-conscious fear of being thought uninformed. He asks all manner of questions without any qualm of misgiving, and exposes his own deficiencies without any feeling of shame and distress. It is by his free and eager inquiries that he improves so rapidly. Were he afraid to show his ignorance, no one could help him out of it. The enforced school lessons would comprise nearly the whole of his edu- cation, and even they could not be adapted to his individual mental needs. As it is, every genial and kind-hearted per- son with whom he comes in contact is interested in adding to his stock of knowledge. The same privilege might be enjoyed by the adult did not a feeling of shame prevent him from seeking knowledge in the same natural and simple way. But as the years pass, he comes to feel that the confes- sion of ignorance will expose him to ridicule, or contempt, or censure, and he therefore hides it under whatever pretext , he can find.

NOTES ON AGRICULTURE HORTI- CULTURE, &c, The Western Counties Agricultural Co-operative Society, started some tiro years ago, nurnbere now over 800 members, and has stores in Truro as well as Plymouth. This enables farmers to buy manures and seeds at reasonable prices for ready money. Farm produce having been of late years so depreciated in value, makes it of primary importance that all purchases should be made on the most advantageous Iterms. The London and North-Western Railway Company have arranged to receive daily at their Kew Bridge station all kinds of farm and market-garden produce, and to forward them in time for the early markets next morning in Bir- mingham, Wolverhampton, Manchester, Liverpool, and other large towns in the northern and midland counties. Seeing that market-gardening, in nil probability, will play a very important part in our future agricultural history, this is a step in the right direction. INTERESTING BANQUET TO AN AGRICCLTURIST.-011 Sunday, the sth inst., the National Agricultural Society of France gave a banquet to their president, M. Chevreul, at the Cafe Riche, Paris, in commemoration of the 50th year of his election. Nearly every member of the society present in the city attended. M. de Mahy and M. Dames recounted the services and discoveries of M. Chevreul, attributing his successes to untiring work, regularity, and moderation in the conduct of life, love of method, respect of imagination, and culture of elevated ideas and search for truth. M. Dumas concluded by wishing the aged but robust president long life and good health. A complete ovation followed. M. Chevreul embraced M. Dumas, and M. Henze presented a colossal bouquet of camelias, which, says the report, hid the person, and blocked the remarks of the president. M. Chevreul is in his 97th year; he was elected a member of the National Society in 1832; and since 1849 has .been 34 times Vice-President or President of the Society. TENANT RIGHT IN LOMBARDY AND PIEDMONT.—On the entrance of a tenant to a farm the proprietor appoints an engineer to make out a list of its fixtures and stock, and to report on the state of every field, its size, cultivation, and condition. Plantations are noted and trees numbered, and everything of a permanent nature stated, and the whole valued, according to a scale of prices. The tenant has the right to associate an engineer of his own choice with the one appointed by the proprietor. When the lease expires the same work is gone over again,and should ameliorations have been made by the tenant, he is credited with these at their value; and, on the other hand, should deteriorations have taken place, he is debited with them, and he either receives from his landlord, or has to pay him, the sum brought out the valuation. . . From what I could learn of the esti- mation in which the method is held, both landlord and tenant seem satisfied. . . Tenants are entitled to assign their leases in the absence of provisions in the lease to the contrary; the consent of the landlord is not required to such assignments; the principal tenant remains bound to the landlord. In the case of loss of crop, or half loss, the tenant is allowed to claim a reduction of rent, which is allowed unless compensated for in the previous year's excess. The tenant for a single year is also so entitled to claim for the whole or half loss of a year's crop. This, or something like it, was understood to be the law of Scotland, although not acted on of late.—Fortnightly Review. Mu. WALLER ON AGRICULTURE.—Speaking the other day at an important meeting of East Anglian farmers, Mr. Waller said he had of late made a few experiments. He had laid down 70 acres in permanent pasture, and he did not hesitate to say that that was an enormous mistake. He had also laid down similar land with good solid ryegrass and clover, and he did not hesitate to say that that was, so far, a grand success. It had now been going four or five years, and he should like some of his farmer friends to go and see it. He had a neighbour near him that evening, and he would challenge that gentleman to show a piece of ryegrass and clover, within 150 miles, that would compare with it. It had been mowed every year, and every succeeding year he had been glad that he had not ploughed it up. He be- lieved that the land of this country would grow ryegrass and clover everlastingly, if properly treated. There might be many advantages in the four-course shift, but he would urge the growth of artificial grasses in large quantities for feeding purposes. Mr. Waller, in the course of further re- marks, alluded to wholesome laws which prevailed in the colonies. For instance, if you were to turn a pair of rabbits down in some parts you would be liable to six months' im- prisonment with hard labour. If your neighbour did not 3nt down his thistles or other seed-spreading weeds, he could be summoned before the magistrates, who would order him to cut them down within a reasonable time, and if he did not do it, it would be done for him at a much greater cost. No man had a right to do anything calculated to in- jure his neighbour. It was a splendid law, and something of the same kind would be beneficial in this country; for why should his neighbour cultivate thistles, docks, dzo., and allow the seeds to blow all over his land? The same might be said with regard to rabbits, which were very nice things to keep, provided they were kept in with a nice piece of wire netting. Why should my landlord, or any other fel- low, keep beastly rabbits to come out at night and eat his neighbour's crops? If he chose to keep rabbits, let him fence them in. POTATOES AND THEIR CULTURE.—A few isolated in- stances of success have resulted from planting potatoes in the autumn; but when the results of experiMents are ob- served over a period of thirty years this very old practice is found to be unsafe. No good cultivators who gave a shilling a pound for potatoes would plant them in the autumn, for the simple reason that they well know that a more profitable return could be had by planting well-pre- pared tubers in the spring. A great deal of argument will be needed to destroy the force of that one fact. Early pota- toes that have commenced growing may be planted at once,, especially in rather light soil, and covered four inches deep; in cold, strong soil it is better to plant later in the month, and cover more lightly, as the tubers if spread thinly in a light place will make stronger and better growth out of un- genial soil than in it for the next fortnight or three weeks. Nearly all potatoes are planted too closely together, both in gardens and fields. In good soil the rows of Ashleafs should be two feet apart; all mid-season sorts nearer three feet than two, and very strong growers nearer four feet than three between the lines, the sets ranging from a foot to fifteen inches apart in the rows. It is of the utmost importance that the subsoil be broken up, so that the rain can pass from the roots freely. A hard "sole" such as in some fields is 'made with the plough, and in gardens often left by defec- tive digging, is in some soils almost impervious to water, and wherever this accumulates about the roots, injury, if not destruction, inevitably follows. In low-lying ground and wet soils generally there is no plan equal to planting on the surface and covering the sets with soil obtained from between the rows, which, in this case, should be 3i or 4 feet apart. It is surprising what fine crops are thus obtained by this method of culture in cold, wet soils. A little Super- phosphate of lime spread in the drills with the sets' just making the ground. white, is always beneficial, and the bene- fit is still greater if a very slight sprinkling of nitrate of soda or sulphate of ammonia, about half an ounce of each to a length of ten or twelve yards, and any quantity of wood ashes are spread in at the same time. The potatoes are then supplied with some of the most important consti- tuents they require for ensuring healthy growth and good crops.

ILLUSTRIOUS IRISHMEN. _ No. XII.—JOHN PHILPOT CURRAN. Oh breathe not his name—let it sleep in the shade, Where cold and unhonoured his relics are laid; Sad, silent and dark, be the tears that we shed, As the night dew that falls on the grass o'er his head. But the night dew that fallsothough in silence it weeps, Shall brighten with verdure the grave where he sleeps, And the tear that we shed, though in secret it rolls, . Shall long keep his memory green in our souls. Thomas Moore. Robert Emmet, whose introduction here arises from the well known episode in his career (strange and mournful as some fiction of romance) that is connected with the name of Sarah Curran and the story of "The Broken Heart," was the son of a respectable physician in Dublin' and the younger brother of Thomas Addis Emmet. From his earliest years he seems to have been a Republican. At the age of 16 he entered the Dublin University, and soon gained for himself not only the respect, but the love of all who had the privilege of his acquaintance. There was a debating club in connection with the College; and here young Emmet endeavoured to mature his oratorical powers against the time when his dream of political regeneration should be realised. Thomas Moore, in a notice of him, says "that when he joined the society he found Emmet in full reputation, not only for his learning and eloquence, but also for the blamelessness of his life and the grave suavity of his manners." A quotation from one of his speeches will show the political bias of his mind. After a brilliant eulogy on the French Republic, he concluded with this remark "When a people, advancing rapidly in knowledge and power, perceive at last how far their Government is lagging behind them, what, then, I ask, is to be done in this case? Why, pull the Government up to the people !" The conse- quence of indulging in such language at such a time may be easily imagined. Emmet, with others, was struck off the College Roll. He was then 23 years of age. This untoward event pnly confirmed him in his Republican principles, and increased his ire against a Government that could not tolerate freedom of speech. After his expulsion he visited his brother, who had been arrested as one of the rebel direc- tory in the year 1798, and Was now confined in Fort George, and then went to the Continent, apparently for pleasure. On his return from the tour he visited Amsterdam and Brussels, where his brother, being liberated from Fort George, was staying, and in 1802 set out for Ireland. No sooner had he arrived in Dublin than he entered into com- munication with the several leaders who had taken an active part in the former rebellion, and explained to them his in- tentions of striking another blow for the Independence of ' his country. We have no space to describe the preparations made on the part of Emuiet and his followers for the fulfil- ment of their plans. Suffice it to say that the 23rd of July, 1803, was fixed upon as the day on which the attempt was to be made. This was not the date originally fixed upon by Emmet. From conversations with Napoleon and Talteyrand he had been led to suppose that in the August of 1803 the amicable relations between England and France would be ruptured, and that the invasion of England would then be attempted, and this was the time he had fixed upon for making his effort, but circumstances over which he had little or no control forced his hand. The fatal day arrived, and when it closed the Insurrection of 1803 was crashed. Favoured by the darkness of the night Etnmet and a few followers contrived to escape from the city to the mountain range of Wicklow. For better security the party separated, each adopting the best meanstwithin his power for evading the now uplifted hand of justice. Emmet might possibly have quitted the country in a fishing boat, but his ardent attachment to the daughter of Carran induced him to return to the metropolis. None but a madman would have risked the dangerous experiment, but Emmet appears to have been influenced in all his actions by the wildest impulse. With the hope of obtaining an interview with her, if possible, before his intended departure, of corresponding with her, and of seeing her pass by Harold's Cross, which was on the road from her father's country house, near Rathfarnham, to Dublin, he returned to lodgings which he had formerly occupied at Mr. Palmer's. He had not been long there be- fore his retreat was discovered, and on the 25th of August Emmet was arrested by Major Sirr. On the 19th of the following month he was tried at a special commission, before Lord Norbary, Mr. Baron Daly, and Mr. Baron George. Curran was invited to act as his counsel, but declined to do so. Emmet resolved on making no defence, so that it mattered little, in one sense, that Curran refused to plead on his behalf. Bat, as Thomas Davis says, "His refusal to see him was framed too harshly." Of this Emmet, in the closing words of a letter written to Curran says—" A man with the coldness of death on him need not be made to feel any other coldness." Some allowance, however, is to be made for Curran. Lord Norbury pronounced the dreadful sentence, ordering the prisoner to be executed on the following day, Tuesday. It was past ten o'clock at night when the prisoner was re- moved from the dock, and conveyed from the Courthouse to Newgate. There he was heavily ironed by the gaoler' and placed, it is supposed, in one of the condemned cells. Long after midnight he was again removed to Kilmainham Gaol, a distance of about two and a half miles. At ten o'clock on the morning of Tuesday he was visited by Mr. Leonard M`Nally. He inquired of the barrister after his mother, whose health had been in a declining state, and who had completely broken down under her recent afflictions. "How is my mother ?" enquired Emmet. Without replying di- rectlk the barrister said, "I know, Robert, you would like to see your mother." The answer was, "0 ! what would I not give to see her ?" M'Nally pointed upwards and said, "Then, Robert, you will see her this day," and he then gave him an account of his mother's death, which had taken place several days previously. Like the mother of the Sheares, she had been hurried to the grave by the calamities which had stricken her sore. Enamel stood silent and mo- tionless for some time, evidently straggling to keep down his feelings, and then said, "It is better so." It was about half-past one o'clock when Robert Emmet was brought forth from his prison and placed in a carriage, accompanied by two clergymen, to be conveyed to the place of execution in Thomas-street, at the end of Bridefoot-street, and nearly opposite St. Catherine's Church. The carriage, preceded and followed by a strong guard, both of cavalry and in- fantry, moved slowly along the street. Throughout the progress Emmet displayed what Curran called the most complete "unostentatious fortitude." The closing scene is so graphically described by Madden that we give the his- torian's words :—" When Robert Emmet alighted from the carriage, and was led to the foot of the scaffold, his arms being tied, he was assisted to ascend by the executioner, but he mounted quickly and with apparent alacrity. He ad- dressed a few words to the crowd, very briefly, in a firm sonorous voice. In the few words he spoke on the scaffold, he avoided any reference to political matters or to the events with which his fate was connected. He merely said: 'My friends, I die in peace, and with sentiments of univer- sal love and kindness towards all men.' He then shcok hands with some persons on the platform, presented his watch to the executioner, and removed his stock. The im- mediate preparations for execution were then carried into effect; he assisted in adjusting the rope round his neck, and was then placed on the plank underneath the beam, and the cap was drawn over his face; but he contrived to raise his hand, partly removed it, and spoke a faw words in a Ipw tone to the executioner. The cap was replaced, and he stood with a handkerchief in his hand, the fall of which was to be the signal for the last act of the finisher of the law.' After standing on the plank for a few seconds, the executioner said, 'Are you ready, sir?' Not yet,' was Emmet's reply. There was another momentary pause; no signal was given. Again the executioner repeated the question, 'Are you ready, sir?' and again Robert Emmet said Not yet.' The question was put a third time. Emmet was heard to pro- nounce the word Not '—butt before he had time to utter another word the executioner tilted one end of the plank off the ledge, and a 'adman being, young, generous, endowed with precious natural gifts and acquired excellencies, with genius, patriotism, a love of truth, of freedom, of justice,— was dangling like a dog, writhing in the agonies of the most revolting and degrading to humanity of all deaths. At the expiration of the usual time the remains were taken down and extended on the scaffold, the head was struck from the body, grasped by the hair, and paraded along the front of the gallows by the hangman, proclaiming to the multitude, 'This is the head of a traitor, Robert Emmet.'" No one can justify the outbreak of 1803. It can only be viewed with absolute and unqualified condemnation. Morality, wisdom, and patriotism can hold but one opinion on the subject. The chances of failure were far greater than those of success, and the conspiracy cannot for a moment be justified. But let us not be harsh in our judgment of Emmet. His errors were errors of judgment. He loved his country with all the fervour of an enthusiast. He had listened to the debates which preceded the Union, and had drunk in with devotion the doctrines which were then pro- mulgated by some of the ephemeral patriots of the day. These were well calculated to inflame minds less ardent than his. "Let iE not be forgotten, then," says Phillips, in , his "Recollections of Carran," "by those who affect to despise hie memory that men, matured by experience, deeply read in the laws of their country, and venerated as the high priests of the Constitution, had but two years before ve- hemently, eloquently and earnestly, in the very temple itself, proclaimed resistance to be a duty.
• Experience, says Jean Paul Richter, is the best school- master, but the school fees are somewhat heavy.

div.head: UNEHAUSTED MANURES.
div.p: UNEHAUSTED MANURES.

At the special request of Lord Rosebery, the Scottish Chamber of Agriculture have prepared a list of suggestions which may be adopted as a basis for computing the com- pensation for manures unexhausted at the termination of a tenancy. The following is the list:- 1. LIIRE.—In all soils to which it would be proper to apply lime, and the proper quantity (over five tons) is ap- plied, it is good—in light soils, for ten crops; in good,deep, loamy soils, for twelve crops; in clay soil, its beneficial effects are not lost in fourteen or fifteen crops; and in peat soils it is good for ten or twelve crops. In new grazings its effects are seen in twenty crops, and in old permanent pas- tures its effects are discernible for thirty years. 2. HORSE, COW, AND TOWN MANURE.—When applied in sufficient quantity (above 15 tons), these manures are exhausted in the ordinary five-course shift. The rate is more rapid in the first two than in the remaining three years—say, half in two years, and the other half in the re- maining three years of the rotation. 3. Guhavos.—lf highly ammoniacal, the exhaustion of the nitrogeneous matter will be rapid in the first and second year. But there are other valuable fertilising elements in good guano, and these are more enduring. Experience de- monstrates that half the manurial value of guano is ex- hausted in the first crop, and the other half left available for the remaining crops of a rotation. Its beneficial effects are obvious in most soils, even in the fourth year of a rota- tion.

4. BONES.—Bone-dust will benefit, according to the nature of the soil, from three to five crops of cereals and grasses. Dissolved bones are more rapid in the rate of exhaustion. The first crop takes about one-third of the manurial value, the second will bring the one-third up to a half, and a third and fourth crop will exhaust the whole.

_ 5. PHOSPHATES decomposed by vitriol will be exhausted at the rate of dissolved 'bones, and ground phosphates at that of bone-dust, and the rate of exhaustion may be taken as that of guano. 6. SULPHATES are volatile, and experience leads to the belief that, when applied in sufficient quantities, these are mostly exhausted by the crop to which applied to the ex- tent of two-thirds, and to the extent of the balance in the next crop, and are of little appreciable value to subsequent crops in Scotland. It is right, however, to state, that Mr. Lawes's experience in England eems to be different. 7. SPECIAL MANI:MM.—These are the manures prepared for special crops, and known by the name of the crop to which they are applied, such as " turnip manures," drc. The rate of exhaustion of these depends upon the ingredients of which they are made up. Experience would class the rate higher in endurance than sulphates, but of less endurance in guanos—say three years—two-thirds first year, and one- third the remaining two years. 8. CLAY.—A well-known application to peat and other vegetable soils, which endures for seven years at least, and which may be held to be exhausted one-seventh of its cost each year. In Scotland the cost of its application is its only cost.

div.head: INCENDIARISM AT A LONDON DOCK.
div.p: INCENDIARISM AT A LONDON DOCK.
LANCASHIRE & CHESHIRE MINERS' PERMANENT RELIEF SOCIETY.

THE EMPLOYERS' LIABILITY ACT. The riinth annual meeting of the Lancashire and Cheshire Miners' Permanent Relief Society was held on Saturday at Wigan. Mr. Alfred Hewlett, of the Wigan Coal and Iron Company, occupied the chair, and there was a large attend- ance of colliery proprietors and representatives from the various local agencies. The Chairman of the Hoard of Management, Mr. C. G. Jackson, of the Chamber Collieries, Oldham, moved the adoption of the annual report. This showed that at the close of 1881 the number of members in the society was 32,184, and the available balance in hand £28,679. The ordinary revenue of the society during the year produced £29,608 2s. 2d., and the expenditure had amounted to £26,861 10s. 3d. The ordinary members had contributed during the twelve months £23,256 2-s. 41- the proprietors by percentages on the amount of th,eir workmen's contributions had subscribed £5,180, and from honorary members had been received £149 193. The expenditure for the year included funeral allowances on account of death of members, £1,262 103. 64; medical aid, £3,674 195.; to widows, £2,721 25.; children of members, £3,568 19s. 64; and on account of disablement of members, £12,871 12s. 64. During 1881 there were 6,725 cases of disablement amongst the members, and 70 fatal accidents by which 117 members were killed. These fatal accidents placed on the funds 68 widows and 157 children, and at the close of the year 249 widows and 627 children were receiving annuities from the society. Of the 6,725 cases of disablement there were 2,624 in which only one week's relief was paid. The report added:—"Con- sidering the circumstances which have attended the year's operations, the Board are of opinion that the members have reason for much gratifica- tion on the fact that there has not only been no diminution in the number of members, but a slight increase. During the first quarter of the year the membership was comparatively low, and nearly the whole of the revenue of the society suspended, owing to a cessation of work through- out the district. CGnfidence in the society was, however, saon regained, and there has since been a steady accession of strength. In last year's report the Board were able to con- gratulate the members on a very low death-rate, the lowest ever recorded by the society; and this state of things con- tinued until the month of December, when, by the occurrence of the Abram explosion, the rate was very materially in- creased, and this year the society has to record an accident death-rate of no less than 3•9 per thousand members. The Board have had under consideration the steady increase of late years in the proportion of disablement cases to the number of persons employed at many of the collieries connected with the society, and they have appointed a committee with in- structions to inquire into all the circumstances, and to as- certain if possible the cause of the excess. Although at large numbers of the agencies the members of the society have entered into a mutual arrangement with the owners of the collieries in view of the recent legislation on this subject of employers' liability, and although at other agencies the old arrangement that the employer shall pay 15 per cent on his workmen's contributions is continued, there are a few at which the only revenue to the society is from the ordinary members' contributions. The Board submit that, in fairness to the rest of the members, the contributions at these colleries should be raised, and they have given notice of an amendment of rule to that effect. In common with the rest of the permanent relief I societies of the kingdom, the society took part in the con- ference organised by the Central Association for dealing with distress caused by mining accidents, and held in Lon- don in August last. The outcome of that conference was that instructions were issued to the Council of the Associa- tion to prepare a scheme for the purpose of dealing with large accidents. The Council appointed a special commit- tee, which is still sitting, and has had before it several pro- posals, but it is certain that before a scheme can be decided upon the very best possible advice legal as well as actuarial—will have to be obtained."—The motion for the adoption of the report was seconded by Mr. NV. PICKARD, and carried. The Hon and Rev. Canen Bridgernan, rector of Wigan, was re-appointed president of the society, and Mr. Alfred Hewlett and Mr. W. Pickard vice-presidents. Mr. HEWLETT, in acknowledging the appointment, con- gratulated the society on its continued prosperity, especially after the dark commencement of the year by reason of the strike. The policy advocated by the society had now so far commended itself to the members that 24,600 of them had entered into a mutual arrangement with their employers in view of the Liability Act, and no one could dispute the fact that the arrangement was working most satisfactorily. Through the instrumentality of the society similar organi- sations had been set on foot in North Wales, South Wales, and South Staffordshire, and these had now some 15,000 members. Their efforts in this direction were for the pur- pose of carrying out eventually a scheme of federation, whereby large accidents would have their costs spread over the area of the united societies. The cost of relieving the distress caused by the lamentable accident at Abram last December had happily been met by the society. Mr.. W. PICKARD, in thanking the meeting, said the action taken throughout the district had now justified the advice he gave at the commencemert of 1881. The 24,000 men who had entered into an arrangement with their employers had not contracted out of the benefits of the Act, but had made it the lever for increasing their power to deal with the distress and suffering caused by mining accidents. The annual subscriptions of these men would amount to £20,000, and the employers' percentage to £5,000. Under the scale adopted prior to the passing of the Act, the employers' con- tributions would have only been .E 3,000 and probably this might not have been continued had not some arrangement been entered into in view of the Act. At any rate the men were clean gainers to the amount of £2,000 per annum, and he should like to know any district, or any similar body of miners, who had benefited to the extent of one-fourth of this amount by adhering to the Act. So far as protection was concerned it was not the Employers' Liability Act, hut the Mines Regulation Act of 1872—(hear, hear)—to which miners must look. The Mines Re eulation .Act was to prevent accidents and punish negligence, and on it miners must rely. The retiring members of the Board of Management were re-appointed, and the proceedings concluded.

div.head: ABOLITION OF THE INDIIN IMPORT DUTIES.
div.p: THE ABOLITION OF THE INDIIN IMPORT DUTIES.

The final meeting of the members of the Association for the Removal of Protection from Indian Manufactures was held on Monday, at Hanover Chambers, King-street, Man- chester, Mr. E. Walmsley presiding. The object of the meeting was the dissolution of the association, the cause of its creation having now been removed. A report was sub- mitted detailing the chief incidents of the agitation for the removal of the Indian import duties on cotton goods. Special mention was made of the part taken in the movement ray the association, which was formed more than four years ago, and the committee said the association might fairly claim an important share in the work that has been done. The gentle- men comprising the acting committee were Mr. J. Alcock (Ashton Brothers), Mr. F. Ashworth (Messrs. Geo. Robinson and Co.), Mr. J. A. Beith, Mr. H. Calvert (Messrs. W. Calvert and Sons), the late Mr. J. Chapman (Messrs. John Nunn and Co.), Mr. J. Garnett, Mr. W. Haworth (Messrs. J. Dilworth and Sons), Mr. I. Hoyle, Mr. E. Helm, Col. R. R. Jackson, Mr. D. E. Micrulachi, Mr. W. Peel (Messrs. J. Peel and Co.), Mr. S. P. schilizzi (Messrs. Ralli Bros.), Mr. John Slagg, M.P., Mr. J. W. Schott, and Mr. J. Thompson, Mr. J. C. Hobbs, of Hanover Chambers, having acted as secre- tary. It was resolved, "That this meeting tenders its thanks to the Right Honouraltle the Marquis of Hartington and the Government of India for the broad and statesmanlike measure by which protection has been entirely removed from the fiscal system of India and its commerce is placed on a Free Trade footing." The meeting also thanked the Marquis of Salisbury "for having initiated the policy of reducing the Indian import duties on cotton goods and yarns, and for his consistent and forcible advocacy of the removal of this obstruction to our trade in India." It was further resolved that the balance at the credit of the association, after paying all liabilities, be handed to Mr. Hobbs, whose services as secretary during the four years the association had existed entitled him to the cordial thanks of the meeting.—The association was then, by resolution of the meeting, dissolved.

div.head: SOCIALISM IN LONDON.
div.p: SOCIALISM IN LONDON.

A meetino•of members and friends of the Social Democratic Working Men's Club, which principally consists of Germans, was held at their rooms in Featherstone-street, City-road, London on Sunday evening, for the purpose of celebrating, in accordance with their annual custom, the 18th of March, on which day, in 1871, the Paris Commune came into existence. The Chairman, Herr Daubenspeek in opening the proceedings, explained the origin of the meeting, which, to- gether with the Commune, celebrated the Revolution of 1793 and 1848, after which Herr Jung proposed the follow- ing resolution: "Considering that the revolutions previous to the 18th March, 1871, were for political ends, they were therefore insufficient to overthrow , the corrupt system of of society; considering that the revolution to come must be for the purpose of abolishing the misery of the working- classes, it must be an economic revolution • it is resolved that this meeting pledges itself to seize all means in its power to make and keep this movement essentially social- economic, that it may avoid the failures of past revolutions and soon make human rights victorious."—M. Peter Lavroff, who spoke in Russian, supported the resolution, as did Prince Irapotkin, who, in saying a few words about the spread of Communistic principles in Europe, alluded to the Russian movement. Its origin, he said, was quite peaceful, and its tendences were socialistic. The dreadful situation of the peasantry and of the working classes was what in- spired the young Russian Socialists. The Government im- prisioned them (1,000 only in 1864), and kept them four years in prisons where, cut of 200 prisoners, eleven died, four committed suicide, and nixie became mad. The exiles were by thousands; but there was no justice for them. When Socialists began to defend their homes from nocturnal raids of police with arms, the Government began to hang them by scores. Two were hanged by Alexander 11. This gave to the struggle its desperate character. Now, the Govern- ment necessarily would extend more and more among the peasantry, and the victory of revolution was sure. THE GRANT TO PRINCE LEOPOLD.—The House then went into committee on the message from the Queen with regard to the Duke of Albany's marriage.—Mr. GLAD.STONE moved resolutions granting Prince Leopold £lO,OOO a year on his marriage, in addition to the amounts he was already entitled to, and providing for an allowance of £6,000 a year to Princess Helen in the event of her surviving Prince Leopold. —Sir STAFFORD NORTHCOTE seconded the resolutions, which were opposed by Mr. Laboucbere, Mr. Broadhurst, Mr. Healy, and Mr. Storey.—On a division, the first resolu- tion was carried by 387 against 42 votes, and the allowance to Princess Helen was agreed to without a division. THE CLOTURE.—Mr. BERESFORD HOPE then resumed the debate on the rules of Procedure, which was carried on in a thin House.—Amougst the speakers were Mr. HUSSEY VIVIAN and Sir MICHAEL HICKS-BEACH, who maintained that the ctoture was not intended to stop obstruction, but to gam the Opposition. Obstruction, he maintained, should be dealt with by action against individuals.

div.head: POLITICAL ITEMS.
div.p: POLITICAL ITEMS.

Sir Michael Westropp has resigned the Chief Justiceship of Bombay. The convention with France securing to this country the "most-favoured nation" treatment was issued among the Parliamentary papers, on Wednesday. The bill promoted by the Associated Chambers of Com- merce to amend the law of bankruptcy, and introduced by Mr. Barran, M.P., is appointed for second reading on April 23rd. A letter has been received at Northampton from the Speaker acknowledging the receipt of the resolutions passed at a meeting held there with respect to the question of Mr. Bradlaugh's seat. A four-line Conservative whip was sent out on Tuesday night urging the members of the party on no account to pair between that date and the 30th inst., when the division on Mr. Marriott's motion will probably be taken. We (Daily News) hear that Mr. Gorst will not now bring on his motion for the release of Cetewayo before Easter, but that he expects to find an opportunity of doing so on the first Monday after the reassembling of the House. It is said that a deputation of his constituents is about to wait on Mr. P. J. Smyth, M.P. for Tipperary, to urge him to resign his seat. In the event of a vacancy Mr. Cowen, son of the member for Newcastle, will be asked to stand. Mr. Dodson, the President of the Local Government Board, assured a deputation which waited upon him on Wednesday that he should endeavour to pass the Floods Prevention Bill during the present session. He attributed much of the opposition to the measure to imperfect acquaint- ance with its details. It is stated that Mr. Sexton will move a call of the house for Thursday, when the cloture division will be taken. It is also stated that certain Irish members will not visit Ireland during Easter, fresh warrants having just been issued for their arrest. Sir Charles Dilke's motion for a return showing the total number of electors on the register in each Parliamentary constituency in the United Kingdom, is the same as he has moved annually during the past eight or nine years, and has no reference, as is supposed in some quarters, to intended Government action. At a meeting of the Irish Parliamentary party, held at Westminster, the following resolution was proposed by Mr. Sexton, seconded by Mr. Healy, and carried :—" That the deputy chairman, secretary, and whips be instructed to issue a special joint circular to the members of the party, setting forth the vital importance of the division on the cl6ture, and the consequences which may follow." It is stated that Mr. Arthur Arnold, M.P.' has not at present any intention of asking for another date for the con- tinuance of the formally adjourned debate on his resolution as to Parliamentary reform. Mr. Arnold and his supporters are satisfied in the meantime with the expression of opinion during the debate, and with the division already taken, nominally on the question of adjournment. Mr. Gladstone, in a letter to the chairman of a meeting in Belfast, respecting intermediate education in Ireland, said he learned with regret that it has been thought necessary to reduce the amount given in prizes, drc., in connection with intermediate education in Ireland; but, in the present state of public business, he fears it may be found impossible to entertaih any proposals involving fresh legislation on this question. Mr. Chaplin, M.P., speaking at a meeting of the Constitu- tional Union, on Wednesday night, at St. James's Hall, London, said there was no doubt that agriculture was the greatest of all industries in England. Prominent among the suggestions made to remedy its depression was the relief of local rates and burdens. On this subject Mr. Edward Ridley read a paper, in which the Land Bill promoted by the Farmers' Alliance was condemned as a mischievous and injurious measure. It is stated that there is a 'desire, not only among the leaders but also on the part of the rank and file of both parties, that the discussion on Mr. Marriott's amendment to the closure resolution should terminate before Easter. It will probably be concluded on Thursday. There will, however, remain no less than seventy-seven other amendments to the proposed new procedure rules. Although there is little doubt as to the Government being able to carry the most vital of them by a majority of over 20, the greater part of the session will probably be devoted to the task. The Deputy Chairman (Mr. Justin M‘Carthy) and the Whips of the Irish Parliamentary party have 'addressed a circular to the Irish members asking them to be in their places on the occasion of the clOture division and vote against the Government. It says that the position of the Ministry may depend upon a single vote, and that the defeat of the cloture involves two questions—first, the resignation of the Government, and secondly, the impossibility of renew- ing the Coercion Act. The circular gives figures to show that "the Government majority disappears in case we can bring up the whole of our party." The Press Association states that in consequence of the recent blackballing of several advanced Liberal candidates, who were otherwise eligible for membership of the Reform Club, a preliminary meeting of Liberal members of Parlia- ment was held on Tuesday afternoon at the House of Com- mons, with the view to bring about some change in the mode of election. No resolution was passed, nor any final conclu- sion arrived at, but it is probable that as a result of the deliberation the next election at the club will be postponed, and representation in the meantime made to the committee with the view to restore to them their former duty of electing new members, instead of leaving the ballot as at present in the hands of the general body of the members. AN EXTRAORDINARY LETTER FROM LORD SALISBURY.— In reply to resolutions passed last week at a Grand Lodge I of the Orangemen of Bradford (Yorkshire) and the district, Mr.' Henry Manners, one of the private secretaries to the Marquis of Salisbury, writes from 20, Arlington-street, London, as follows :—"Sir,—A copy of the resolutions passed at a meet- of loyal Orangemen of Bradford and the district, held last week, has been received by the Marquis of Salisbury, and I am directed by him to assure the Orange Lodges of Bradford of his sincere thanks for them. His lordship feels that the present time is a most critical one. Liberty of speech in the House of Commons for the representatives of the people is proposed to be abolished ; Mr. Bradlaugh is virtually sup- ported by the present Government and Mr. Gladstone; and the uncontrollable temper of the Prime Minister has almost brought the two Houses of Legislature into conflict, simply to gratify that gentleman's overweening vanity. Ireland is in a state of rebellion, for which the present Government is solely responsible. Such a condition of affairs calls for the attention of every loyal subject; and Lord Salisbury hopes that by the co-operation of all those who support constitu- tional principles, Mr. Gladstone's dangerous and reckless projects may be defeated.—Mr. William Walters, Bradford."

At the Manchester Police Court, on Thursday morning, Mary Ellen Kirk was bmught up on remand, charged with stabbing her husband, John Kirk, on Saturday last. Prisoner had been undergoing nine months' imprisonment, and on being discharged, her husband declined to receive her. She smashed the windows, and afterwards purchased a large pen- knife. Again being repulsed, she attacked her husband with it, and inflicted such wounds on his neck that his life was in danger. She was committed to the assizes. EDUCATION IN ENGLAND AND WALES.-A Parliamentary return has been issued showing various details as to the ex- penditure from the education grant in England and Wales during 1881. From this it appears that the expenditure for 1881 was £2,614,883 13s. 6d., being an inctease of £117,667 Os. Bd. over that of 1880, the greater portion of the increase being £112,345 10s. Bd. in the grants for day scholars. The grants to schools connected with the Church of England amounted to £1,252,017 7s. 5d., an increase of £16,913 Bs. 6d. over 1880 ; to British, undenominational, and other schools, £224,747 2s. 10d., an increase of £9,687 4s. 6d.; to Wesleyan schools £111,023 18s. 10d., an increase of £3,375 63. 81: to Roman Catholic schools £125,601 13s. 4d., an increase of £1,720 83. 11(1.; and to Board schools £706,429 35., an increase of £79,347 193. 9d. The total granted to Church of England schools since 1839 has been £17,846,671 14s. 4d., to Dissenters' schools £4,679,510 16s. 3d., to Roman Catholic schools £1,447,746 ss. 7d. and to Board schools £3,155.841 19s. ,4d.; the grand total of educational grants since that date having been £30,256,344 2s. 3d. From the tables of attendance at inspection it appears that the total number of schools annually inspected are 18,062, of which ' 11,589 are Church and 3,692 Board schools. The total num, her of scholars for whom accommodation is provided is 4,839,633, and the average number in attendance is 2,863,535, of whom 1,490,429 attend Church scheols, and 856,351 Board schools. The rate of expenditure per scholar in average attendance is £1 15s. 11d. in Church of England schools, £l. 15s. 2..'7d. in Wesleyan, £1 10s. 8,(1. in Roman Catholic, £1 16s. 3?cd. in British. and £2 is. 6d. in Board schools; giving an average of £1 16s. lthld.
