div.head: EXAMINER SATURDAY, MARCH 25, 1882.
div.p: THE EXAMINER SATURDAY, MARCH 25, 1882.
FOREIGN INTELLIGENCE,

within the palace were playing; electric lights of every con- ceivable design were shining; a gorgeous bank of flowers grown in the palace grounds unfolded its beauties, and seemed to gliv in the brilliance of the scene ; while pre- ceded by a posse of police, and followed by Lord Dprby, radiant with smiles, and the other members of his party, Mr. Gladstone passed from point to point. It may be safely said that the International Electric Exhibition was never seen to such advantage as it was on Monday evening, for all along the palace itself and in the various courts the exhibi- tors had evidently put forth their full power, remembering, no doubt, whose eyes were seeing their work. In spite of almost being mobbed at times by the warmth of welcome on the part of his friends, some of whom were insisting on shaking hands with him, it must have been a real refresh- ment to a we cry parliamentary chief to turn aside from the question of clotatiy, and the endless talk of the Irish mem- bers, to the splendid triumph of applied science, in which, through the heartfelt appreciation of the people, he was after all the principal figure himself. Having dined at the palace, the right honourable gentleman returned to the House of Commons, and it needs no gift of prophecy to say that we have not heard the last of Mr. Gladstone's visit to the finest demonstration yet given of what promises to be the light of the future.

We learn from Durban that there has been fighting on the south-western border of the Transvaal between Boers and natives, and that the warfare continues. There was a revolutionary demonstration at Berlin, on Sater- day, when a large crowd visited the graves of those killed in the insurrection of 1848. Fortunately no disturbances occurred. A slight accident happened to the German Emperor on Friday. His Majesty, on leaving the Academy, slipped on the bottom stair and fell, receiving slight contusions on the right elbow and knee. The Vienna Presse learns from St. Petersburg, in a letter sent by post to the frontier, that several Nihilists have escaped from Siberia. Amongst them- is a very "dangerous" man named Zwetkow. A partial strike has taken place at the Pacific Cotton Mills, Lawrence, Massachusetts, which employ 6,000 opera- tives. The hands objected to a reduction of wages on the ground that the mills are prosperous. A telegram received from Constantinople announces that three strong shocks of earthquake were felt on Tuesday on the island cf Chios. The population have taken refuge in tents. The temperature is excessively high. Among the literary remains of Berthold Auerbach the beginning of an autobiography has been found, containing a, series of portraits of the writers of the post-classical period in Germany ; also a Socialistic novel called "Per Meister and Seine Gesellen," which will remain unpublished by Auerbach's desire. On Wednesday, the 85th anniversary of the birth of the Emperor William was celebrated with the accustomed en- thusiasm. The members ,of the Royal Family, the great men who are at the head of the various departments of the State, the Foreign Ambassadors, and a throng of lesser nota- bilities hastened to the Palace to pay their respects to the aged Sovereign. It is officially estimated that 85,000 persons are destitute owing to the floods in the Western American States. Yazoo city, Mississippi, is completely overflowed, and the inhabi- tants have had to take refuge in the upper rooms of the buildings, from which they were rescued by steamboats, 1,200 having been removed on Saturday night. The two Italians oharged with having attacked the Chancellor of the French Consulate and the gentleman who accompanied him, in Tunis some days ago, have been re- leased by the Italian consular judge, on the ground that the chancellor and his companion :were not engaged in their official capacity, and were not recognised in ,the darkness. A private telegram which has been received at Rangoon, states that three high functionartes of the Burmese Court have been imprisoned—namely, Kampa Kinghee, the Foreign Minister; Pagan Atwinworon, Minister of the Interior, and the King's father-in-law ; and Yenoung Mintha, an honorary Prince, chief favourite, who carried out the notorious atrocities perpetrated at King Theebaw's accession. Diffi- culties are expected to follow. The Embassy leaves on the Ist of April. The Belgian papers promise the disclosure of important improvements in the telephone by M. Van Rysselberghe, as soon as the necessary formalities for securing the patent rights are completed. The improvements enable the inventor to use for long distances the wire of the telegraph services, all induced sounds being suppressed. Satisfactory experi-- ments have been made on the wires connecting Antwerp and Brussels, the telegraphic service being in full activity at the time. No return wire is required. A scientific expedition to Persia is being despatched from Austria, under the command of Dr. J. C. Polak, formerly physician to the Shah. The expedition will include Dr. Wahner as geologist, and Dr. Pichler as botanist, and a sub- vention has been granted to these gentlemen by the Vienna Imperial Academy of Sciences. The expedition will proceed via Odessa, Poti, Tiflis, Baku, and Rescht, to Hamadan, the ancient Ecbatana. The expedition is to return in about six months. The 75th birthday of Longfellow was celebrated in many parts of America. At Atlanta, Georgia, selections from his poemswere read in the public schools, and the exercises were participated in by nearly five thousand children, white and coloured. At his native city of Portland, Maine, there were great rejoicings. Mr. Wm. Gould, of Windham, in an ad- dress to the Maine Historical Society, showed that the poet inherits the blood of five Mayflower pilgrims, including Elder Brewster and John Alden. The following reply to a telegram sent to the poet was read :—" Cambridge, Feb. 27, 1882.—Your telegram received. I return cordial thanks to members of the society, and am very grateful for this signal mark of their remembrance and regard.—HENßY W. LONG- FELLOW." At his own home there was no celebration. During the day friends called to offer their congratulations, but, owing to the recent illness of the poet, it was not deemed advisable to make any demonstration. BRIGHAM YOUNG NOT DEAD.—A CURIOUS RUMOUR FROM SALT LAKE.—An Omaha letter in the New York World says :—A Josephite Mormon lately from Salt Lake ex- presses the opinion that Brigham Young is not dead, but that he is concealed, and will in due time appear to his people and pretend that God has "resurrected" him to lead them out of their troubles. The gentleman in question saw the alleged body of the prophet, and says that while there was a strong resemblance, it was not in reality the corpse of Young. He declares that he is not alone in this view, as not less than a hundred of his acquaintances express a similar belief. While here he visited some of the Omaha

Josephites, and it was to them he made the revelations of the plan by which Brigham Young is to create the greatest sensation of modern times. He had many business dealings with the prophet, and was intimately acquainted with him. He asserts that, with the complete organisation and secret workings of the church, it would be an easy matter to keep Brigham Young concealed for almost any length of time, and reproduce him when most needed to revive the faith of believers by his alleged resurrection. ANOTHER THEATRE DESTROYED BY FIRE.

At half-past nine o'clock, on Sunday night, the Theatre of the French Opera Bouffe, recently constructed in the Demidoff Garden of St. Petersburg, caught firein the middle of the performance of "La Perichole," and in less than ten minutes from the time of the alarm it was enveloped in one eaormous blaze. The rapidity with which the fire spread was owing to the building being en- tirely of wood. But in spite of this dangerous fact no one appears to have been burned or seriously injured. ARREST OF A SPANISH CAPTAIN.

A Madrid telegram says :—The Spanish Government have addressed a remonstrance to the British Government against the arrest and imprisonment at Singapore of the captain of the Spanish mail steamer Leon XIII. From the report of the circumstances of the case which has reached Madrid it appears that while the steamer was on her way to Manilla, the engineer, an Englishman, refused to obey the orders of the captain, and was in consequence put in irons. On the vessel reaching Singapore the captain communicated the facts of the case to the British authorities, who demanded that the man should be set at liberty. This the captain re- fused, saying that the mutinous engineer must be tried by the maritime authorities at Manilla, his offence having been

committed on board a Spanish vessel. The English 'autho- rities then caused the captain to be arrested. The Corres- pondencia expresses the hope that the matter will be satis- factorily settled. BOSNIA AND HERZEGOVINA.

A Prague telegram says :—The Politik states that the idea of convening a congress for the final settlement of the Bosnian and Herzegovinian questions is seriously engaging the attention of Euxopean diplomatists, and that an agree- ment exists on the subject between England and Russia, whose views meet with the concurrence of France. The journal continues as follows :—" The moment chosen for raising the question will be when Austria proceeds defini- tively to the work of fortifying Herzegovina. This pro- posal is, however, opposed by another scheme advocating the solution of the question by the voluntary cession of the occnpied Provinces by Turkey through a special convention." A correspondent at Vienna gives currency to a report that Russia has proposed to the British Government a new Euro- pean Congress to consider the Bosnian and Herzegovinian questions, and afterwards notify to Austria how long the oc- cupation by Austrian troops should last. A telegram received through Reuter's agency, however, affirms the question has not been tnooted in any quarter.

Edith Watson, described as a married woman, was brought , up for further examination at 111arylebone Police Court, on Tuesday, charged with receiving a quantity of wearing apparel and other articles, knowir.g them to have been stolen. Evidence showing her connection with the man Watson, or Vanderstein, who, it was alleged, had obtained the goods in question from Mr. Whiteley, Westbourne-grove, was adduced. The prisoner's landlady also deposed to see- ing a quantity of jewellery and diamonds in the prisoner's possession. The case was remanded. On Tuesday, at the Preston Police Court, Messrs. Woods and Hampson, manufacturers, Fitzroy-street mills were summoned to answer seven charges of breach of the Factory Act. The defendants were fined £1 and costs in each of two cases, and ordered to pay costs in others.—Nine charges or infringing the Factory Act were then preferred against Mr. George Paley, manufacturer, Hopwood-street mill. The Bench inflicted a fine of II and costs in each of two cases, and ordered the defendants to pay costs in the other seven cases.

THE ATTACK ON CAPTAIN SELnv.—A correspondent has been published regarding the attack on Captain Selby, whereby his life was lost. Captain Grenfell furnished par- ticulars of the attack, and Lord Dufferin expressed the opinion that the Albanians had been irritated by the distur- bance of their flocks by the shooting party. Captain Selby might have defended himself, having his gun, but he deli- berately lowered it, to show that he bad no Earl Granville hoped the criminals would be punished, and Earl Dufferin replied, on behalf of the Porte, that arrests had been made, and punishment would follow in due course. The Paris correspondent of the Times says a Lyons Legitimist paper has the following The Jesuits of the province of Lyons who took refuge in England are about to begin evangelising the rural populations of Wales, a vast province situated at the south-west extremity of the king- dom. Missions organised by them have already given the best results." On this paragraph betraying rather hazy geographical notians, which induced distrust as to the accuracy of it, the Te/egraphe remarks:—" Our best com- pliments to the reverend fathers. We cannot but wish them to stay where they are so well received." Mr. F. H. O'Donnell, M.P., speaking on Saturday after- noon, on the occasion of the laving of the memorial stone of Catholic schools at Fairfield, said that compared with the Catholic past of England the Protestantism of this country was but a passing incident in the history of the nation. He had no doubt that• with the progr'ess of enlightenment, a larger and larger number of their English friends would come to recognise the superiority of the claims of that Church which was the Church of old England in the past, and which, please God, would be the Church of old England before long again. The hon. gentleman strongly urged the necessity of children receiving a religious educa- tion.

TERRIBLE TRAGEDY AT BRADEORD.—A terrible and mysterious tragedy occurred at Bradford on Tuesdev mora. ing in the house of Mrs. Yeoman, a widow, who resided in a cottage in Holling's Road, and maintained herself by taking in lodgers. One of her lodgers was named William Bairstow, a man about 35 years of age. On Tuesday morning on a lad going into the cellar kitchen of the house he found both Yeoman and Bairstow lying dead with their throats cut. Upon the table was a large knife covered with blood. It is believed that Bairstow first cut the woman's throat and then his. own, but it does not appear, although several other people were in the house on Monday night, that any of them had been alarmed by sounds of struggling or quarrelling. It is said that Bairstow bad recently been heard to threaten that he would number Mrs. Yeoman's days. Upwards of 700 officers and men of the Ist Manchester Regiment of Volunteers attended divine service at the Cathe- dral on Sunday. The Bishop of Manchester preached a special sermon, in which, baeing his discourse upon St. Paul's counsel to Timothy that he should " endure hardneis as a good soldier of Christ," he pointed out the necessity of dis- cipline, order, and obedience to the law. He observed that the greatest of all dangers was the enervating progress of luxury. It was, he said, altogether a false and ignoble con- ception of Christianity whichrepresentecl it as only fit for women and children, and they might depend upon it that a man who had the fear of God before his eyes would not be a worse soldier or worse citizen on that account. The decision of the judges was given in the Ascot prize fighting case on Saturday. The defendants were tried and convicted before Mr. Benvon, chairman of the Berkshire sessions, for aiding and abetting at a prize fight which took place in a field at the close of the last summer Ascot races. The defendants accidentally saw a crowd of persons as- sembled in a field, and from curiosity went to see what was the matter, when they found two men fighting. They were afterwards charged with "aiding and abetting " at a prize fight, and on the ruling of the chairman that they were guilty of a common assault by so doing the jury found them guilty. The question for the consideration of the court, the prisoners having appealed against their conviction, was whether the fillipg of the chairman was correct. The majority of the judges were against the conviction, and it was quashed. At an early hour on Thursday morning, the body of a man, who was then unidentified, was deposited at the Dead- house at the Prince's Dock, Liverpool, having been brought from tho steamer Galvanic, which had just arrived from Belfast. It appeared that on the previous afternoon, a boat one o'clock, when the steamer was off the Mull of Galloway, the man at the wheel saw the deceased, who was a passenger on board, jump into the water. There was a heavy sea on at the time owing to the gale; but, nevertheless, a boat was promptly lowered, manned by Hugh M'Clure, Robert Hey- burtie, James Hudson and James Durrey, and after great difficulty they succeeded in rescuing the deceased. He was got on board the steamer still alive, but he shortly after- wards cuccumbed to the effects of the immersion. The body, during the morning, was identified by relations as that of Robert Doherty, who lived at 7, Wrexham-str eet, Liverpool. About four o'clock on Thursday morning, the alar n was brought to the Central Fire Station, in Hatton Garden, Liverpool, that a fire had broken out in an oil mill in Rigby- street. Superintendent M‘William immediately turned out with a manual engine, followed by the two 'fire steamers • Livingston and Clint, and on reaching the place it was found that the oil mill, 25, Rigby-street, belonging to Messrs. R. and J. Wallace was in one mass of flames. 'The building is a seven storey one, and was full of linseed and I ether inflammable material. Eight branches were set in play from the mains and the steamers, but it was feared from the first that it was impossible to prevent the destruc- tion of the whole premises with their contents, and ail the firemen could do was to keep the flames from extending to the adjoining premises; and in this, fortunately, they were successful. The mill was at work at the:time, but the men, who were all in the lower story, are unable to say how the fire originated. BOILER ExPLOSION IN CORNWALL—MANY PERSONS IN- Jul/ED.—A serious boiler explosion occurred at Gunnislake Clitters Copper Mine, Tavistock. on Saturday. It is the largest copper mine in Cornwall. There are three boilers used for propelling the machinery of the mine. It has for • some time been found that the two oldar engines could not last much longer., and three new ones had been obtained. Early on Saturday morning builders were employed in erecting an engine house for the reception of these new boilers near the old nes, when an explosion occurred. The roofs of the three houses containing the eld boilers were blown off and carded a distance of several hundred yards. Some of the debris fell on the builders, and some on a number of men and women working on the copper floors. Most of these people were afterwards lying about insensible, and many had sustained very serious injuries. The stokers were frightfully scalded. One had his shoulder dislocated, while anether had his collar bone broken. Two or three of the injured persons lie in a precarious condition. Those employed underground were at once informed by signal of the calamity, and all at once rushed up the foot ladder to the surfece. After the injured had been attended to notice was drawn to the agonising cries of cattle belonging to the manager of the mine, and it was found that steam and boil- ing water had gone into the building they were in, and that they were frightfully injured. The condition of the engineering branches of trade in this district shows improvement, and although this is not to the extent which enables any materially better prices to be ob- tained for the finished work, the reports emanating from the employers on the one hand, and the various agencies repre- senting the trades societies of the men on the other, are more cheerful in tone. There is a continued gradual de- • crease in the number of men out of employment and the last month's returns of the Iron Founders' Society, which to Isome extent represents the basis of the engineering, trades, although only returning trade as actually good in very few important centres, are more encouraging on the whole. In Salford, Liverpool, and Rochdale, trade is returned as good, and in Manchester, Birkenhead, Bolton, Barrow, Oldham, and Stockport, as :noderate. Reports as to the general en- gineering trades, tool makers, locomotive builders, and boiler makers, are to the effect that works are for the most part well employed. Machinists have also a good deal of work in hand, and althomah the activity in this branch of trade is largely due to foreign orders, the number of new mills either projected or in actual course of erection in the district must place a very fair amount of local work in the market. With regard to wages matters for the present seem to be pretty well settled in the neighbourhood of Manchester and Salford, but in some other districts the attitude taken by the men causes employers to some extent to be cautious in tendering for new work.

PALACE. On Monday night, the Prime Minister was the subject o a great demonstration at the Crystal Palace, Sydenham. As is well known, much interest has been excited for some time past in the International Electric Exhibition there, com- bining the different systems of electrical lighting, which are shown in the various corridors halls, and transepts, as well as throughout the whole length of the palace itself. *Mr. Gladstone had a wish to see the exhibition, and on Monday evening Mr. render arranged for the right honourable gentleman leaving Victoria station in the Pullman drawing- room car' about a quarter past seven o'clock, direct for the palace. The Prime Minister was accompanied by a dis- tinguished party, including Mrs. and Miss Gladstone, the Earl of Derby, dx., and reached the low level station of the Crystal Palace about a quarter to eight o'clock. Walking up the covered way from the station to the entrance of the palace he had an adinirable opportunity of witnessing the effect of the electric light within a comparatively narrow space, coupled with a singular and sur- prising steadiness, as compared with recent experiments elsewhere. div.head: TRADE NOTES.
div.p: TRADE NOTES.

SCOTCH COLLIERS. Notices were posted on Saturday at all the collieries in the counties of Fife and Clackmannan of a reduction of wages to the extent of 1.21 per cent., to come into operation a fortnight hence. This reduction will probably be stoutly resisted by the men, who were lately demanding an advance of wages. In consequence of a strike of spinners at Messrs. Smet- hurst's mill, at Chorley, the employers have decided to lock out the whole of the operatives in the district unless the men return to their work. The strike arose through the re- fusal of Messrs. Smethurst to adept the indicator. Some thousands of operatives willbe affected. A petition for liquidation has been filed in the Bradford County Court on Monday by Thomas and William H. Holmes, spinners and manufacturers, of Baildon near Brad- ford. The liabilities are estimated at £60,000, but it is stated that the creditors are few in number and that they are largely secured. The firm is of long standing and highly respected. The failure is consequent upon the long depres- sion in trade, which has forced a realisation of stock at a heavy loss. DURHAM MINERS.—At a meeting of the council of the Durham miners, held at Durham, on Saturday, the reply of the coalowners to an application of the federation board for a new sliding scale or a rise in wages was discussed. After• a long conversation it was agreed that the executive com- mittee of the association should at once apply to the coal- owners for an advance of wages equal to 20 per cent. on the present prices paid. THE CORN TRADE.—The Mark-lane Express says "During the past week the weather has been that of the month of May—foggy mornings, cold nights, and brilliant sunshine, with something more than spring-like temperature. The wheats are not growing too fast, but are tillering and keeping close to ground in a most satisfactory manner, their colour being excellent. Barley sowing is drawing towards completion, and is everywhere the order of the day. The scarcity of fine samples of English wheat has enabled sellers to obtain 6d. to is. per quarter advance in several provincial markets towards the close of the week, but inferior lots,which comprise the greater part of the offerings, have not shown any improvement in value, nor are they easier of sale. Flour has become steadier in value towards the close of the week. Our barley season being nearly over, buyers are less eager to possess themselves of the few fine samples that may be offer- ing, and barley for grinding meets very sluggish demand at drooping rates. Malt is difficult of sale,and,oats beans,and peas remain at the same level of values which they have main- tained for some little time past. Trade for foreign bread. stuffs off stands has slightly improved during the past week." THE LANCASHIRE IRON TRADE, MANCHESTER, WEDNES- DAY.—The somewhat stronger tone noticed in the iron trade a week ago has not been followed by any actually increased amount of business, and, if anything, prices are again rather easier. What little business there is doing in pig iron has been chiefly confined to small lots of district brands, which can be bought at low prices. Lancashise makers of pig iron, who have been holding out for 49a. and 505., less 21, for delivery, equal to Manchester, can book little or no iron at these figures, as they are undersold by Lincolnshire irons, which in some cases can be bought at 475. 6d. to 48s. per ton, less ; whilst Derbyshire brands are offering in the market at prices ranging from 483. to 505., per ton, less 2-?2. There is still a fair amount of activity in the finished iron trade but the leading makers still hold out for their prices. Slightly improved reports come in from some branches of the engineering trade, and generally, there is a fair amount of activity throughout this district. THE LANCASHIRE COAL TRADE, MANCHESTER, WEDNES- DAY.—There is but little variation from last week in the con- dition of the iron and coal trades of this district. The coal trade continues very dull, and there are comparatively few of the Lancashire collieries working more than three or four days a week. The lower qualities of round coal for iron- making and steam purposes move off much the same as of late. To move away stocks extremely low figures are so frequently taken that prices generally are more or less affected, and it is difficult to ascertain what sellers in many cases are taking beyond the fact that sales are reported con- siderably under the nominal list rates. The average quoted prices at the pit mouth may be given at Bs. 6d. to 9s. for best coal, 6s. up to 7s. for seconds, and ss. to ss. 6d. fot common round coals. The demand for engine classes of fuel continues tolerably fair. Good burgy at the pit mouth is steady, at about 4s. 6d. to ss. per ton, and good slack is fetching from 3s. 9s. to 4s. 3d. per ton. Local-made cokes continae in fair demand for manufacturing purposes, at about late rates; but gas cokes are a drug. THE LABOUR MARBET.—The laboar market has entered on few important changes during the week, and on the whole the great industries remain well employed. At Birmingham the various branches of the hardware trade show improve- ment, and at Sheffield the electro-plate and cutlery trades are well employed. Some sections of miners are asking for advance in wages, but miners generally are fairly settled. Several large railway works are still in want of navvies, and important contracts are being entered on in yarions direc- tions. In the textile trades there is again same complaint of want of orders at Bradford, and at Halifax immediate prospects are not very good. At Kidderminster the carpet trade shows no changes and at Nottingham lace manufac- turers remain well employed. Shipbuilding and marine en- gineering at all the leading ports remain brisk, and various classes of engineers are freely advertised for. The boot and shoe trade remains bad at Norwich, but there is again a slight improvement at Nottingham. Emigration to the United States has now set in with great briskness, and is likely to continue high for some months. Advices from St. Louis indicate great activity in the building trades, and several sections of wprkers throughout the United States are asking for advance in wages. Railway labour is in great demand, and new undertakings in Neva Scotia are likely to draw further on the English labour market.—Labour News.

is futile to hope for any progress being made with this or any other reform. It needed no great effort on Mr. Arnold's part, or that of the seconder, Mr. Elliot, to make out a strong case in favour of a change. The arguments have been repeated again and again, they carry conviction with them, and the wonder is that effect should not have been given to them before now. The anomalies of the present franchise are manifold. It is almost incredible that in one part of a !county an agricultural labourer should, in order to meet 1 particular exigencies, be invested with the franchise; Iwhile in another part of the same county another of the same class is deprived of the privilege. /t is I rather remarkable that while a labouring man in a borough, who has a house of any value whatever over his head, has a vote, should he from force of circum- stances be obliged to remove into a county he would be robbed of the franchise unless he inhabited a house worth £l2 a year. It is also remarkable that inl counties the possessors of freeholds of the value of only 40s. each have a voice in the election of members of Parliament; and that only in certain boroughs do freemen have a vote. In Ireland the franchise, strange to say, is more restricted than in either Eng- land or Scotland, and it is even more anomalous, for in the sister isle, while a £lO rating is necessary on the part of the burgesses who elect a town councillor, a DI rating suffiees in the case of the election of a member of Parliament. It is anomalies of this char- acter that will be removed by a measure of electoral reform such as that shadowed forth by Mr. Arnold. At the present time, as that gentleman pointed out, the proportion of the electors to the population in England and Wales is one in ten; but this is very much within a fair proportion, as Mr. Arnold's figures indicate. In the Parliamentary boroughs of England and Wales there are 2,098,892 inhabited houses, but the electors number only 1,595,461. There is consequently an excess of more than 25 per cent, of inhabit:d houses over electors. Fifteen per cent. of this may be accounted for by thejact that many of the householders are females, but there still remains ten per cent. of the occupiers who have no voice in the election of Parliamentary representatives. In the counties the proportion is still more marked, and the disfranchisement still more complete. The number of inhabited houses in the English and Welsh counties iS 2,724,912, while the electors number only 932,860. Allowing the same proportions and deductions that obtain in boroughs, Mr. Arnold argues that if uni- formity of the franchise be adopted 1,334,000 electors would be added to the register in England and Wales, 500,000, or nearly twice as many as are at present on the register, in Ireland, and in Scotland the increase to the register would be 150,000. In round figures the increase to the register of electors in the United Kingdom would be 2,000,000, the number of occu- piers at present unable to vote in the election of members of Parliament. By the Act of 1867 the number of voters added to the register was 1,200,000. Mr. Arnold would addthat number and 800,000 more. It should be borne in mind that the great majority of persons disqualified pay rates in the county just as voters in the borough pay them, and that tney.vote in the election of Guardians and for members of School Boards, and there can, therefore, be no valid reason urged why they should not have their political rights oonceded them, At the present time there are 27 boroughs tettirning /I members io Parliament by votes of only half the number of electors found in Manchester, and a great deal less than in Warring- ton ; and again, while the:average representation in England and Wales is one seat to every 41,000 votes in the boroughs, it is only one to every 73,000 votes in the counties, whilst in Ireland there is one seat on the average to 50,000 votes, and in Scotland one seat on the average to 64,000 votes. The objections offered to Mr. Arnold's proposals are none of them serious so far. Mr. Blennerhasset's Select Com- mittee, if appointed, would not, it seems to us, do any arm, seeing that the question cannot be settled just now; and it might have the effect of eliciting much useful information which would be of value in the framing of any future Reform Bill. Mr. Albert Grey's alarm is 'altogether unnecessary, there is no danger of the class to which he belongs being entirely swamped; but 'even if there were, there is as much reason in the representatives of labour mantaiuing the supremacy, as there is in the land- lords dominating as they now do in the I counties. Mr. Stanhope, with evident gusto, quoted Lord Sherbrooki-o as an opponent of the ex- I tension, but surely Mr. Stanhope must have for- gotten that Lord Sherbrooke's opinions are con- , siderahly modified, and that the noble lord is now satisfied that an enfranchisement of the agricultural labourer in counties must follow as a necessary 1 corollary of household franchise in the boroughs. So also with Mr. Goschen. He has long been a strenuous opponent of the extensioncrf the franchise. This fact alone has, it is said, precluded him from taking a seat in the present Liberal cabinet, bat he, too, is now believed to be very nearly if not wholly in entire accord with the occupants of the Treasury Bench on this question. As we have said there is no doubt the resolution proposed by Mr. Arnold will be carried by a large majority. Although no action will be taken upon it for some time, it is satisfactory to have the decision of the last Parliament reversed ; and as the Premier said, the passing of the resolution will be a "visible sign)' to the constituencies that their representatives and the Government are prepared, whenever the oppor- tunity arises, to fulfil their respective promises on this important question of Parliamentary reform.

Most of your readers are aware that it is proposed to carry the Widnes seweragevorks from the river Mersey up to and through Ditton-road. This plan will, of course, include a considerable part of the Hutchinson estate, and it is stated that the trustees of the land have intimated that they can- not allow the 'Local Board to carry out the work unless they are prepared to make concessions which many of the rate- payers consider of a most important character. Various reports are in circulation on the subject, one being that the trustees ask that the Local Board shall take over Ditton- road, and the other that a considerable sum is asked for wayleave. I understand that the matter will probably go to arbitration, and if this only proves as expensive as a somewhat similar case which has been dealt with by the Runcorn Rural Sanitary Auhority, the Widnes Ratepayers' Association will in future have a theme which will find them opportunity for no end of speech-making.

_ A fortnight ago I intimated that the Tories in Mid. Cheshire were speculating on the death of Lord Egerton of Tatton, and the probable summons of the Hon. Wilbraham Egerton, M.P. for Mid-Cheshire, to the Upper House. I also said that in the event of a vacancy thus arising, Sir Gilbert Greenall would be invited—if he had not already 'been—to contest the seat. The latter part of the statement was perhaps premature, but so far as regards the first part, on which doubt has been cast—because it is said the Tories could not do such a thing as speculate on a person's death —I leave my readers to draw their own ,conclusions from a circular which has been sent round to the leaders of the Conservative party, and a copy of which I append :

It does not require much discernment to detect thet the date of the circular corresponds exactly with the period at which the noble lord's condition was most critical; and seeing that the cument had been sent round a clear day before the pubilcatiou of The Examiner, it is not difficult to account for the mention of Sir Gilbert's name in connection with the anticipated vacancy. I think the Tories, who profess to be so very circumspect in all their dealings, might have allowed my Lord Egerton to depart this life before casting about for a successor for his son. The circular is positively one of the most indecent productions which it has been my lot to peruse. It cannot be justified on any grounds whatever; and I think it may fairly be accepted as an indication that the Conservative cause in Mid-Cheshire 15 in a very shaky condition. But Lord Egerton. lam happy to see, is im- proving in health. I wonder what he or his son will thint

_ (Private.) Warrington, 9th March, 1862. Dear Sir,—As it is tot improbable that there may shortly be an election contest in Mid-Cheshire, we shall be greatly obliged by your holding yourself in readiness to act in the Con- servative interest on a short notice, and by your discussing the matter with your political friends and synapithisers in the meantime —Yours faithfully, Nicitor.soze, WHITg, and NICHOL- SGN, Conservative agents. if a copy of the communication should drop across his path. The circular was, as will be seen from the above, marked "Private," which word—as if to impress upon the recipient the strictest secrecy—was written in red ink, while the body of the circular was printed.' -FA good Tory was so disgusted that he handed it to me for publication.

My lord Salisbury has recently taken rather kindly to writing letters, for what reason he thus spends his valuable time is best known to himself. The Conservative associa- tions at Oldham, Cireneester, Bristol, Nuneaton, and a host of other places which might be mentioned, have each sent his lordship a political communication of some kind or another, and the noble marquis has felt bound to make some reply. I have not yet seen anything that the Warrington Conservative Association has done, but I sh,4uld think that if they do not bestir themselves soon " my- lords" pen, ink, and paper will have been used up. It need scarcely be said that his lordship's effusions cover a multitude of questions, all of which are spoken of very flippantly and as becomes the noble lord. So far, however, the Orangemen of Bradford seem to have been singled out for special favours. It is to the Orangemen of this Yorkshire town that Lord Salisbury speaks with the greatest freedom of that liberty of speech which he declares Mr. Gladstone is wishful to abolish ; and it is to them lord Salisbury seys "the uncontrollable temper of the Prime Minister has almost brought the two Houses of Legislature into conflict, simply to gratify th et gentleman's overweening vanity." "Uncontrollable temper," and" over- weening vanity!" Why lord Salisbury is, I think, about the last person who should talk of an " uncontrolable tomper," and so far as regards the overweening vanity " of the Premier, everybody knows Mr. Gladstone 's present position was thrust upon him' but such a position is never likely to be thrust upon lord Salisbury, whose "overween- ing vanity " will always, I am afraid, remain unsatisfied. Judging from appearances, the "unholy alliance", which has been formed between the Conservatives and Home Rulers is to be more closely united on the division on the culture resolutions. At the instigation of the deputy chair- man, the whips, and the hon. secs. of the Irish Parliamen- tary party, a circular has been sent round to all the Irish members imploring them to vote against the Government on the rules of Procedure. In this communication it is pointed out that the fate of the Ministry "may denpend upon a single vote," and that the defeat of the cl<lture involves, it is said, two considerations of great importance—first, the resignation of the Government; and, second, the impossi- bility of renewing the present Coercion Act. Irish members will not So be gulled. They know very well that they have never anything to hope for from the Conservatives now— and it is questionable whether they will obtain anything better at any other time—but Coercion, which is one of their standing orders ; and with reference to the expected resigna- tion of the Government, there is no likelihood at present of the Irish members being able to bring that about. Tb e present "unholy alliance" exists only for an obvious pur- pose—the overthrow of the Government. That purpose is not now to be attained, and I should imagine that it never will be by such a miserable combination. The marriage of Prince Leopold, or rather, I should say, the grant to be made from the State thereupon, was the chief topic of discussion in Parliament on Thursday even- ing. The grant was opposed by Mr. Labouchere and other advanced Liberals, it was never expected the opposition would be successful, but it served as a respectful protest against public money being diverted into what is considered by some a wrong channel. Three valid grounds were urged against the grant. namely, that the Civil List is sufficient to support the children of the Crown, that there is no State reason why Prince Leopold should marry, and even if he does take Uhto himself a wife, that his present income of £15,000 a year is quite sufficient without more. Mr. Labouchere was only able to muster 42 votes, and I rejoice to think that the member for Warrington was on this occa- sion in the minority. He has had the courage of his con- victions, and for voting accordingly I believe he will receive the sympathy and support of the majority of his con- stituency. His conduct forms a marked contrast to that of Mr. Chamberlain, Mr. Courtney, Mr. Mundella, and Mr. Fawcett, who walked out of the House without voting. Very different would their action have been had they been sitting on the front Opposition bench; but as the poet says,—
To place and power all public spirit tends, In place and power all public spirit ends, - VLAOCUS.

HALTON CHURCH SERgONS.-At Halton Church, on Sun- day, the Rev. H. B. Blogg, vicar of Frodsham, and the Rev. Canon Dodd, vicar of Stretton, preached on behalf of the Chester Diocesan Institutions, and the collections realised £6 4s.

RUNCORN AmaTErrn, BICYCLE CM/E.—The following have been appointed officers of this club for the next twelve months :—President, Mr. Thomas Norman; captain, Mr. F Bate; sub-captain, Mr. A. B. Norman; and secretary, Mr. J. Timmins.

WIDNES BOADD.—A special meeting of this Board was held on Thursday afternoon, Mr. Eustace Carey in the chair. There were also present Messrs. Heyes, Gaskell, jun., Handley, Kershaw, Forster, Shuttleworth, O'Keeffe, Sadler, and Allen (clerk). The recommendation of the Finance Committee of the 25th ult. as to paying off certain bonds was adopted. Some of the bonds paid off were at 41 per cent., and they have been renewed at 4 per cent. This con- cluded the business.

WIDN'ES LOCAL BOARD Erxeraorr.—On Thursday even- ing, the nominations for this election were sent in. The Owners and Occupiers Association, who are making an effort to return their men, nominated the following :—Mc. James Cross, civil engineer ; Mr. H. Gaskell, junr., alkali manufacturer; Mr. John Matthews, boot and shoe manu- facturer; Mr. P. Longton, brewer; and Mr. B. Brown, iron- founder. The candidates of the Ratepayers' and Property Owners' Association are :—Mr. J. Midwood, gentleman ; Mr. E. Martley, bookseller and estate agent; Mr. E. John- son, grocer and provision dealer; Mr D. Wright, baker and grocer ; and Mr. R. Webster, grocer and provision dealer. The voting papers will be distributed on the 31st inst. and collected on the 4th prox. The counting up will take place on the following day. RUNCORN YOUNG MEN'S 011RISTIAN ASSOCIATION.— CODLING ENTERTAINMENT.—We have pleasure in calling attention to the fact that on Thursday evening next, a musical and elocutionary entertainment will be given in the Public Hall, Runcorn, under the auspices of the Runcorn Young Men's Christian Association, for which tickets may be obtained at Mr. Bellamy's, The Examiner otilce. Miss Lambert, a Warrington contralto of acknowledged merit, and who is very fairly known to Runcorn audiences, will sing several songs; and Miss Ada Hindley, a Liverpool soprano, who is highly spoken of, will also be present. Captain Haolehurst, of the well-known firm of Messrs. Hazlehurpt and Son, will sing" The old Sacristan," and Parker's 'Close to the threshold." We hope that the health of Mr. Morrison, of Widnes, who is so popular a tenor in the neighbourhood, is thoroughly re-established, as he has consented to be present. Mr. Sansom (London and North-Western stationmaster at Widnes) is a finished reciter, and he will give several selec- tions from Shakspeare. which will, without doubt, give much delight. Mr. E. Rhodes will also favcur the audience with's "taste of his quality" in the same direction; and a very good glee party is to be present, who will be accom- panied by Mrs. Heal, an organist of more than ordinary ability. Dr. Steele wilt preqide. In conclusion, we express a hope that the Runcorn public will interest themselves in this matter, for the sake of the asscociation in connection with which it will be given.

WMNES SCHOOL RUED. - On Thursday afternoon, the monthly meeting was held at he Board-room, Victoria- ioad. Mr. T. Sutton-Timmis presided, and there were also present the Rev. Thos. Finegan, Messrs. W. Bradshaw, H. Wade-Deacon, R. H. Davies, and G. H. Danby (clerk). The repert of the District Education Committee showed that dur- ing the month of February the number of cases summoned before them had been 348, of which 118 were applications for payment of fees and 230 for contravention of the Education Act. Fees were recommended to be paid in Ot cases. Twenty- four applications had been refused, and there had been 2.5 prosecutions before the magistrates, in each of which a con- viction had been obtained.—Mr. Wade-Deacon, in moving the adoption of the report, which was agreed to, said he regretted the committee bad had to summon a larger number of parents than usual before the Bench during the month. They had,in a measure, been compelled to adopt this course, owing to the fact that such a large number of parents appeared to be totally indifferent to the education of their children. It seemed 'probable to him that the number of such cases would be even larger in fnture.—The Chairman expressed his regret at the remarks which had fallen from the last speaker.—At a later part of the proceedings Mr. Wade-Deacon said that the mem- bers of the District Education Committee had visited the in- dustrial schools at which the children committed upon the Board's application to the magistrates were kept. They found all of them in a fair state of healtb,with the exception of two, who were in the hospital, and one of these had since died. He was in Plymouth some few days ago, and visited the truant school for lads, and made several enquiries in regard to it. He was informed that the moral effect of the school upon the boys was so great, that only one per cent, of those who left were returned. There was one of those schools at Liverpool, and he thought it would be as well for the Board to send children there rather than commit them to an indus- trial school. Certainly the cost would be rather mere-Bs. 6d. per week—but it would be better to let them go there for a few weeks rather than pay for their maintenance at an indus- trial school for a term of five year. He added that he might possibly have to bring this matter before the attention of the members again at a later part of the year.—The Rev. T. Finegan read the report of the School Management Commit- tee:—The Sitnm's Cross managers recommended that the resignation of Miss J. Richardson, head mistress in the in- fants' department, be accepted • also that Miss Henderson he appointed head mistress in the infants' department of the Simm's Cross schools at a salary of £5O per annum, and one- third of the Government grant. The West Bank managers recommended that the salary of Misa B. A. Hughes, assistant- mistress in the junior girls' department, be increased from £35 to £4O per annum.—The various recommendations were adopted.—The Finance Committee's report,which was agreed to, showed that the accounts recommended for payment were .£242 45.31., and during the month £ll5 Os. 10d. had been paid into the bank. It was also recommended that Arthur Hough be engaged as a junior clerk at a salary of Cs. Bd. per rnonth,—lbis concluded tbe business.

div.head: FRODSHAM.
div.p: FRODSHAM.
HIGH TIDE.—The strong wind on Tuesday caused the river Weaver to overflow, and the land at Sutton, between the river and the canal, was flooded to an extent which has

not been known for some years. DRAMATIC PERFORMANCES AT THE TOWN HALL, FROD- smuf.—The select character of the audience is a sufficient guarantee for the tone and character of the entertainment provided by Mr. Stanley Warde's Dramatic Company during the third week of their visit, and we pave no doubt they will receive a hearty welcome when they next come to Frodsham.
TRINITY WESLEYAN BAND OF IioPE.—A meeting of the :emperance friends iu connection with the Trinity Wes-

leyan Chapel was held in the Victoria Hall, Frodsham, on Thursday evening, when addresses were delivered by the Chairman, Mr. Thomas Hough, and the Rev. F. Haines, of Northwich, who was formerly resident minister at Frod- sham. The usual vote of thanks to the speakers brought the meeting to a close. ANNUAL MEETING OF RATEPAYERS AT FRODS HAM.

The annual meeting of ratepayers in the township of Frodsham was held in the Overseers' Office, in the Town Hall, Frodsham, on Thursday evening, when there were present Messrs. Thomas Davies (chairman), Henry Linaker, John Ashton, C. E. Linaker, John Challoner, E. Ashworth, T. Andrews, T. Riley, R. Bate, S. Spencer, S. Aston, T. Lewis, G. H. Danby, J. Cunnah, H. They, J. Percival, and R. Andrews (assistant overseer). The Proposed Petty Sessions for Frodshant : The Assistant Overseer read the following letter in this matter, viz. :—" Clerk of the Peace's Office, Chester, 28th March, 1881.— Dear Sir,— The application for (the magistrates of the petty sessional division of Eddisbury to hold a petty Sessions at Frodsham, should be made to the magistrates of the division through their clerks, Messrs. Blake, Trafford, and Cooke, of Northwich, and not to the Court of Quarter Sessions. If they entertain the proposal, and think it neces- sary to make any application to the Court of Quarter Ses- sions, they will no doubt do so.—Yours truly, (signed) C. W. POTTS.-Mr. R. Andrews, Overseers Office, Frodsham." The Assistant Overseer reported that he had communicated with Messrs. Blake, Trafford, and Cooke, Northwich, but had not received any reply thereto.—Glea2elians: Messrs. John Ashton and Themes Andrews were again nominated as Guardians.—Overseers: On the question of nomination of overseers being submitted, Mr. John Challoner inquired the aueeent of balance in the hands of the retiring overseers, which was stated to be above £loo.—Messrs. James Andrews and Thomas Davies were unanimously recommended for appoint- ment as overseere. by the Justices.— Waywai'den: Mr. Henry I . Lmaker was also unanimously returned as waywarden.— I Frodshaan Sewerage: Jfr. Wright's Arbitration.—ln re- ference to this matter, Mr. Linaker made a personal explana- tion. He stated that the whole of the proceedings had been carried out by him in compliance with the instructions of the Rural Sanitary Authority, and in the manner prescribed by law; and he submitted particulars, detailing the progress of the proceelings, for the consideration of the ratepayers. The following resolution, proposed by Mr. John Challoner, and seconded by Mr. James Percival, was carried, and ordered to be recerded-on the minutes :—" That, having heard the explanation given by Mr Linaker, respecting the false rumours reported in Frodsham and Frodsham Lordship in reference to the sewerage and arbitration, this meeting entirely exonerates Mr. Linaker from all blame in the matter, and considers that he has acted honourably through- out the whole affair."—S'pecial Sanitary Rate : The Assistant Overseer reported that the special rate required in connection with the sewerage scheme, during the ensuing half year, was £2OO, and applied for the remuneration to be fixed for making and collecting the rate. Mr. John Ashton proposed, and Mr. Thomas Lewis seconded a proposition that the remuneration be .£l5, an amendment fixing the amount at £lO being defeated.—Lighting Rate: A meeting of ratepayers comprised within the Lighting District was held at the close of the above meeting, when the following account of the Lighting, Inspectors was submitted, viz.: —Receipts: Balance, £lB 19s. 10J. ; cash from overseers, £36 58. ; total receipts, £55 ss. ,Ad. Expenditure: Frodsham Gas Co., £42 55.; secretary's salary, £2 10s. ; sundry repairs, £4 13s. 4d.; balance in hand, £5 17s. od.; total, £55 ss. 41d. The accounts were adopted, Dr. F. P. Weaver and Mr.. J. W. Rothwell, were re-elected inspectors, and a sum not exceeding £5O was authorised to be raised duiing the ensuing year.—A vote of thanks to the chairman brought the meeting to a close.

div.head: LYME
div.p: LYME

LYATAI LOCAL BOARD ELECTION.—A. meeting of rate- payers was held in the Assembly Rooms, on Saturday night, . but was very poorly attended, there being no more than 40 persons present. The meeting was called by Messrs. Hall and T. H. Taylor, for the purpose of selecting three candi- dates for the above Board, on the retirement of Messrs. Hall, Richardson, and Simpson. It had become well known during the week that the Ratepayers' Association had de- cided to nominate Mr. J. D. Dewhurst, Col. ROSS, and Mr. Arthur Callender, therefore the meeting was convened to propose three other candidates to oppose these gentlemen. Mr. J. Marsh, of Bradley Hall, was called to the chair, and at once called upon Mr. James Holt, who explained the objects of the meeting.—Mr. Hall followed, and gave what . he called a complete history of the Lymm sewerage scheme. He (Mr. Hall) was in favour of the small scheme, and what he should like the meeting to do, was to nominate little . scheme candidates to oppose the big scheme candidates.— Mr. South and Mr. Bickley both opposed Mr.llall, and said they were at a loss to knoß what the meeting was for, they having understood that the Ratepayers' Association had called the meeting.—Eventually, Mr. Smith proposed, and Mr. Bickley seconded the candidates. The result of a show of hands was in favour of Mr. Dewhurst. Mr. Marsh, of Bradley Hall, Mr. David Forster, Rush Green, and Mr. J. Hall, Statham, were also selected as candidates. The meet- ing was soon afterwards brought to a close with the usual vote of thanks to the chairman.

div.head: VISIT OF MR. THOMAS E. MURPHY TO, WARRINGTON.
div.p: VISIT OF MR. THOMAS E. MURPHY TO, WARRINGTON.

It affords us much gratification to learn that on Sunday, April 16, Mr. T. E. 'Murphy will commence a Gospel Tem- perance Mission, in the Warrington Public Hall, and that it will be continued for 14 successive nights. Mr. Murphy, who is the son of the founder of the great blue ribbon move- ment, was born in New York, on July 18, 1859, and is con- sequently in the 23rd year of his age. Though young, Mr. Murphy is endowed with wonderful gifts, and happily they are exercised in an exvilent cause. He has already con- ducted a number of missions in England, at all of which thousands have taken the temperance pledge, and we doubt not that equal success will attend Mr. Murphy's mission here. We are told that "As a speaker Mr. Edward Murphy is very brilliant, intensely earnest and full of enthusiasm. His thoughts are arranged with exactitude and expressed with considerable rhetorical skill. Some of his perorations are, from the sublimity of their pathos, irresistably impres- sive; and to an unusual degree he has the power, which he exercises with rare sagacity, that every natural orator pos- sesses, that of moving his audiences as he wills, to laughter or to tears." We bespeak for the talented gentleman a cordial welcome and a patient hearing.

div.head: 411t3.-
div.p: WARRINGTON POLTCE COURT. FiZIDAY. - Before Capt. Reynolds (chairman), Major Cartwright, Mr. Jos. White, and Mr. Ziba Armitage.

ATTEMPT TO DEFRAUD THE CHESHIRE LINES COMPANY. —Thomas Clyues, mouNer's dresser, Sheffield, was charged with riding from Sheffield to Warrington on the Cheshire Lines Railway without having previously paid his fare, and with intent to defraud the company. On the arrival at Warrington, on Thursday, of a special train from Sheffield for the Liverpool races, the prisoner was found underneath the seat of a third-class carriage—lie was fined 20s. and costs, or in default a month's imprisonment. A REFRACTORY APPRENTICE. Wm. Warburton, glass manufacturer, summoned Daniel Tobin, on a claim of £5, for failing to perform his contract according to the terms of his apprenticeship deed.—Mr. Percy Davies appeared for the complainant, and said that on the 13th inst. the defendant had to make 150 ice cream glasses to a pattern which Ile himself had made, but he made them too much too large. They were consequently useless, and the order for the goods was lost. He was ordered on another occasion to make some paraffin lamp chimneys. He had sufficient metal to to make 40 dozen chimneys, whilst he only made 14 dozen, and then threw the remainder of the metal up and down the shop.—Two witaesses were called whose evidence went to show that the defendant had wilfully spoiled his work.— defendant contended that it was impossible to always make good work, and alleged that on the night he had to make the paraffin lamp chimneys be had not been asleep for 24 hours.—An order for £3 was made upon the defendant, to be paid at the rate of ss. per week, and he was also ordered to fulfil his contract.

THEFT FROM A PROVISION SHOP.—Mary Hughes, a tramp from Huddersfield, was charged with stealing a tin of sardines, and a tin of salmon of the value of is. 6d. from the shop of Richard Birchall, provision dealer, Butter- market street. At a quarter to nine on Friday morning the prisoner went into the prosecutor's shop and asked the boy at the counter for an ounce of coffee and tea. Whilst be was weighing the purchase, the boy observed the prisoner take up the tins of fish produced and "make off with them." Sentenced to a month's imprisonment. ASSAULT.—Thonaas Moran, a youth living in Erwood- street, for assaulting Margaret Larliin, a married woman of the same neighbourhood, on the 20th instant, was fined 55. 7d.

THE MAINTENENCE OF CHILDREN.—Patrick Farrell, a labourer, was summoned to show cause why be should not be committed to prison for the non-payment of £1 lie. 6d., being the arrears of an order made upon him to contribute towards the maintenance of his son who is in an industrial school.—The Bench, after hearing the evidence, remarked that the defendant was evidently determined to set the order at defiance, and committed him to goal for a month.-- Ralph Norman was brought up on a similar summons, the arrears being £2 6s. Gd., and the Bench ordered him to pay 2s. per week.
LATEST NEWS.

The steamer Toronto, N%, ich has art ived at Liverpool from Portland (Maine), reports heavy weather on the passage. She lost 77 cattle, out of 276 shipped, alai 36 sheep, out of 223 shipped. • A Standard Alexandria•telegram says :—A paper usually well-informed says the Egyptian Govanment intend to con- struct an arsenal at Suez, and that an engineer has arrived there to prepare his plans. The committee having charge of the science classes at the Hall of Science, London, have decided to write to Mr. Mundella stating that they have not withdrawn Mrs. Besantie name as teacher, as stated by him when replying to Sir Henry Tyler in the House of Commons, and to request that the error may be corrected. Sir Stafford Northcote has written to the Bradford Orange- men acknowledging the receipt of resolutions passed by them approving of the steps taken by the Conservative party in the House of Commons in opposing the admission of Mr. Bradlaugh.
A TOWN CONSUMED BY FIRE. ME PERSONS BURNT TO DEATH.

A terrible calamity has occurred in Hungary, ;;ulting ia the total destruction by fire of the town of Emved. Only the manor house, in fact, has escaped the flames. Not only have all the dwelling houses; with stables and outbuildings„ been burnt to the ground, but the four churches, with the,- clergy-houses attached, have been reduced to at:hes. Five old women and four children were burnt to death. The in- habitants are compelled to camp in the open fields. RETORTED DIFFERENCES IN THE CABINET.

The Loudon correspondent of the Fiycntan's Journal says :—Thl rumour is again revived that Mr. Forster will shortly retire from the post of Irish Chief Secretary. Seri— ous differences exists ia the Cabinet over Irish affairs and a renewal of coercion and farther land legislation cannot well take place with the. Ministry as at present constituted.

div.head: NEW CONSTITUTION FOR CYPRUS.
div.p: A NEW CONSTITUTION FOR CYPRUS.

A new Constitution for Cyprus is officially announced. The Legislative Council will consist of six official and twelve elected members, nine ef the latter being Christians and three Mallornedans. The duration of the first Council will be three years. The franchise qualification and the right of voting are placed on a broad basis.

div.head: CHESHIRE CONGREGATIONAL UNION:
div.p: THE CHESHIRE CONGREGATIONAL UNION:

The annual meetings of the Cheshire Congregational Union were held en Thursday at Hyde. The Chairman (the Rev. G. K. Walker, of Middlewich) in his opening address pleaded for greater " enthusiasm " in the prosecution of the work of the churches, and instanced the results that are attending.the labours of the Salvation Army as evidence of what may be accomplished by increased zeal. Although they might have their individual opinions as to the pro- priety of some of the means the Army employ, he advised that the:movement should be watched and the work aided and utilised where possible. The reports showed that there had been an increase during the past year of 11 per cent in the membership of the aid-receiving churches After the tran- saction of the usual business, a discussion took place on the :neans of drawing young people into the fold of the churches. A resolution was passed expressing gratitude to God at the preservation of the Queen from the recent attempt upon her life. In the evening a public meeting in connection with the Union was held in Zion Chapel; Mr. W. Milne, of Powdon, in the chair.

div.head: COL. BURNABY'S BALLOON VOYAGE.
div.p: COL. BURNABY'S BALLOON VOYAGE.

The Central News stees a telegram was received at Dover yesterday from Col. Burnaby by Mr. T. Wright, the aeronaut, stating that the Saiden had descended safely last night about six o'clock at the Chateau de Montigty, Nor- mandy, and will at once return by train to London. Ac- cording to the telegram, which is brief and somewhat obscure in some particulars, Colonel Burnaby, after arriving on the French coast, in Boulogne, was carried out to sea. Again the balloon, however, returned inland in a southerly direction from Dieppe, and the aeronaut finding night coming on descended in the neighbourhood of hfontigny. The balloon behaved fairly well, and rcquired but little expendi- ture of ballast on the journey. The following is the tele-. gram from Col. Burnaby to Mr. Wright :—" Your ballom ' uninjured; wind changed mid-Channel; afterwards was time becalmed. Over sea; eventually found southerly current at high altitude; descended Chateau de Alontigny7 Envermea, Normandy. Voyage difficult, but very amusing." The distance travelled by Col. Burnaby, supposing he had proceeded in a straight line to Caen Calvados, would be 250 miles, and the rate at which he proceeded would be about thirty miles per hour. re does not appear, however, to have made a true course, as after passing over the French coast near Boulogne, the balloon must have been taken by the wind in a more Westerly direction, and was then again carried over a por- tion of the English channel before being brought to earth in Normandy.

At a meeting of the Baloon Society of Great Brit yesterday the president read two telegrams relating te, the Colonel's successful trip across the channel. The first follows :—"Chateaux de Monligny, Normandy. was as Colonel Fred. Burnaby descended in the balloon Eclipse in meadow near this place, about six o'clock last evening. A numleor of persons witnessod the arrival of the aer Me Colonel was ot, wh, has been loaed for all along the coast. loudly cheered and received a hea welcome." The second telegram which was read —was one which had been sent by a friend of the Colonel's, who lives near the spot, and conversed with the eeeranaut, who said :—" Eclipse behaved splendidly. Passed over Boulogne at noon, and proceeded in a south south-westerly direction. Threw out more balast in order to find a current to take me on to club at Paris over Letonquet. At a few minutes to two o'clock still proceeding south-west. Wind chopped round and became becalmed in the channel. Again threw out ballast, of Icloielf. I bad taken the precaution to have plenty, and providentially getting into a favourable current was carried with expedition to Chateau de Montigny, having been about eight hours in the air." The reading of these telegrams was received with ; cheers, and the meeting closed by the president delivering a few remarks on the subject of military balloon invasions,

HOUSE OF LORDS.

Lord CAuPERDowN moved that their lordships should commence business at 4 instead of 5 o'clock. A discassion ensued, and it was ultimately agreed that 4-15 should be the hour at which their lordships would assemble. • Their lordships adjourned until 12-30 to-day. HOUSE OF COMMONS.
MR. BRADLLUGII.—A petition was presented from Nor- thampton, praying that Mr. Bra.'laugh might be permitted to take his seat.

ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS.—Mr. CHAMBERLAIN, replyinq to Mr. Buxton, said the Act 7 and 8 Vic., which imposed an obligation on railway companies, to run cheap artizan trains, and relieving such from passenger duty was in force.— Mr. LrrEvnE, replying to Captain Aylmer, said it was true that a meeting of members of the Reform Cub was lately held in committee room fifteen, but non-members of Parlia- ment were not present.—The SPEAKER, replying to Mr. Labouchere, said he would not be in order in moving the issue of anew writ for Northampton. NOTICE OF MOTION.—Mr. FIRTH gave notice for an early day to move that the electors of Northampton, in accordance with petition presented, be heard at the bar against the exclusion of flit-4r member. GROUNDING OF THE EDINBCROTL—Mr. TREVELTIN said he hacLreceived information as to the grounding of the ship Edinburgh. The vessel went on a mud bauir, but fif,,ated off when the tide rose. The vessel had sustained not the, slightest damage internally. An examination exte!nilly would take place immediately.

AILERICA AND HER CITIJIENS. - Sir C. DILLE said representations from the G•werninent of the United States had been made to Her Majesty's Gov, rnment with regal d to the trial or release of American citiz,ns imprisoned under the Coercion Act, and such communication was now under 'consideration.

The Consolidated Fund Bill was read a third time. FOREIGN TARIFFS —Mr. RITCHIE called attention to the effect of Foreign Tariffs on the trade of EnOand. Be in- sisted that for some time the prosperity of this country had not been progressing, but on the contrary it was retrogres.,- sing. The cause of our going back was the commercial policy of this country and the want of confidence engen- dered. He did not ask that there should be a return to protection, that was impossible; but what he did require was that there should be a general inquiry into the whole sub- jezt, and oe extremely regretted that his motion for appoint- ment of a Select Committee was to be opposed y the Govern- ment. He concluded by moving that a select committee be appointed to inquire into the effects which tariffs in force in foreign countries had upon the principal branches of British trade and commerce, and into the possibility of removing by legislation or otherwise any impediment to the fulkr de- velopment of the manufacturing and commercial industry of the United Kingdom.
