div.head: Tatttr to flu editor.
div.p: Tatttr to flu editor.

iTEiFROM A WARRINGTONIAN IN AMERICA. INTE RESTING, REMINISCENCES. Sir —I have just received a copy of the Warrington Examiner. I also received a copy in 1880, giving an account of your election and the noble victory you 'had gained, once more throwing overboard the old representa- tive of no progress, and sending a gentleman to Parliament of the right stamp; one who is able and willing to assist in pushing forward the noble principles of progress, and one possessing sound judgment, activity, and discretion. I had aLso sent me a good-sized photograph of your worthy member. with whom I was in times gone by a fellow-worker in the Liberal cause. I have Cobdeu and. Bright hung in my sitting-room, and shall add Mr. McMinnies', so that the three worthies will be in company in this western country. I was very glad to see, and must congratulate him on, his healthy and robust appearance. I hope he will continue healthy, strong, and able to represent the good old town for many years to come. lam old enough to remember the first , election in 1832, being then 27 years old. I took an active part in that and every other contest up to the defeat of Mr. Allcar d, who was half a Whig. After the first election we were nearly always beaten by small majorities, owing to the influence of the brewery, the bank, and the combined influ- ence of the Tories over their tenants. It therefore, does me good to hear of the progress of the good old town. How much I should have enjoyed being present at your victory, I trust the final overthrow of Toryism in old Warrington. The reading of it brings to mind old times, old struggles, but always defeat. Those times are, I trust, past; and ought to have been long ago. Thus I thought when the franchise was extended, and Mr. P. Rylands was returned, "Now all is over with the Tories." lam sure his career in Parliament was, such that all genuine reformers could approve, there being no comparison either in intellect, sound principle, or activity between him and the worse than dead representative he had dethroned. But what was my surprise • when, at the next election, I saw the talented and active P. Rylands replaced by the redoubtable G. Greenall. I thought "How is this? Have the workingmen of Warrington lost both principle and common sense ?" for everyone with the least intelligence knows that the rights of the masses have always been opposed by the Tories; and that whatever has been got from them in the shape of reform or progress has been wrung from them in spite of themselves. They have always looked upon the masses much the same as our slave holders looked on their slaves, and I was certainly astonished when I saw Mr. Rylands replaced by Mr. Greenall. But Burnley showed genuine reform principles and sound judgment by replacing Mr. I.tylands in Parliament; and the good old town made some atonement by returning a genuine live reformer the first chance it bad. And here I would say: And ye who now. are enfranchised, ye noble sons of toil, be true; support those noble men who did you enfranchise. The principles advo- cated on your platform are the right sort- -Free Trade, peace with all nations, and Land Reform at home. Were Parlia- ment comprised of such men as the three who addressed you years ago, the above reforms would soon be brought about, but come they will, together with a purging of the House of Lords. I see the Fair Trade policy is making a little stir; it is nothing more than a bait to get the votes of the labourer by trying to persuade him it will keep up the rate of wages. The Protectionists of this country are trying to show through the Fair Trade advocates of England that Free Trade has been a complete failure. We old members of the Anti-Corn Law League know better. They ccmplain that the Free Traders of England are flooding this country with Free Trade literature, and warn the people to be- ware of them. I would say, "pour in all the argument you can; it is needed here." I see you had on your platform a number of napes which bring to my mind's view a number of old familiar faces. Some were scholars, some teachers in our Cairo-street school, with whom I there, and in the Mechanics' Institution, spent many busy hours. They are now men_of mature years, active lives, and sound principles. Some are the descendants of staunch defenders of liberty and Liberal principles when it was dangerous to avow them. each was old John Rylands, Joseph Crosfield, H. Gaskell, and many others I might name. With what an amount of pleasure and satisfaction they would view your last election. In conclusion, let me wish our good old town success. I shall always feel interested in its welfare, and I still remain so much of an Englishman as to feel an interest in the welfare of the old country. I would here just say I think all yoar M.P.'s who gave Mr. Gladstone their full support are acting very judiciously. He is the right man at the head of affairs. I think there is sufficient common sense combined with self-interest in the Irish nation, to appreciate what he is doing. Everyone must see that he is doing all that is possible to be done at present. Now, with wishes of success to the Liberal cause, properity to the good old town, love and respect for all old friends, I remain, yours, THOS. MOULDING. Blackberry Station, Illinois, Feb. 20, 1882. a

div.head: WARRINGTON POLICE COURT.
div.p: WARRINGTON POLICE COURT.

SATURDAY.—Befoce Mr. Aid. Chandley and Mr. Aid. Burgess. REMANDED CASE.—William Hart, bricksetter's labourer, 16, Jockey-street, was charged with stealing from Char.dos Foundry, between five and six o'clock on Fiiday night, 1012 lbs. of brass, value 45., the property ef Messrs. Samuel Hor- ton de Co.—Remanded. bioerbeun—Before the Mayor, and Deputy Mayor (Coun- cillor Fairclough), and Major Cartwright. DRUNRENNESS. Sarah Saunders, of Liverpool, was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Howley-lane,on Saturday morning, and she was ordered to leave the town at once.—For being drunk in Hill-street, on Saturday night, Jas. Howarth, who made his fourteenth appearance. was fined 5s and costs.—A similar charge was made against Alfred Jackson and he was fined 1087 and costs.— The following persons were also fined for being drunk : Jas. Gardner, Mary Ann Foy, Michael Folly, Wm. Amblett, Edward Lewis, John Rogan, Thomas Goulden, and Jane Runcorn. OBSTRUCTING THE STREET. Henry Allcock, a salt -dealer, was charged with obstructing the free passage of Bridge-street, on the 9th March.—P.C. Corbett proved the case and the defendant was ordered to pay 9s. Costs. STONE THROWING. Michael Flynn, Michael Corfield, Vin. Barnes, and Francis Ford, young boys, were charged with throwing stones.—P.C. Shaw said the boys on the 10th inst, were sending stones at an errand boy who was walking down Bewsev-street.—Mr. Hunt said the police were con- tinually bringing up boys for sending stones, endangering the lives of foot passengers and doing damage to property, and the magistrates were just imposing the penalty of 35.6 d. costs. The offenders had no idea that they were liable to a fine of 40s. and costs.—Major Cartwright: It is becoming an intolerable nuisance, especially in the outskirts of the town.—Each defendant was fined 2s. 6d. and ss. 6d. costs. A SUSPICIOUS CHARACTER. —A young fellow named Patrick Kilroy, of Jolly's-yard, was charged with being a person of suspicious character, having been found in pos- session of a hat supposed to have been stolen, and of which he could not* give a satisfactory account. The prisoner was seen' in Bridge-street late on Saturday night with a new hat in his hand, whilst he was wearing a cap. P.C. Shaw stop- ped him, and asked for an explanation, when he used threatening language.—As no one claimed the hat, the prisoner was discharged.—Mr. Hunt said knowing the character of the prisoner, the officer was justified in the course he took. FAMILY DESERTION.—Joseph Bibby, an ironworker, was charged with running away from the borough on the 19th October, leaving two children chargeable to the common fund of the Warrington Union.—Mr. Garnett, relieving officer, proved the case, and stated the prisoner Lad previously left his family. His family had received £9 12s. 4d. in rellef.—Prisoner was sent to gaol six weeks. PITCH AND Toss.—Alfred Starkey, a boy was chargedwith playing pitch and toss in Bennett-street on Sunday morn- ing. From the evidence it appeared the prisoner was trying to • knock a half-penny from a ring with a peg top. The Bench considered it a game of skill, and on the boy promising not to offend again, he was discharged.—Wm. Barlow was charged with playing at pitch and toss in Aiken-street, on Sunday morning.—The case having been proved, the Bench inflicted a fine of 55., and ss. 6d. costs. EXTRAORDINARY CASE.—:THROWING BOILING WATER.— John and Mary Dempsey, man and wife, residing in Trafalgar-court, off Church-street, Were charged with unlaw- fully -wounding Patrick Brannon by throwing a quantity of boiling water on his face, thereby doing him grievous bodily harm.—The prosecutor, who is a tailor, and has a wife and six children living in Ireland, has lodged with the prisoners for the last three months. On Saturday night the piosecutor went to his lodgings at 9 o'clock; but the door being locked he went to the house of a person named Rabbitt, in Union- street, off Dolman's lane. There he stayed until about eleven o'clock, when he again went to the prisoners' house. A scene of mutual recrimination ensued, and the male prisoner seized the prosecutor's coat. The prosecutor thought' it best to get away, and said he was going to bed. "I want you," said Mrs. Dempsey, who seized a cup, and from a saucepan poured boiling water on the prosecutor's face and bosom. W ith the rolling pin she then gave prosecutor several blows on the arm,tore his collar and shirt, and pushing him in the street gave him a blow on the eye, saying "Now you have had enough." The husband, while this was being done, was standing on one ie deof the fire. The prosecutor then returned to Eabbitt's house, where he slept that night. At about eleven o'clock next morning he went to the police station, and P.C. Neill sent him to the Infirmary to have his injuries attended to. i rho prosecutor appeared n court with his face completely oandaged up, a small race only being left for him I-7a breathe through.—Dr. Richmond, house surgeon at the In- firmary, said the prosecutor was scalded on the face, both arms, and the right shoulder, hut not very severely. They were superficial scalds. The right eye had been scalded. but he did not think the prosecutor.would sufler much injury from that. He apprehended no serious consequences whatever.— Major Cartwright Would it be very painful ?—Dr. Rich- mond: Oh, yes.—The Mayor : Has he any pain now ? Yes. —The Bench reduced the charge to one of common as4ault, and the prosecutor having given his evidence, he was cross- examie.2.l by Mr. Moore, who appetred for the prisoners, to show that there was some family feelitag between, the par- ties, who are related by marriage.—The prosecutors evidence was totally uncorroborated.—P.C.'s Neill and Jones gave evidence as to the apprehension of the prisoners. Mrs. Pernpany admitted to the latter officer that she threw the water at the prosecutor, adding that he shou:d not call her such names as he did before her husbind. Her husband, she stetted, never interfered in the matter at all.—Mr. Moore, for the defence, submitted there was no case against Dempsey. There was some bad feeling between the prosecu- tor and the prisoners' family, who had got it into their heads, whether rightly or wren& that the prisoner wee

unfaithful to his wife. The prisoners were honest hard- working people, and were the main support of the prosecu- tor's family. The prosecutor had been orared to leave the house some time ago. On Saturday night he went in the house in an excited state leading Mrs. Dempsey, who was, alone, to believe that he had too much drink. He used some of the vilest expressions a man could use to a woman, and tried to take improper liberties with Mrs. Dempsey. The husband then came in and ordered him out. Mrs. Dempsey had no idea the water she sent at the prose- cutor was so hot, and was sorry that he should have been injured. She was willing to compensate hi:n.—The police gave the prisoners good characters.—The Bench considered there was no case against Dempsey, and discharged him. They had no doubt Mrs. Dempsey was in a passion when she sent the water, through the provocation she had received from the prosecutor. She was ordered ta pay 40s. damages and costs. SCHOOL ATTENDANCE CAsEs.—At the instance of the Schooi Attendance Committee, the following persons were summoned by Mr. Riley for neglecting to send their chil- dren regularly to school, and a fine of ss. was imposed in each case :—George Peach, railway inspector; Samuel Thomason, bricksetter ; William Lamb, railway inspector; Peter Baguley, hawker; Bernard Conroy, forgeman ; Wm. Moffatt, tanner; Junes Miley, Wakefield-street ; Joseph Grant, flatman ; Pat Rooney, forgeman ; Robert Garrett, wireworker, Whitecross.—A warrant was ordered for the apprehension of Mary Knockton. A THIEF NICELY CAUGHT.—Edward Hart, a bricksetter's labourer, was charged, on remand, with stealing 10?-31bs. of brass from Chandos Foundry. the property of Saml. Horton and Co.—For a few days last Week prisoner was working at the Chandos Foundry, and on Friday night he offered to sell some brass to two marine store dealers, but they would have nothing to do with it. Shortly afterwards P.C. Pace met him in Winwick-street with something rather bulky in his possession, and stopped him. He found he had some brass castings in his possession, and took him in custody. It was afterwards ascertained they had been stolen fr.om the Chan- dos Foundry.—The prisoner pleaded guilty, and he was sent to gaol three months. TUESDAY.—Before Councillor Monks. BICCIIALIAN FOLLOWERS.—MichaeI Cummins, Friars Green, a labourer, was charged with being drunk and dis- orderly in Bridge-street on the previous afternoon, and he was fined 7s. G. and costs, or in default seven days.—For being drunk and disorderly in Bank-street on Monday after- noon, Andrew Walsh, a gatherer of rags, Percivaf's Fold, was fined ss. and costs, with the alternative of seven days' imprisonment.—A fine of ss. and costs was imposed upon Michael Galvin, 9, Farrell-street, for drunkenness and dis- orderly conduct in Challoner•street.—John McDonald, Major Cross-street, was mulcted in the penalty of ss. and costs for being drunk and disorderly in Buttermarket-street on the previous night. WEDNESDAL—Before Alderman Chandley and Captain Litton.

THE ALLEGED FRAUD BY TRADESMEN. Edward Mackie, sen., Edward Mackie, jun., and Eliza Mackib, lately carrying on business as linen drapers in Orford-street, were brought up, on remand, charged with conspiring to defraud Messrs. Mclntyre, Hogg and Co., of Manchester, and others. —Mr. Percy Davies represented the prosecutors, and applied for a further remand of eight days, until after the meeting of the prisoners' creditors had been held, when some course of action would be decided upon. If the prisoners were not prosecuted under this charge they would be under the Debtors Act of 1879. In addition to what has been pre- viously published, it may be stated that Mackie, sen., in 1874, filed his petitien in liquidation in Chesterfield County Court. He owed £5OO for goods similar to those he had obtained in this instance, and without paying a penny of the claims he disappeared, and it was reported he had gone to America. He afterwards "turned vup " in Liverpool, in 1878, and took a shop in Netherfield-road, which he left , without paying his rent, coming to Warrington. It had been I discovered that the younger Mackie was not the son of the other prisoners, but a man named McGowan' who a short time ago was discharged from the Liverpool police. The male prisoners had no objection to a remand, the elder stating he was guilty. The female prisoner said she was very ill and delicate, and characterised Mr. Davies' remarks as a concoction against them.—The prisoners were re- manded to Walton Gaol until next Wednesday. ROBBERY BY A WomAx.—Emily Barclay, a woman of re- spectable appearance, was charged on remand with having, between the 22nd and 23rd Dec., 1880, stolen one black cloth shooting coat, a vest, shirt, two shawls, and a blanket, of the value of £2 10s., from the house of Elizabeth Shaw.—The prisoner pleaded guilty.—On the 19th December, 1880, the prisoner represented herself to Mrs. Shaw as a tailoress, and obtained lodgings with her at 5, Egerton-street. Four days later she suddenly disappeared, and with her the articles named. Every inquiry was made, but neither the prisoner nor the goods could be traced. In March, 1881, Mr. Hunt receiveda communication from the Chief-Constable of Man- chester, who informed him that the prisoner had been com- mitted for trial at the sessions on three charges of robbing her lodgings. She was sentenced to twelve months imprison- ment, and on Tuesday morning her term expired. When re- leased from Knutsford Gaol she was met by P.S. Bowen,who apprehended her on this charge.—Considerine the sentence she had just undergone the Bench committed the prisoner for a month with hard labour. A SHOCKING TALE.—John Austin, a strapping young fellow, was charged with having, on the 18th March, as- saulted his wife Mary Ann.—Prosecutrix said at midnight on Saturday her husband went home drunk. She had his supper ready, but because she did not fetch some "onions and things" he struck her on the face.—Prisoner : It's the first time in the fourteen years since we were married.— Prosecutrix : Oh, that's nensense.—ln reply to Alderman Chandley, the prosecutrix said her husband habitually ill- used her and the children by " clemming them and drunken- ness." A few weeks since he caught her by the threat and nearly choked her because she took half-a-crown from his pocket when he went home drunk. He did not take home money sufficient to keep the family. There was no food in the house now, and when she left the court she would have to go to the parish. The children had had a bit of breakfast given them that morning.—Prisoner said be had done no work for six weeks. He promised to get employment at once I and treat his family properly.—He was bound over in his I own recognizances of £5 to keep the peace for six months. THURSDAY.— Before Captain Litton and Alderman Webster.

PETER BAGIILEY MARES HIS 61ST APPERANCE.—Peter Baguley, who it was stated "does not work hot sells oranges," made his Gist appearance on a charge of being; drunk and disorderly in Bank-street.—He was fined 53. in- cluding costs. RETURNING FROM LINCOLN RACES: CHEATING THE CHESHIRE LINES COMMITTEE--James Willis, described as a labourer, from London, was charged with having, on Wed- nesday, ridden in a third-class carriage on the Cheshire Lines, from Lincoln to Warrington, without having paid his fare.—A ticket collector stated that on the arrival of a special train from Lincoln about twenty minutes past eight on Wednesday night, he found the prisoner concealed under the seat of a third-class carriage. He got the prisoner out and asked him for his ticket, but he had none.—The prisoner said he got under the seat to have a sleep.—The ticket col- lector replied that the prisoner was fonnd under the seat wide awake, and that four men at the end of the c ompart- ment, who were playing cards, had a newspaper over their knees trying to conceal the prisoner.—The magistrates' clerk said the trick was tried every year.—The prisoner was fined 20s. and costs or a month.—James M'Corrnick, hawker, Liverpool, and William Pannett, confectioner, Stockton, were charged with a similar offence from Godley Junction. On the arrival of a train from Hull shortly after eight o'clock, P.S. Bowen saw the prisoner hurriedly left the com- partment in which they were, and mingle with the persons on the platform. The tickets were all collected and when the train was about to start the prisoners attempted to enter a compartment, but were prevented.—The prisoners pleaded guilty, M'Cormick remarking that they had been to the races and. lost ,their money.—They were each fined 201. and costs, the alternative being a month's imprisonment.

div.head: ITAYDOCK,
div.p: ITAYDOCK,

ALLEGED THEFT OF A WATCH.—At the Wigan County Police Court, on Monday, before Mr. J. Leyland, Anne Johnson, a middle-aged woman of no settled address, was charged with stealing a silver lever watch and chain from the person of Joseph Swift, at Haydock, on the 14th inst.— Prosecutor, who is a collier, residing at Lime-kiln, Haydock, stated that he met the prisoner at the Owl's Nest beerhouse, Haydock, on the afternoon in question. She came begging, and he asked her to sit down and he paid for her a glass of ale. He had never seen the prisoner before that day. He subsequently paid for more glasses, but how many he could not say. He left the Owl's Nest and went to the Waggon public-house, kept by George Platt. He was not sober when he left the Owl's Nest. The prisoner accompanied him to the Waggon, and they had some more drink there, for which he paid. He did not know how long he was there. They left the Waggon together, and went a little down the road and returned again to the Waggon. They had some more beer, and shortly afterwards he left the house, the prisoner being still there. When the prisoner came to the Owl's Nest to him he had the watch produced in his pocket, which he had been fetching from being cleaned, and he also had it in his possession when he went to the Waggon. After he had left the Waggon with the prisoner he missed his watch, and asked the prisoner if she had seen his watch, and she said she had not. He then went home.—Cross-examined by the prisoner: I did not offer to pay your expenses to INlanchester.—Moses Martin, peddler, Spring-view, Lower Ince, stated that he was at the Walmsley Arms Hotel, Lower Ince, last Thursday morning about eleven o'clock, and while there the prisoner came in. She said her brother had gone to New York, and had given her the watch before he went away. She offered to sell it for £l. 155., but witness could only give her 255. for it. She declined to take it, and witness said " Well, I'll give you a sovereign, it is all I have got." He gave her the sovereign and she gave him the watch. He afterwards handed the watch over to Police- sergeant Holden.—Sergeant Holden deposed to apprehend- ing the prisoner at Lower Ince and charging her with steal- ing a silver lever watch from the person of Joseph Swift at Haydock, on Tuesday, the 15th inst. She replied, "I never saw the man." After the remand on Friday last she said, "I wish I had never seen the old man. He paid for me a drink, and said he would give me 2s. or 3s. to help me on the road. I went up the road with him, and he then said he had got no money, so I took his watch." 'the watch witness received from Moses Martin.—Prisoner, in reply to the usual charge, admitted that she took the watch, but said she bad been deluded by the prosecutor, who had promised her money and then declined to fulfil his promise.—Committed to the Sessions for trial.

div.head: EXAMINER SATURDAY, MARCH 25, 1882.
div.p: THE EXAMINER SATURDAY, MARCH 25, 1882.

RUNCORN RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY. STORMY MEETING. The members of the Runcorn Rural Sanitary Authority held their fortnightly meeting on Tuesday afternoon, at the Dutton Workhouse. The Rev. Canon Barclay occupied the chair, and there were also present the Rev. J. W. N. Tanner, Messrs. Ashton (vice-chairman), Rigby, Jackson, Midwood, Andrews, Darbyshire, Weir' Challoner,•CamPkin, Highfield, Hall, Wright, Henry Linaker (clerk), and W. H. Linaker (deputy clerk). MR. WRIGHT'S ARBITRATION CASE: HOT WORDS. The DEPUTY Cisme read the following (copy) letter, which he had forwarded to the Local Government Board, in regard to this matter : Runcorn Rural Sanitary Authority, Clerk's office, Frod- sham, 10th March, 1882.—Frodsham Lordship sewerage.— Arbitration as to wayleave —My Lords and Gentlemen,—At a meeting'of this authority, held on the 7th inst., the umpire's award in reference to wayleave required for Frodsham Lord- ship sewerage scheme, through land belonging to E. A. Wright, Esq., was submitted, and a letter was read from Mr. Wright's solicitors demanding payment of the costs paid by them in taking uo the award, viz., £5 3s. 2d.. when a resolution was carried that the said sum of .295 3s. 24. be not paid until your lordships' opinion has been taken in the matter, and the follow- i^g motion was also put to the meeting* and passed. viz., "Resolved that the clerk write to the Local Government Board and state the whole affair to them both for and against the Authority; telling them about the inquiry meeting being held, and Mr. Wright putting in no appearance at the time, to ask them their opinion on the matter." In compliance with the above resolution, I have the honour to enclose herewith, for the information of your lordships, a copy ot the minutes of the proceedings of the Authority, recorded herein at the last meet- ing, and also a copy of the award. which recites the action in the matter of easement required for Frodsham Lordship sewer, both by this Authority and Mr. Wright. The inquiry referred to was held by G. J. Smith, Esq., on the 29th April, 1880. The next meeting of the Authority will be held on the 21st inst., and I have to request yourgordships' opinion in the 'natter for the information 01 the Authority at the said meeting.—l have the honour to be, my lords and gentlemen, your most obedient servant, (signed) H. LINAKER (clerk). The following (copy) reply had been sent:— Local Government Board, Whitehall, S.W., Bth March, 1882. —Sir,--I am instructed by the Local Government Board to acknowledge the receipt of your letter of the 10th inst., requesting their opinion as to the payment by the Rural Sani- tary Authority of the Runcorn Union of the costs in taking up the award of an umpire in an arbitration tinder the Public Health Act, 187,5. " The Board direA me to state that, whilst they are desirous of affording the best advice and assistance in their power to local authorities, so far as regards the general application of the law to the performance of their duties, they cannot always undertake to act as the legal advisers of local authorities with respect to their actual proceedings in particu- lar cases, especially where such proceedings affect the rights or obligations of individuals, who would have no opportunity of being heard on the subject, and who might be prejudiced by an expression of opinion by the Board on an ex parte statement. In such cases the Board recommend that local authorities should obtain the advice of their own legal advisers. In the present instance, the Board do not think that they can pro- perly advise on the subject to which your letter relates.—' am, sir, your obedient servant, J. F. RorroN, Assistant Secretary. MISCELLANEOUS.

On the proposition of Mr. Minwoon, seconded by Mr. DARBYSHIRE, it was resolved that Mr. Bancroft be written to as to why the man-hole, &c., were not shown upon the plans above mentioned when they were first made. Mr. JACKSON gave notice of motion to the effect that the salary of the Clerk should be fixed at the next meeting. This concluded the business.

Mr. ToMYINSON, who was loudly cheered, moved :—" That this meeting hereby expresses continued confidence in Her Majesty's Government, and trusts that the new rules of pro- cedure may be speedily adopted, in order that the promised legislation on questions of pressing importance, including the Corrupt Practices Bill, may receive immediate attention. The meeting is also of opinion that the recent action in the House of Lords indicates that the Upper Chamber is not in accord with popular progressive principles, therefore the question of its reform demands the consideration of the con- stituencee." Mr. D. DUNCAN (Gayton Hall, Weston) seconded the resolution. Mr. G. W. LATHAM, speaking in support, said the resolu- tion expressed their desire to support the honour and dignity of Parliament. The House of Commons was the embodiment of the people, and if the people wished to have their credit maintained they must support the dignity of the House of Commons. (Cheers.) First of all they desired that that body should be free to conduct ita own business with decency; secondly, they wished that its members should be elected in a perfectly honest and upright way; and, thirdly, that that body should not be interfered with by any other body. (Cheers.) He had little to say about the closure, but he thought it due to the hon. member for West Cheshire to apologise for a little joke lie had made about the members for that division never speaking. Mr. Tollemache had referred to that joke, and especially that portion of it with relation to Baalam's ass—(laughter)—say- ing it was "only to be expected of Mr. Latham, &a." (Laughter.) He (Mr. Latham) begged to assure the hon. member that he only said Baalam's ass did speak. (Loud laughter and cheers.) The age of miracles was passed, but no miracle ever yet wrought was so great as to make the members for West Cheshire speak. (Laughter and cheers.) Therefore he apologised to Mi. Tollemache, whom he die not compare to Baalam's ass. (Laughter.) There was no use in talking about the closure. Crewe men would have read the speech of the Marquis of Hartington, who said in a few words that the time of the House of Commons was its own, and must not be interfered with by any fool, or bore, or other conceited fellow who wished to take up an undue pro- portion of it. (Applause.) Discussion could not be stopped so long as we had a free press and the right of open meeting—(hear, hear)—and in spite of all the talk about freedom of speech, he did not believe we should lose one atom of our liberty by these measures being carried. (Cheers.) The next thing they desired was that the Cor- rupt Practices Bill might be carried. (Cheers.) In his opinion that was a most important object, but he thought that when we had larger constituencies and a greater spread of education, corrupt practices would of themselves die out. (Hear, hear.) A great change in public opinion was needed, in addition, on the question of cheapening the cost of elec- tioneering, and of placing the expense of contests on the rates—(hear, hear)—becauae under the present system many eligible workingmen and tenant farmers were pre- vented absolutely by the cost of fighting a borough or county from seeking to obtain admission to the House of Commons. (Cheers.) With regard to the third branch of the resolution—the interference of the House of Lords with the votes of the House of Commons—that was a subject upon which at the present moment they were all bound to speak out pretty boldly. It had been suggested that if the House of Lords were swept away, we should have a second chamber. He did not see the necessity. (Cheers.) If there was to be a second chamber, would any man out of a lunatic asylum ever make it like the House of Peers. (Laughter and applause.) Because a man was born the eldest son—because he was born a man and not a woman— (laughter)—and because he happened to come in priority of all the other brothers he might have—(laughter)—whether that fellow were a knave, or a fool, or a spendthrift, when his father died he went up into the House of Lords and legislated for the country. (Laughter.) He need not have one single ounce of property; he might be perfectly landless and penniless, and yet he would go into that House. (Applause.) And more than that, so long as he was not guilty of absolute crime—he might be notori- ous on the turf as a cheat—yet he could legislate for the country. And now he asked—was an assembly like that, composed as it was in a very considerable proportion of men Who had grown so old that their wits were gone—(laughter) —and of men so young that they had not yet come to their sober senses—(great laughter)—whether such an assembly, elected on the hereditary principle, was one that any man could put any confidence in ? ("No," and cheers.) People said that it had gone on for a great many years, and there had been no conflict between it and the Commons. The reason was obvious—that up to 1832, when we got the first Reform Bill, the two Houses were almost entirely composed of the same class. (Applause.) The peer kept half a dozen or less members of the House of Commons in his pocket— (laughter)—and elected them when necessary, or sold the seats to other persons if he thought fit. Other people said, "Oh, it is all Gladstone's fault. (Laughter.) If he were out of the way it would be all right." To many, Mr. Glad- stone seemed to be a sort of magician, who was always con- juring up evil, whereas the fact in ills opinion was that the Prime Minister was the great controlling power at the present time against the rush of democracy. (Cheers.) In later years the two Houses had been in perpetual conflict, and if that contest was continued, the will of the people being irre- sistible, it could have but one ending. (Cheers.) The resolution was carried with cheering, and the proceed- ings soon afterwards terminated. ACTION AGAINT ALDERMAN HARRISON. At the St. Helens County Court, on Wednesday, before Mr. Thompson, judge, William Ashcroft, quarry-man, of Pemberton, sought to recover from Joseph Harrison, high bailiff of the Warrine ton Court, £l3 4s. 11d., the amount of damages sustained by the defendant neglecting to serve a warrant of execution.—Mr. Barrow, of Wigan, represented the plaintiff, and Mr. Riley, of St. Helens, the defendant.— Mr. Barrow said that on the 16th November last his client obtained judgment against one David Hughes, stonemason and shopkeeper of Warrington, for £9 168. 6d. and costs, and that was ordered to be paid forthwith. The execution was issued, and on the same 16th November the warrant was transmitted by post to Warrington to be executed by the defendant. In the ordinary course it would arrive at War- rington on the following morning, Thursday, the 17th November, and it was defendant's duty to attend at thei Registrar's office to receive the warrant, and by section 29 also bound to execute that warrant as soon as possible. Those words were expressly stated in the section. No at- tempt was made to execute the warrant until it was too late to do so by reason of the judgment debtor having filed his petition for the liquidation of his affairs by arrangement. The petition was filed on the same day the warrant was re- ceived. This being judgment for less than £5O, his client would have been protected in the event of seizure as against the trustee in bankruptcy. His client (the plaintiff) was deprived of the benefit of his judgment. He ought to say in all fairness to the defendan that the petition was filed on the same day the warrant was received by him • but not- withstanding that circumstance if, it was possible for the defendant to have executed that warrant after its receipt before the petition was filed, he said in all confidence that the defendant was as much answerable to his client for the amount of his claim as if he had neglected it two or three days. He contended there was ample time for him to have executed it had he properly attended to his duty. The onus of proving that it was not-possible for him to execute the warrant lay with defendant. On the 18th -November the plaintiff brought to him (Me. Barrow) the notice he had re- ceived, and on the morning of the same day, pursuant to his client's instructions, he (Mr. Barrow) wrote the defendant informing him of the receipt of the notice and expressing the hope that the defendant had levied the execution and secured his client's priority. To that letter he received a reply from the defendant—and he would draw his Honour's particular attention to the reply, because it was most material to the plaintiff's case. Had it not been for that letter this action would not have been commenced. The defendant as high bailiff was bound to answer all enquiries and give every information to the plaintiff's solicitor or agent ;' and it was his duty to answer his enquiries in a satisfactory manner. On the following day he received a reply from the defendant saying that " Hughes, he regretted to saw, had succeeded in riling his petition in the Warring- ton County Court early on Thursday, the 17th inst., the very day the warrant was issued to him. He at once gave orders for lb immediate execution, and the officer on his way was told that the defendant (Hughes) bad filed his petition." If the statements in the letter had been true the present action ,vould not have been commenced. His client, the plaintiff, was inclined to believe that he was acting with a man of integrity, and did not assume for a moment that he would make any statemeatthat was not true. Nothing more was. thought about the matter until the sth December when his client went to Warzington for the pur- pose of attending the first meeting of the judgment debtors' creditors, but prior to attending that meeting he went to the County Court and examined the file of proceedings, and he discovered that the petition was filed, not as defendant said, early in the morning, but so late as half-past three in the afternoon. That caused, his client to pursue further en- quiries,and requested that he (Mr. Barrow) should ,lommuni- cate with the defendant, telling him what they had dis- covered and demanding an explanation. He wrote the defend- ant to that effect adding that he, therefore had ample time to execute the warrant; under which circumstances he was in- structed to say that be (defendant) was held personally re- sponsible for the amount, and he would be glad to hear what he proposed to do in the matter. The defendant offered no further explanation, and notice of action was then given. He obtained leave to administer interrogations to him and they were administered. With reference to that matter the defendant either showed gross ignorance c 2 his duty or wil- fully refused- to comply with the terms of the order of the court. Unfortunately his Honour the last court day thought the answer sufficient. Since that day, so late as Saturday last, he received a letter from the defendant which he thought to say the least, was a most impertinent one, and which contradicted entirely all the statements in that first letter ; and on this correspondence. be based his case. The letter said that the defendant did not wish to take advantage of his client in any way, but he could not fail to lose the case. It further stated that the defendant Hughes had left hie address given in the warrant nearly three months previously;

div.head: WIGAN.
div.p: WIGAN.

The workmen employed by Mr. R. G. Dean, painter, Standishgate, decided on Saturday to adopt the weekly con- tribution plan on behalf of the Infirmary. A CCIDENT TO A VoLuNTEmu.—On Saturday afternoon, the local volunteers met for united company drill on the vacant ground in Dicconson-street, north. The new mode of attack was practised, and while the men were being manoeuvred Private Watmough, by some mishap, was in- jured by one of his own company's rifles. He received a cut on the forehead, though not by any means a serious one, and he was at once attended to by Dr. Unwin, the surgeon of the battalion. THE ALBION IRON WORKS, ASPULL.—In January last a case of special importance was heard before the learned judge of the Wigan County Court, in which Mr. Ellis, on behalf of the Manchester County Banking Company, Limited, asked his Honour to declare that the mortgage given by Mr. Edward Hale, whose estate was in liquidation, included, in the security, the lands, buildings, and fixtures of the Albion Iron Works, Aspull. Tne bank claimed under this mortgage the whole of the machinery in connection with the works, and they applied to the court to declare that they had such a title. On behalf of the trustee in the liquidation proceed- ings, Mr. Ackerley objected to a portion of the application on the ground that trade machinery could not be considered as fixtures, and could not be deemed to be a bill of sale within the meaning of the Act. His Honour gave a decision against the trustee, and in favour of the bank, and on behalf of the former Mr. Ackerley gave notice of appeal. We learn, however, that within the past few days the matter has been amicably settled by the bank agreeing to hand over 1.2:1- per cent. of the total amount realised by the sale of the whole , building and fixtures to the trustee for the benefit of the ; estate.— Wigan Observer.

div.head: WINSFORD.
div.p: WINSFORD.

AN AMATEUR CONCERT, WINSFORD.—In the Town Hall, Winsford, an amateur concert was given, on Wednesday evening last, by the members and friends of the Station-road Primitive Methodist Chapel organ fund. The selections were chiefly from Handel, Mozart, Bliss, Wilson, Glover, ttc., and were very nicely rendered by the members of the choir and a few friends. The Station-road string band did good service by the manner in which" Gloria "was rendered as an overture, and by the violin solos of Mr. Bloor, and Mr. Sproston. The one took "In my cottage near the wood," and the other "Pin Mesto," and both were highly appre- ciated. The anthems and glees by the choir gave great satisfaction • of the former may be instanced "I will praise Thee," "Hallelujah chorus," "I love the Lord," and "All we like sheep," while amongst the latter were "To the Woodland Grem," "All among the barley," "The fisherman's glee," and "The Red Cross knight," Two duets pleased much, namely, "What are the wild waves saying," by Miss Dodd and Mr. J. Hickson; and "Beautiful rain," by Miss Newall and Mr. Whitney, was encored. Amongst the songs we may instance Mr. Percival's "Mill May," Mr. Pimlet's "Friend of the brave," Mr. Mason's "Life is a river," Miss Dodd's "Jessie, the flower of Dttnblane," and Miss L. Percival's "At the gate of heaven " was warmly encored, as was the" Wishing cap." The attendance was good, and the admission moderate, and, as an addition, there was a popular and liberal chairman to keep all going to the best advantage in the person of Mr. Edmund Leigh. There is no doubt but a good round Sum was the outcome of the etfort for the new organ so much wanted by the Station-road chapel.

After tea the chair was taken by. the Rev. William Mellor (president of the Association), who was accompanied by Mr. G. W. Latham, Mr. J. Tomkinson (Willington Hall), Mr. J. Briggs the Rev. A. W. Potts, Alderman Heath, Mr. G. Wallis, Mr R. Pedley, and other gentlemen. There was a very large attendance.

RUNCORN POLICE COURT. MONDAY.—Before Messrs. S. B. Chadwick (chairman) and, Charles Reynolds. SERIOUS CHARGE AGAINST A RUNCORN CONTRACTOR. Mr. W. H. Linaker, solicitor, addressing the Bench, said there was a case down for hearing that day, in which Mr. Thomas Cliff e, street cleansing contractor to the Board of Commissioners, who lives in Ross-street, was charged nith having, on the 16th inst., assaulted his wife, Mrs. Hannah Cliffe. He appeared for the defence, and wished to state to the Bench that the summons was only served on Friday evening. He was consulted on Saturday, but he was not prepared to go into the defence that morning, as he had not had sufficient time to give the necessary notice to the wit- nesses whom he intended to call. There was also a further ground on which he might press for the adjournment, and that was that Mr. Burton, who represented the complainant, had served him with a notice that Mrs. Cliffe intended to apply for a judicial separation. Mr. Burton remarked that he was not obliged to give Mr. Linaker such notice, but he had done so in order that he might not be taken by surprise. Mr. Linaker replied that that the case was of such a character that there would necessarily be a great deal of evi- d•lce to be taken on both sides. Witnesses would be called by him for the defence who would put a very different light upon the case. The Chairman thought Mr. Linaker had received reason- able notice, as he was instructed about ten o'clock on Satur- day morning. Mr. Linaker said that on first looking into the matter this might appear to be so, but he must remind Mr. Chadwick that he had several engagements on Saturday which pre- vented his doing anything in regard to Mr. Cliffe's case. It simply came to this—that if the adjournment could not be granted, though defendant had given such a btief notice, Mr. Cliffe would have to go undefended as ha (Mr. Linaker) should withdraw from the case. Mr. Johnson (deputy magistrates' clerk) said it had been _ _ _ . .

held that one day's notice was sufficient time. Mr. Ashton (magistrates' clerk) asked where the com- plainant (who appeared in court with her face bandaged) was now living. Mr. Burton replied that she was living with her friends. Mr. Linaker suggested that if the Bench could not see their way to adjourning the hearing of the case for some days—say Monday—they might adjourn it to the following Thursday, defendant giving an undertaking that he would not communicate with complainant in any way in the mean- time. He (the speaker) had no wish to interfere with the action of the court in any way. Mr. Ashton, after consulting with the magistrates, said they were wishful that Mr. Burton should give them a brief outline of the case, and then they would consider whether it was one they ought to adjourn. Mr. Burton said Mr. Cliffs and his wife had been married 20 years, and during the last six of that period, they had lived very unhappily together owing to the drinking habits and violent conduct of defendant. In December, 1880, pro- ceedings were taken in that court by complainant against defendant, for assault, but at his (Mr. Cliffe's) urgent solici- tation, the summons was withdrawn. At several other times, defendant had been guilty of violence, and owing to this Mrs. Cliffs had on four occasions been obliged to put herself under the care of a doctor. The offence with which defendant was now charged was the most serious of which he had hitherto been guilty. On the occasion referred to, Mr. Cliffs threw a shovel over a wall at his wife, and hit her on the forehead, causing a wound which penetrated the bone, and was two inches in length. Theshovel,which would be produced for the inspection of the magistrates, was a most dangerous weapon for defendant to use. He should call several witnesses who would bear out the statement which he had now made to them. Mr. Linaker submitted that he ought to be allowed time to obtain witnesses to meet the application of complainant for a judie,al separation. The Chairman said that the Bench, after carefully con- sidering the case as it affected both the people concerned, had determined to adjourn the hearing of it until the follow- ing Monday. They should, however, require a promise from Ur. Cliffs that he would not interfere with the due course of justice. Defendant would have to be bound over, himself in £4O, and two sureties in £2O each to appear on the follow- ing Monday. The magistrates also wished to intimate that they should not permit the case to be settled out of court. Mr. Linaker observed that after what had fallen from the Bench, he would promise, on his own part, to withdraw from the case if he found there was any attempt at negotiation between the parties concerned. Defendant and Mr. Brookes, secretary to the Commis- sioners, and Mr. Dutton market inspector, entered into the necessary sureties; and defendant was told he would have to pay ss. as the cost of the recognizances. Mr. Burton applied for costs on behalf of his client, but the Chairman said that this matter had better stand over for consideration at the adjourned hearing.

SELLING BUTTERINE FOR BUTTER, AT ROCK SAVAGE.— Joseph Didsbury, Rock Savage, was charged with having sold to the prejudice of James Bossons, police constable, 1 lie. of butter, which was not of the nature, substance, and quality of the article demanded by the purchaser.—The Officer said that on the 16th tilt., be called at defendant's shop, and asked for a pound of butter. He was served by the defendant's daughter, and, on obtaining the article, he told her that it was bought for the purpose of being for- warded to Mr. J. Carter Bell, the county analyst, for ex- amination. He offered to divide the butter into three parts, on which the daughter, who did not appear to understand what he meant, called her mother, who remarked "If she has made a mistake, well and good, but I am the mistress." —Superintendent Williamson said that on the 22ed ult., he forwarded the sample to Mr. Bell, who forwarded a certifi- cate stating that it was adulterated with 80 per cent. of foreign fat.—Mrs. Didsbury appeared, and said the article bought by Mr. Bossons was butterine, and she always told the customers this when she sold it. She gave similar in- formation to the police officer.—The Chairman said the case had been clearly proved, but as this was the first conviction recorded against the defendant he would only be fined 55., the costs being Ll 163. Bd. A PROFANE FELLOW.—John Walsh, a young man, was summoned under the Runcorn Improvement Act, for having, on the 11th instant, made use of profane laeguage in High- street.—P.C. Noden proved the case, and stated that on telling defendant he must either cease using such filthy language, or move away, if he did not wish to be locked up, he said he was quite willing to be taken to the police station.—Defendant was fined 10s. and 9s. 6d. costs, with the alternative of 14 days' imprisonment, with hard labour. THE OLD CLOTHES DEALER AND THE MARKET INsPEe-ron.—Roger Rooney, a dealer in second-hand clothes, , who has a shop in Regent-street, was summoned for having, on the 11th instant, not being a licensed hawker, sold, or ex- posed for sale in Bridge-street, within the limits of the town of Runcorn, as defined in the Improvement Act of 1852, but not within the limits of the market, on a piece of laud outside the market (not being a dwelling-house or shop) certain marketable articles in respect of which toll was authorized to be taken in the market.—Mr. W. H. Linaker. clerk to the Board of Commissioners, appeared on behalf of that body, and said that on the date mentioned the defendant put up a mock auction on land outside the market, for which he was liable to a penalty of 40s. under the Markets' and Fairs' Clauses Act, 1817.—Mr. Dutton was called, and proved seeing defendant selling second-hand clothes on a piece of private ground in Bridge-street, which was not part of the market.—ln reply to a question from Mr. Johnson, deputy magistrates' clerk, the witness said be believed that old clothes were articles liable to toll.—Mr. Linaker quoted a clause from the Act showing that the things named as liable to toll embraced almost every description of goods.—Wit- ness, in answer to further questions, stated that the land on which the defendant was selling the goods belonged to Mr. Robinsen, photographer, whose place of business was imme- diately below Wilson's Hotel.—ln cross-examination by de- fendant, witness admitted that he had charged him toll before.—Rooney said he had only sold about three times in two years on the land, and he maintained that, as it was private property, he was entitled to do so. Ile also alleged that during the evening he saw the witness in the street and asked what he would have to pay for selling.—Mr. Linaker said that when the hawking question, and other matters connected with it. was raised some time ago, he distinctly told the Board of Commissioners that they had no right to charge a toll to people who used any land outside the market. It was no doubt quite tree that defendant had paid toll when using the land in the past, but he had done so wrongly.—Defendant took the matter in very good humour, and occasionally gave vent to the mirth which seemed to be brewine within him by a subdued laugh. The cool manner in which he argued the case, and tried the in- fluence of soft sawder " on the magistrates, several times raised a hearty laugh in court. This came to a climax when the magistrates proceeded to consult with one another. evi- dently with the intention of deciding upon the amount of the penally, on which defendant shrewdly observed that "if the case was going against him " he should like an adjourn- ment, as he had communicated with a solicitor before coming to the court, but the gentleman had not been able to put in an appearance.—The Chairman said the magistrates con- sidered Rooney guilty of an attempt to avoid payment of the market toll, and he would have to pay a fine of 55. and costs.—Mr. Unaker said the defendant's contention was that he had a right to sell upon the land in question, whereas it must have been well-known to him that the very point he miffed had been frequently discussed in that court, and a oentrary decision invariably given. Considering that such people knew prrfectly well that they were breaking the lee-. it was not equitable that the commissioners should be called upon to pay the advocate's fee, and he asked the Bench to allow it. The magistrates said they would do so, and include it in the costs, making them 21s. (total, with fine, 263).

div.head: THIIP.SDAY.--:Before Mr. R. M. Brooke.
div.p: THIIP.SDAY.--:Before Mr. R. M. Brooke.

A WIDNES. 7YOUNG MAN'S ADTENTURE IN RUNCORN.—A SMART WARRINGTON POLICE SERGEANT.—A young woman I named Hannah Radford, who has for some time beer. living in Widrres, and David Jones, her stepfather, were chaNed with having on the 20th inst., stolen a silver watch, and a photograph, the property of James Murray, of No. 7 Cathe- rine-street, Widnes. The prisoners were also charged vnth receiving the same knowing them to have been stolen. The progecutor said that on Monday night he met the prisoner at Widnes, and came to Runcorn, about seven o'clock with her. The watch produced was his, and he had it safe when he left Widnes. He carried it in his waistcoat pocket, and attached to it was an albeit chain. Before be left Widnes, he bad a glass of whiskey and two glasses of beer.. He remembered going acrossthe brid;e to Runcorn, and arriving safely, on the Cheshire side of the river; but he did not recollect anything that occurred for a considerable time after that. The first occnrence which came to his re- collection was meeting a police sergeant in Runcorn, and

therefore, declared elected. Ott the motion of Mr. COLEBURN, seconded by Mr. P. SPEAKMAN, the meeting decided that the books should be ready for the auditors on the 30th inst. ; and the 13th pros. was, on the proposal of Mr. JOHNSON (organist), seconded by Mr. THOS. NORMAN, fixed as the date of the adjourned meeting. It was also resolved that public notice of the date of the meeting should be given. The following gentlemen were nominated as overseers : Mr. William Handley, Mr. William Whittaker, Mr. Briscoe, and Mr. Forrester. Mr. William Sutton was appointed assessor and collector of taxes for the year 1882-3, and Mr. John Simpson assessor ' of taxes, both unanimously. Mr. Handley then vacated the chair, as he had an impor- tant engagement to attend, and on the motion of Dr. Mc- Dougall, seconded by Mr. F. A. Lake, Mr. Henry Coleburn was elected to the position. Mr. CoLEetrare said that it appeared that there was at present no proper room in which the books belonging to the Free Library could be stored, and the matter which they had now to consider was a notice of motion given by Dr. McDougall in respect to finding proper accommodation for the books. Dr. McDotroarz, who was —received with a round of ap- plause, first of all apologised for again coming before the ratepayers on this question after such a very short time had elapsed since the proposal to have a Free Library was so fully considered in that room. He paid a compliment to Mr. W. Handley for the exertions he had put forward on this question. He regretted to say that though the Act had been adopted by a very large majority, it seemed to be very clear that certain gentlemen bad determined to frustrate the ob- ject of the promoters. He was deeply sorry that he found himself opposed to any gentlemen for whose private charac- ter he had a very great respect. However, the importance of the question to the town was so great, that he considered It was the duty of everyone who was interested in the wel- fare of Runcorn to do what they could to aid in promoting it, and so leave behind him a better state of things than formerly prevailed. They must admit that when the question was considered in that room on a pre- vious occasion, the flower of the ratepayers were present,and in spite of the intrigues which were taking place at the time behind the scenes, with the object of preventing the adop- tion of the Act, they carried the resolution in favour of it. He spoke in strong terms of the vacillating policy which had since been adopted by some members of the Board of Commissioners in respect to this question. Amongst the various methods brought forward by some of the gentlemen of whom he spoke was the favourite one of re- ferring the business to a committee; and they knew if they wished to extinguish any proposal, this was about the most effective course they could possibly adopt. He ridiculed the suggestion of Mr. Robert Shaw, that a room might Le taken for the purpose of providing accommodation for the library at an annual rental of £32; and remarked that I they had no wish to have books put away in some place that I would only be worthy the name of a dungeon. (Laughter.) Having read a letter received from Mr. Robert Davies, of Warrington, in regard to the gift of Thackeray's works to the library, and paid a compliment to that gentleman for his generosity, he proceeded to speak at length on the manner in which the Commissioners bad obtained posses- sion of Waterloo House, which he contended was admirably adapted for the purposes of public offices. He maintained it would be a wise thing to use the present offices for the reception of the books of the public library. During the course of his speech, some of the observations of Dr. McDougall appeared to irritate several of the Commissioners who were sitting near the platform. The Doctor spoke very strongly in regard to the interruption. Mr. ROBERT ROBERTS urged on the Chairman to see that Dr, McDougall had a fair hearing, as he was, he believed, simply telling them the truth, and it was not very often they could obtain all the information they required as to the action of the Commissioners on any particular question. For his own part, he was of opinion that if they " upset " a few members of the Board, and put others upon it—even if they were a little more donkey-bred—it would be more advantageous. (Laughter.) • Dr. McDonow, apparently referring to an interruption by Mr. Lake, solicitor, said he thought it would be well if some of the Commissioners present would take a leaf out of the books of the workingmen as to the manner in which I they should conduct themselves at a public meeting. He was sorry to have to make such an appeal to individuals who , ought to know better. (Sensation.) He then referred to I certain gentlemen on the Board who were fond of making' bullets for other people to shoot. In conclusion, he moved that in the opinion of the meeting the present Commis- sioners' offices and Board-room were, from their central position, the most suitable for the purposes of a Free Library, and they suggested to the Board the advisability of adopting the premises for such purpose. Mr. ROBERT FOULKES seconded the resolution. Dr. STEELE severely criticised the line of remark which had been pursued by Dr. McDougall. He said it was too personal altogether, and very unfair of him to try to make it appear that many of the Commissioners who were favour- ably disposed towards the library held a decidedly opposite opinion. Dr. McDougall must know that nearly every mem- ber of the Board, now that the Act was adopted, was desir- ous that it should be properly carried out. Mr. PHILIP SPEAKMAN followed in the same strain as Dr- Steele, and during • his remarks • Dr. McDougall frequently interpolated observations to the effect that the speaker knew very well he had done all he could to thwart the wishes of those who wished the library to succeed. Mr. GEORGE MOSS Said hit idea of a Free Library was much more comprehensive than that which appeared to be entertained by some of the speakers. The ought most cer- tainly to be in connection with the Library a free reading room, where the working men would have an opportunity I of carefully studying the best newspaper literature of the day. Mr. CURZONS was in favour of the library beinglopened every day at all hours. and he remarked that he hoped to see the day when the masses of the people of Runcorn would be sober and enlightened. Mr. THOMAS NORMAN said he had never beard one single dissenting voice in regard to the Free Library of the Board of Commissioners. He supposed the present Commissioners' rooms were worth £l,OOO at least. [Dr. MCDOUGALL : No they are not.] Therefore, if they used them or the pur- poses of a Free Library there was at once £5O sunk in in- terest which must come out of the library rate. He thought that the proposal before the meeting was one which required more consideration. If they could sell their present public offices and the town's yard, then they might migrate to Waterloo House with advantage. Mr. LAKE defended his own action on the Board in respect to the Commissioners' property, and said that the commit- tee which had been appointed on the question had not been constituted with any view to obstruction. In proof of this he stated that when proposing the committee he was careful to nominate upon it Mr. Handley, who might be described as Dr. McDougall's henchman on the library question, to- gether with Mr. flazlehurst and Mr. Briscoe. He contended that the statements of the doctor as to the ability of the Board to let off part of Waterloo House, and so bring in an income to repay them for the occupation of the building, were not correct, and would not hold water when viewed from a legal aspect, because the Local Government Board would sanction no such course of proceeding. He reminded them that they had not got the hospital as vet, and until it was erected it was highly probable the London authorities would not allow Waterloo House to be used as an office. He scarcely thought that a meeting of that character, which might be said, to a great extent, to be listening to an ex parte statement, could scarcely be looked upon as the best judges to decide on a matter of so much importance. He moved an amendment to the effect that it was inopportune to come to a decision that evening with reference to the library question. Mr. ROBERTS : I am afcaid the gentleman who has just spoken does not give the working claves of Runcorn the credit of being able to think for themselves. Mr. J. J. SPEAKMAN considered that Dr. McDougall had not put the matter fairly before the meeting. He contended they bad to face a difficulty in dealing with this matter, and he advised a prudential course of conduct. Where did they go when the wind was blowing ? Did they stand in front of it? No. They tried to find a shelter behind some friendly wall. Mr..CIIRZONS (vehemently) : There's been wind enough at this meeting. We want to hear nowt about wind. (Great laughter and loud applause). Mr. J. J. SPEAKMkN : I am afraid Mr. Curzons has been troubled with wind on his brain all the days of his life. Mr. MEADowcnorr, who was received with applause, aid he thugl,t the present public offices were not suitable or the purposes of the public library. He then proceeded to make some observations in respect to the manner id which he alleged the Doctor had led the public to believe the expenses connected with adopting the Act would be very small.
RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The fortnightly meeting was held on Tuesday afternoon. at Dutton Workhouse, when there were present the Rev. Canon Barclay (in the thair), and Messrs. Handley, Hazle- hurst, Midwood, Ashton, Andrews, Henry Linaker (clerk), and W. H. Linaker (deputy clerk).

'MASTER'S REPORT. The report of the master (Mr. R. Jones) showed that there were 183 inmates in the house, against 165 in the corres- ponding week last year. Eighteen vagrants had been re- lieved during the week. There were 30 boys and 29 girls in attendance at the Workhouse school, and 12 boys and 17 girls receiving industrial training. There were 16 imbeciles in the house. Out-door relief had been paid, during the week, to the amount of £65 16s. N. to 649 persons.

INCREASE IN THE COUNTY RATE. The following accounts were submitted for payment, by Mr. William Handley :—County Rate £1,032 3s. 6d., hospi- tal extension £3OO, petty cash payments £lB 14s. Id. Mr. Handley said the increase in the county rate for the quarter was rather more than 50 per cent, as compared with the corresponding period last year. The increase in this rate was becoming a very serious matter. In fact, the quarter's increase amounted to £326 14s. id. A letter had been re- ceived from Messrs. Potts and Roberts, stating that there was an error in the communication forwarded by them say- ing that the rate for the ensuing quarter would be £822. It would be £1,032. Mr. MIDWOOD objected to paying such a large amount of money unless they knew upon what ground the increase was made, and what it was for. Mr. HANDLEY said the usual particulars in regard to the rate were given in the statement now laid upon the table; and he believed the authorities were not obliged to give any further details. In fact, particulars had been asked for in the past, but they had not been supplied. The only course thoee who were dissatisfied could adopt, was to hurry on the formation of county boards. (Hear, hear.) Mr. MIDWOOD moved that the clerk be instructed to apply for information as to how the increase was caused, and that the cheque for the precept be withheld until it was given. Mr. RIGBY seconded the motion, with pleasure. Mr. HAZLEHURST suggested that if the latter part of the resolution were passed, it would place the authority in a bellicose position in regard to the managers of the county rate. He proposed that the latter part of the motion be left _ _ _

Mr. ANDREWS seconded the amendment, which was carried unanimously. Mr. CHALLONER moved that the cheque, which had been signed, should be held back. The CLERK explained that such a course would compli- cate the accounts very much, and make them nearly incomprehensible to the majority of the ratepayers. Mr. RIGBY said the increase would be about £1,300 per year. Such an increase was monstrous, ridiculous, and absurd.

The amendment was ultimately agreed to. The following contracts were signed :—Coffins, William Lightfoot; beer and spirits, Robert Rigby; beef and mut- ton, Joseph Dobson; milk, &c. (including carting), Joseph Roberts; brushes, William Chester; coal, Garswood Colliery Co. ; boys' and men's suits, R. Oldbury; meal and flour, J. Cowap ; groceries, S. Sutton; drugs, S. Smith and Co.; drapery, F. Fairhurst. This concluded the proceedings.

div.head: PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The usual fortnightly meeting of the Prescot Board of Guardians was held on Thursday at the Board-room, Whis- ton Workhouse, Mr. S. Marsh presiding. There were also present the Revs. T. Chambers and J. Barnacle, Messrs. Tyrer, Fidler, Hall, Leatherbarrow, Paris, Dobell, Rowe, Birchall, Jackson, Buckley, Syder, Longton, Gilbody, Penketh, Ranson, and Gerrard; with Mr. S. H. Hartlgy (clerk.) The minutes of the last meeting were read and con- firmed.

div.head: NEW WORKHOrSE CHAPEL.
div.p: THE NEW WORKHOrSE CHAPEL.

The CLERK read an entry from the chaplain's report book giving the details af the tening of the Workhouse chapel, and mentioning that over £26 was collected at the close of the service.—The Rev. T. CHAMBERS said that the sum had been made up to £27.—The CHAIRMAN asked whether the Roman Catholic inmates had yet held service in the chapel. —Mr. LEATHERBARROW said the master had informed him that they had had service in the chapel on two occasions.— The CLERK reported that he had that morning received from Mr. Gandy, the architect, a certificate that £B3 10s. Od. was due to Mrs. Harrison, ironmonger, of St. Helens, on ac- count of hot water apparatus for the chapel; also a certificate that Mr. Gore, the contractor, was entitled to £316, balance of contract. The architect also sent in his own bill for plans, specifications, and superintendence of chapel, which amounted to £47 14s. 6d.---The accounts were referred to the Building Committee. :APPOINTMENT OF TREASURER. The CLERK read the following letter, dated Whitehall, March 10th, from the Local Government Board I am directed by the Local Government Board to acknowledge the receipt of your letter of tht, Ist inst., in which you report the resignation of Mr. Edward Chrimes, the treasurer of the Prescot Union. I am directed to call your attention to Article 184 of the General Order of the 24th of July, 1874, and to request that, in reporting to the Board, the result of the next election of a treasurer you will inform them as to the amount of the security which the Guardians propose to require from him for the faithful discharge of the duties of his office; and whether any salary or remuneration is to be assigned to him for his services.—EDWAßD Surrox."—Mr. W. TYRER reported that the committee appointed at the last meeting went over to Warrington on Tuesday last and saw Mr. Dun, manager of Parr's Bank, Warrington, and made arrangements with him to their entire satisfaction. In accordance with that interview he begged to move that Mr. C. W. Corner be appointed treasurer to the Union at a salary of ,C3O per annum.—Mr. HALL seconded, and the motion was carried.—At the suggestion of Mr. HARTLEY the amount of security (£1,000) was put in the motion.

div.head: FIRES AT WORKHOUSES.
div.p: FIRES AT WORKHOUSES.

The CLERK said he had received a letter from the Local Government Board stating that their attention had been drawn by their inspectors to the want of appliances in poor law institutions for meeting any outbreak of fire or ensuring the safety of the inmates. The letter went on to state that buckets ought to be provided on the landings, ezc. The Clerk observed that they had a lot of appliances, but it was deqirable they should be tested to see if they were in proper order.—The letter was referred to the building committee.

div.head: MAKING SHORT WORK OF A LUNATIC'S -FORTUNE.
div.p: MAKING SHORT WORK OF A LUNATIC'S -FORTUNE.

The CLERK remarked,,that no doubt the Guardians would remember that Thomas Winstanley, an inmate of the Rain- hill Nsylum, had become entitled to a sum of money, and that he was instructed to take proceedings with a view to recovering some of the money. On the previous day he attended °before two justices at Liverpool, and made an affidavit that the Guardians wanted 230 for Winstanley's maintenance, and the Guardians would doubtless get that amount.—ln answer to the Chairman, the CLERK said that Winstanley's money amounted altogether, at first, to nearly £5OO, but the solicitors had swallowed about £lBO already.

div.head: REDUCTION OF MAINTENANCE OF LUNATICS.
div.p: REDUCTION OF MAINTENANCE OF LUNATICS.
The CLERIC read a communication from Lancaster County Asylum: stating that the charge for maintenance for pauper patients would be reduced from the Ist of April from Bs. 2d. to 7s. 7d. per weck.

div.p: APPOINTMENT OF MEDICAL OFFICERS FOR HALE END
StITTON.

On the motion of the Rev. T. CHAMBERS, seconded by Mr. DOBELL, Dr. Ricketts and Dr. Tattersall were appointed medical officers of health, the former for Sutton district and the latter for Hale district.
ILLNESS OF AN ASSISTANT OVERSEER.

The CLERK read a letter which he had received stating that Mr. Edmund Range, the recently appointed assistant overseer for Whiston, was very ill. Dr. Morris certified that he would not be able to cemmence duties for a month at least.
