div.head: RUNCORN STARR-BOWKETT BUILDING SOCIETY.
div.p: RUNCORN STARR-BOWKETT BUILDING SOCIETY.
LECTURE AND APPROPRIATION MEETING.

On Wednesday evening, a meeting was held in connection with the Runcorn and District 400th Starr-Bowkett Society, in Bethesda Congregational schoolroom, for the purpose of hearing a lecture on the principles of the association, by Mr. J. Barcroft, and also making the second appropriation. On the motion of Mr. J. D. Jones, seconded by Mr. Booth (Bridge-street), Mr. S. C. Beckett was voted to the chair. Amongst the gentlemen upon the platform were :—Messrs. J. Poole, W. Armstrong, J. K. Digges, and W. Handley, who was a short time ago appointed secretary. The CHAIRMAN, in opening the proceedings, referred to the facc that Mr. Barcroft had lectured on the same subject in Runcorn on a previous occasion, but he had not had the pleasure of hearing him. He, however, heard his remarks spoken of in terms of high commendation. He had pleasure in calling upon the gentleman to address them. The LECTURER said it was not his intention in an any re- marks he might make that night to say anything with the object of damaging any building society in the town; and he hoped that if he happened to let any observation fall which pinched the toes of any gentleman present, the listener affected would consider he did not mean to do so. Permanent building societies had done a great deal of good, and he believed there was a great future before them. He first referred to the advantages of thrift, and urged those present who might be inclined to sneer at small savings not to despise the day of small things. There were thousands of people who to-day were contemplating a dismal future because their health add strength were failing them, and they were convinced that they could not very much longer continue to follow what had for many yelts been their daily task. Why was it that these people weru in this despondent condition? Simply because in the days of their vigour they had refused to give any attention to the importance of small savings. His object that night was to cause some of them who had not hitherto thought of providing fora rainy day to do so; and he should be glad to answer any questions they might choose to put to him at the close. He then entered at great length into the advantages of Starr-Bowkett societies, and gave a large number of facts, most of which were laid before our readers at the time when Mr. Starr visited Runcorn for the purpose of startihg the society. He was pleased to state that in his own district he had been the instrument of causing very many to join such societies, and he felt that in so doing he had not only conferred a benefit upon these men, indivi- dually, but he had benefited the entire neighbourhood in which they lived. There were two of these organisations in the little place to which be referred, and during the year they had advanced as much as £3,000 upon property, though the population was only about 8,000. As an illustration of what might be done by saving, he would suppose a case in which a young man determined to save one shilling per day, which would be no very great effort for some who were in receipt of fair wages, if they would only decide to do with- out some at those luxuries which did them much harm. Suppose that a young man began saving his one shilling per week, and went on doing so until he came to the age of 50, he would be in possession of accumulated savings amounting to £547 10. Five per cent. added to this amount for thirty ye rs, would give a total sum put away of £1,212 108. 2d. Now, if any one of the,a had got such an amount as that, he would not take very many snubs from his foreman. (Laugh- ter.) The Starr-Bowkett society which had been formed in Runcorn and of the 500 other similar organisations estab- lished throught the country, had been for the purpose of giving the members an opportunity of each getting a house of his own in which to live, and so avoiding the payment of rent. They proposed to do this by 500 members coming to- gether and putting into °se common fund every week as many sixpences as they might be enabled to spare. For the loan of the sixpence a member had the chance of getting an appropriation whick would entitle him to the loan of £lOO for 10, or for 121 years, without interest. No member was, however allowed to have more than four shares in one group. In the district where he lived, two housei of an average character, suitable for a workingman's family, could be put up for about £l5O each house. Some of them might say they wanted some sort of a guarantee as to the time in which they would obtain an appropriation before they joined. Well, he could not tell them when they would do that, for they might have to wait a very long time; but it was satisfactory to know from calculations which had been most carefully made, that the last man in Runcorn would get his appropriatioa in 18 years. A person might say that during all this time he would be paying into the society and getting nothing; but be thought it was possible so show them that they were not quite to badly off as that, if they joined. The lecturer then explained that the secret of the society lending money to members without interest was that the cash paid in was turned over in a four-fold manner. He next dwelt upon the admirable system displayed under the society's rules ; and the fact that they provided for nearly every contingency whiet,h might overtake a member by allowing him to reduce the number of his shares without losing anything he had paid if he became the victim of mis- fortune. The election of offieers was entirely in the hands of the members, and if they became dissatisfied they could choose new ones He knew of a'case where a certain building society had put £30,000 of the members' money "down a coal pit "—(laughter)—but such a proceeding could not have been carried out under the Starr-Bowkett rules. If a member died, and left a number of children totally unpro- vided for, the money which had teen paid into the society by him was given back without one farthing being deducted. (Applause.) Several objections were next taken up and dealt with in a very effective manner; and the speaker, who is without doubt one of the ablest exponents of the princi- ples of the Starr-Bowkett building societies who has visited Runcorn—not excepting the founder; Mr. Starr—concluded amidst applause. It was then requested that anyone who desired ta ask questions as to what had been stated, or to criticise the principles of the society, might do so. One or two interro- gations of very minor importance were put, which Mr. Bar- croft answered as easily as if he had been repeating the multiplication table, At the close of his observations, he said the friends in Runcorn had now been at work a little time, and the nnmber of members only reached 190. He, however, wished them to know that they were not anything like so badly off as some of the societies, which were now working most successfully, had been in the past. He pro- phesied that the Runcorn society had before it a much brighter future than many of them anticipated. (Applause.) The balloting for the appropriation then took place in the usual form. Messrs. Thomas Faulkner and Arthur Riley acted as scrutineers. On the application of a member of the audience, those assembled were requested to state if any of them would like to join before the ballot° was taken. None came forward; and much amusement was caused by 192 proving the winning number. This, of course, proved that if new members had joined that evening, one of them would have immediately been placed in a position to have a large sum advanced. The balloting had now to be gone through

again. When this had been done, Mr. Barcroft said the winning number was 180, whose shares were taken up oil the 20th inst. Subscriptions had been paid for four weeks' entitling the holder of the share to an advance of £2OO for 12-!2- years. It would no doubt strike some of them as singular that the winner was Mrs. Ilaunah Handley, the wife of Mr. Wm.

Handley, secretary. Mr. HANDLEY immediately stepped forward and said he would, for the present, hand back the appropriation to the society—(loud applause)—but reserve the right of his wife to use it within 12 months. Mr. Ihricuorr expressed his great gratification at the course adopted by the secretary, and said the members could have another balloting within three weeks. After the passing of the customary vote of thanks, the proceedings terminated.

A point of great importance under the Employers' Liability Act arose at the Oldham County Court, on Wed- nesday. , A spinner shed a millowner for £2Bl for personal injuries sustainp,d by a machinery accident. The question of negligence does not appear to have been gone into, objec- tion being taken at the outset on behalf of the defendant that the notice of claahn was not a proper one, aa it did not in- dicate the nature of the accident, and plaintiff's counsel admitted tha he could not fight the case in a superior court supposing he got a verdict now. The Judge (Mr. Crompton Hutton), while feeling that no obstacle ought to have been thrown in the.way of the beneficial operation of the Act, said he felt sure that the notice was a great difficulty, and eventually it was arranged that the plaintiff should receive £l5, and each side pay its own costs.

div.head: WIDNES POLICE COURT.
div.p: WIDNES POLICE COURT.

MONDAY.—Before Messrs. Holbrook Gaskell and George Pilkington. Two WARRINGTON DESERTERS.—Wm. Shannon and John Ratcliffe were charged with deserting from the 40th regiment of foot, stationed at Warrington.—P.C. Skinner and Sergeant Robinson gave evidence as to apprehending the men on Saturday evening; and each of them was re- manded to Walton gaol to await an escort. WEDNESDAY.—Before Messrs. Blinkhorn and H. 8. Hall. STEALING £7 ss. FROM A FELLOW LODGER.—Michael Berry, a young man, was charged with stealing ,E 7 55., the money of a fellow lodger, named Patrick Claffey.—Prosecu- tor said he was a labourer, and lived in Catherine-street, ' and on Saturday he was at his work, and returned home about two o'clock. The prisoner lodged in the same house. He twitness) kept his savings in a box in his bedroom, and on the day of the robbery there were £7 ss. in it. At three o'clock in the afternoon he saw that his money was safe and locked the box; and on the following morning he found it gone, the box having been broken open. On making enquiries for the prisouer he found that he had not been seen that morning. This aroused his suspicion, and he and a man named Leary went to Liverpool, and found the prisoner immediately outside Lime-street station. He asked Berry for his money, and he, at first, denied taking it, but subsequEntly admitted his guilt. Since then the pri- soner had given £l4s. of it to the landlord.—Mrs. Leary, wife of Thomas Leary, gave corroborative evidence as to what happened at the house. —P.C. Anderson said he appre- hended prisoner in a back yard off Margaret-street.—The Chairman said the case was a vary bad one, and the Bench did not think it would be met by anything less than a sentence of six months' imprisonment with hard labour. THE gCHOOL BOARD AT WORK.—Several people were summoned by the Widnes School Board, who were repre- sented by their clerk (Mr. G. H. Danby), for not sending their children to school, and the following were each ordered to pay ss. including costs :—John Kinsella. Michael Hand- ley, John Healey, John Kehoe, Robert Hoey, and John Cooney. A DRIVER ASLEEP ON HIS LURRY. WM. Palin was fined ss. and costs 12s. 6d., or, in default, seven days' im- prisonment, on the evidence of Sergeant Robinson, for hav- ing been found asleep on his harry whilst driving along Vic- toria-road, on the 27th ult. ALLEGED UNPROVOKED ASSAULT. Mary Ann Conner was charged with assaulting Catherine Conner, widow, on the 13th inst.—Complainant stated that the defendant walked up to her as she was sitting on a doorstep, and, without any provocation, gate her a violent blow on the back of the head.—Defendant was fined ss. and costs. KEEPING DOGS WITHOUT HATING LICENCES. The fol- lowing were each ordered to pay ss. and costs (making 175.), for keeping dogs without licenses :—Friend Thos. Simcock, Wm. Mack, John Kehoe, Michael Handley, Joseph Greaves, Wm. Findlow, Thomas Ireland, Joseph Jamieson, Peter Kensie, and Patrick O'Brien. ASSAULTING A NEPHEW. Charles Taylor, a powerful- looking young man, was charged with assaulting James Taylor. Complainant, who is a greengrocer, said that de- fendant came to his shop and quarrelled with him about some money he (deefendant) owed. Defendant asked him if he intended to make him pay the amount, and he said yes, and told him that he ought to have discharged the debt long before. Defendant then used most disgusting language to him, and raised such a disturbance that he was obliged to close the shop door and threaten to send fer the police.—Defendant said the complainant had caused him a great deal of trouble, and stated that his wife and himself were dirty people. Defendant was ordered to enter into sureties; himself in £lO and two sureties, of £5 each, to keep thepeace for three months, or, in default, to be impri- soned fourteen days. A CONVICT FAILING TO REPORT HIMSELF. Michael Leevey was charged with having, whilst the owner of a licence granted to him under the Penal Servitude Act,unlaw- fully remained in Widnes for 48 hours without notifying his place of residence.—Prisoner pleaded guilty.—Superin- tendent Barker stated that Leevey was some time ago sen- tenced to five years' penal servitude in Dublin, and the licence he held, as a returned convict, would expire in April 1883. Prisoner left Dublin on the 11th inst., and ought to have reported himself at Liverpool, but he failed to do so. He arrived in Widnes on the 15th inst., but did not report himself until Tuesday. The fact that he had to do so with- in 48 hours of arriving in a strange place, was clearly stated upon his licence, so that he had no excuse for his conduct. —Prisoner was sent to gaol for three months. OBSTRUCTING THE FOOTPATH.—WM. Massey was fined ,fined ss. and costs 7s. 6d., for obstructing the footpath on the 11th inst.

div.head: RATEPAYERS' MEETING AT PENKETH.
div.p: RATEPAYERS' MEETING AT PENKETH.

On Thursday evening a well attended meeting of the ratepayers of Penketh,was held at the Red Lion Inn, for the purpose of examining the overseers' accounts fAr the past half-year, to lay the rate for the succeeding half, to nominate overseers, guardian, and waywarden, and to trans- act any other business for the benefit of the township. Mr. A. Thorpe was voted to the chair' and amongst those pre- sent were Messrs. Jas. Turner and Jones Foster (overseers), D. Garnett, B. Hobson, J. Mainly, P. Johnson, A. Bennett, J. Kerfout, and T. Garnett (assistant overseer).

div.head: TIES ACCOUNTS.
div.p: TIES ACCOUNTS.

The accounts which were certified to be correct by the auditors, Messrs. B. Hobson and Jas. Watson, showed that the receipts for the half year had been £398 is. 41d., pay- ments £379 Os. Bd., leaving a balance of £l9 O. 8.12 d. There were no arrears of rates. _

Mr. TURNER said that during the year March 1881 to March 1882 the overseers had collected £729 18s. 7d., and had paid to the Union £418; sanitary rate, £33 3s. ld.; highway, £238; and sundries, £34 13s. 3d. There had been lost through empties and per centages £26 4s. id. The accounts were unanimously passed on the proposition of Mr. A. BENNETT, seconded by Mr. P. BOARDMAN. THE RATE. • Mr. TURNER explained that the amount required for the ensuing half-year would be :—Poor-rate £278, last half £229; highway rate, £119; sanitary rate, £4O 4s. Bd., last half 7s. 11d.; allow once for empties aad percentages, £25; sundry expenses, £l7 55.; total £459 9s. Bd. A rate of is. sd. in the pound would realise £458 13s. 7d., which with the balance from last half would be amply sufficient, and probably leave a balance of £l7. The rate last year was is. 3d. in the pound. On the proposal of Mr. Wm. HANKINSON, seconded by Mr. JOSEPH ASHBROOB, it was decided to lay the requisite rate.

div.head: NOMINATIONS.
div.p: THE NOMINATIONS.

The retiring overseers, Messrs. James Turner, Geo. Segar, and Jonas Foster, were unanimously nominated for re-ap- pointment. Mr. Robert Garnett, the retiring guardian, was nominated for re-election, Mr. Kerfoot observing that if they nominated a hundred they would not get a man who would perform his duties better, though he had "fought shy " when the increase of salaries came on, as he saw an "A " instead of a" P " beside his name. (Liughter.) Mr. James Turner was nominated to again fulfil the office o" waywarden.
DESIRABLE IMPROVEMENTS. Mr. B. HOBSON suggested the desirability of petiltioning

the directors of the London and North. Western Railway Co., to widen the road approaching the railway station at Fidler's Ferry from Limefield Gate, Penketh, without further delay, because at present the narrow road was not only dangerous and inconvenient to foot passengers but also to vehicles. The new station was appreciated by the residents, and if the company would at an early date make the desired improve- ment the comfort of the passengers who resided in Penketh, Caerdley, and Sankey, as well as those who arrived and de- parted from the station,would be still further promoted. The CHAIRMAN moved a resolution asaing the London and North-Western Railway Co. to consider the propriety of making a better foot-road than the existing one from Penketh Hall bridge to Fidler's Ferry stations foot-pas- sengers having at present to use a private road which was shortly to be closed. _
It was agreed to incorporate Mr. Hobson's suggestion with the Chairman's resolution, which, having been seconded, was adopted. The meeting afterwards terminated.

div.head: MILTON CONGREGATIONAL CHAPEL,
div.p: MILTON CONGREGATIONAL CHAPEL,
WIDNES.
ANNUAL TEA. MEETING AND SALE OF WORK.

On Wednesday afternoon, a sale of work on a small scale was held in the vestry of Milton Congregational Chapel, I Simm's Cross, Widnes, for the purpose of raising a sum of I about £5O. It will be remembered by our readers that some three years ago negotiations were entered into with the trus- tees of the chapel by the Widnes Loc il Board for the pur- pose of acquiring a number of yards of land at the side of the edifice, so as to make the highway the proper width at this point. Several rather insignificant offers were made by the Board, but the pastor of the church and some of the trustees firmly resisted these attempts to secure a consider- able advantage at what was thought a ridiculously cheap rate. After much bargaining, and appearances of deputa- tions before the Board—which interviews were all fully reported in The Examiner at the time—the Local Board agreed to pay the trustees a sum of £2OO for the land. With this the church and congregation agreed to erect a wall round the building, which beforetime was very much ex- posed to the adventurous small boys who abound in the neighbourhood of Simm's Cross, and other parts of the town, and who are a terror to many property owners by their Van- dalism. A very neat and substantial wall has been put up by Messrs. Barran and Brookes, contractors, from designs by Mr. Rimmer, architect. Limestone chippings will be placed immediately round the sacred edifice, and flags in front of the Main door. Some £3O remains in hand from the last sale of work, and it was expected that about £5O would be realised by the effort on Wednesday afternoon. We may add that within the last five years, during which time the Rev. T. Peters has been pastor of this church, about £1,550 have been raised—a highly creditable performance on the part of a congregation which is not very strong numerically. It is hardly necessary to say, in the face of such a stete- ment, that there must have been no lack of zeal on the part of both minister and people. The room in which the sale was held is about twenty feet long, and it was very well stocked with goods, and presented an attractive appearance. The proceedings were opened at about three o'clock by the Pastor, who gave out the 1,257 th hymn, which was sung with consideraele heartiness. Mr. Peters next offered an appropriate prayer, after which, with- out any further preface' he requested the ladies in charge of the stall to commence business. The names of the ladies were Mrs. Greive' Mrs. Lewis, Mrs. Chapman, Miss Edwards, Miss Peters, and Miss Travis. Mrs. Morris had charge of the refreshment stall. Amongst the goods was an imitation wedding cake, of Brohdignagian proportions, which received much attention from the fair ladies who thronged the room; and it was filled with sweets and other attractions, which the curious were allowed to select at a charge of threepence each. Some of the bachelors who were not successful in getting anything of value revenged themselves by saying they were afraid the pretentious cake was very much like many other things matrimonial—a little delusive! A pair of oleomphs representing landscape scenery, and four illustrateetexts, were given by Mrs. Edwards, and two very neat brackets, suitable for a toilet table, were presented by Miss Evans. • In the evening the annual tea meeting was held in the chapel, and the wants of the 350 persons who were present, were well provided for by the ladies who had charge of the tables. Their names were as follow :—Mrs. Lewis, Mrs. Rimmer, Mrs. Kiddie, Mrs. Hignett, Mrs. Phillips, Mrs. T. P. Doming, Mrs. J. Doming, Miss Hirst, Miss Timmins, and Miss Morris. At the public meeting which was subse- quently held, Mr. R. Webster presided, and he was supported by the Revs. T. Peters (pastor), J. Tesseyman (Wesleyan), J. Thomas (Congregationalist, Runcorn), and Mr. T. Sad- ler. Devotional exercises having been engaged in, The CHAIRMAN said it was with great reluctance he ac- cepted Mr. Peter's invitation to occupy the position he did that night, knowing his inability to worthily occupy the post, and being convinced a more suitable person could have been found. But Mr. Peters assured him a speech would not be expected from him and ha consented. It was a posi- tion' he thought, of which he need not be ashamed; for he felt he was trying to do something for Him who had done so much for him. (Hear, hear.) The chapel was an orna- ment to the neighbourhood, to which, he was convinced, it would at some time or another be a great blessing. Workers in connection with the chapel would find much scope for their labours, and he trusted the tineb' was not far distant when they would see it filled to overflowing with the wor- shippers of the true and living God. He understood the members of the church had a voice in its affairs, and their interest in its welfare being thllh enhanced he was sure they must work heartily together. (Applause.) It would be unwise in him to make any further remarks, surrounded as he was by men more able than himself to e atertain them, and he had great pleasure in calling upon the Rev. J. Tesseyman to address them. The Rev. J. TESSEYMAN said he was glad to be present that night to speak a few words of congratulation and sympathy with them in the work which they had in hand in connec- tion with the church, and to bid them God speed. He under- stood the proceeds of the bazaar and public meeting were to be used towards the removal of a debt which had been in- curred, and he hoped the encumbrance would be removed. He was not one of those who thought there was nobody else in the world besides Methodists. He gave himself credit for possessing a little more charity than the man who prayed one day "Lord bless me and my wife; our John and his wife; us four and no more." (Laughter.) He was thankful to say he had a greater charity than that. He had a place in his heart for other people besides Methodists, and he had often been told he preached more like an Independent than a Methodist preacher. (Hear, fear.) Why he did not know, but he be- lieved he was a very good Methodist for all that. He could preach in their:chapel as well as in his own. He had preached in Primitive Methodist and Baptist Chapels; in fact in all kinds of places. He loved all good people by whatever name they were called. Often he questioned whether Christian people—Methodists, Independents, Baptists, Church people and all the rest—were doing all the good in Widnes they ought to do, or that they were capable of doing. Certainly there was in the town a great deal of Sabbath breaking and ' profane swearing. He thought he had seen more of these things in Widnes, in relation to its size, than in any other town with which he had ever been acquainted—notably as regarded profane swearing. This was carried on to an enormous extent. Scarcely ever did he go out without hear- ing terrible words uttered, not only by men but by boys and girls, and even by mothers, who cursed their little children. Did they when they heard this profane swearing, speak to the people about the bad habit. Some people said that if they did so they would only get insulted. He was never insulted in Widnes yet, and he had reproved a good many people for swearing. The worst he had received was in the case of a boy who simply laughed at him; and surely any- body could stand to be laughed at. On another occasion he reproved a man, who admitted it was a bad habit. He (Mr. Tesseyman) told:the Man that he thought there was more swearing in Widnes than in any other town he was acquained with. "Then," replied the man, "I assure you , you have never been in Wigan, for lam sure Wigan is worse than Whines a long way." (Laughter.) Did not they think they could do something more to check this bad habit? It was every Christian's duty, he thought, to reprove an badly:- dual ; the only thing was to do it in a kindly manner, and
he di'd not think anybody would insult them, or thinl any the worse of them for doing it. Each one of them must do
something to bless and save. their neighbours; each one of them was responsible Wore God for the talents they pos-

messed; they were responsible to God according to their ability • and if they did not work, if they did not make themselves useful, if they did not seek to bring sinners to Christ, how should they dare to face the Lord at last? It seemed to him that heaven's happiness would be great:y enhanced, greatly increased in proportion to the good we did, in bringing sinners to Christ. Let them try then to bring people tD Christ. It might be important to make people Independent Methdists or good Church people, but it was infinitely a more important matter to make them good Christians. It would be a grand thing at last to have saved many souls from death. It would make us die easier; we should be able to meet death, Rot with grief, but joy. He hoped none of them when they were about to die would have thorns in their pillow because they had neglected their duty and not been as useful as they ought to have been and might have been. Let them live earnestly, prayerfully, as if each day were their last—live in view of a grand and-glori- ous destiny hereafter. (Applause.) The Rev. J. THOMAS congratulated the meeting on the large gathering, and upon the improved appearance of the outside of the church. He was glad to see that at last they had a good wall, and so me excellent palisading round the church. They were now as a garden, walled round, which Le hoped did not mean that they were going to exclude the people outside, but rather that they intended to gather them in and win their affections, se that the beautiful building in. which they were congregated should shortly be filled to overflowing with anxious and earnest hearers of the Gospel. He urged upon them the necessity of their earnestly work- ing for the Lord, and made an appeal for aid in reducing the debt which existed, hoping that on the occasion of the annual gathering next year they would be entirely free from debt and with a good round balance in hand. (Ap- plause.) The proceedings were agreeably diversified by 50nga,,,..,,1ee5, and recitations. With their customary ability the Farn- worth Gleo Party sane the glees, "As the moments roll," " Night, lovely night," "Foresters' sound," and "By Celia's harbour." Miss Travis was heartily applauded for the song, "Ivy green." For a girl so young she possesses a voice unusually powerful, and with a little cultivation she will doubtless make an accomplished singer. Mrs. Lea (Miss Davies) sang with undiminished power "The better land" and' The Lost Chord," and Mrs. Watson was very success- ful in her rendering of the songs "Joyous life" and "The beating of my own heart." songs were also given by

• forte Messrs. J. R. Lea, Schofield,and Large, aril a duet, PIAI°.,;Ss a m and harmonium, was performed by Miss RlMlller and B )1.. ennett. The duties of accompanist were efficiently Per formed by Mr. Mahon. The proceedings terminated with the thanks. Olaf votes of

Insurances against Loss by Fire and Lightning are effected by the PHCENIX COMPANY upon every description of Property, In every part of the world, on the most favourable terms. I only found in the whole sample one or two seeds of Trefoil, which had probably fallen in accidentally; and it appears to be quite free from sorrel, which is almost always found, more or less, in White Clover. Weeds 0 per cent. Germi- nates quickly and evenly up to 91 per cent. "No, 3. ALSYKE.—A good coloured well-ripened, and heavy seed, almost free from weeds, and very free from broken grains. What few weeds there are (and it is quite impos- sible to avoid a few) are the common Daisy, a very few seeds of Sorrel, and here and there one of Timothy Grass. The weeds, however, amount to 0 per cent.; ge minates up ' to 85 per cent. "These samples of Clovers, therefore, are most satisfac- tory, as regards cleanliness and general quality, and they likewise show a high percentage of vitality. "No. 7. CRESTED DOGSTAIL GRASS.—This is a very fine well-ripened sample, heavy, quite true to kind and almost absolutely clean. I only found a seed or two of rye-grass In the sample. Weeds 0 per cent. " No. 5. COCKSFOOT.—A heavy sample'of light colour, quite true to kind, and quite clean. Weeds 0 per cent. " PERENNIAL RYE-GRASS.—A fine coloured, bright, and very heavy seed. True to kind, and quite free from weeds. Weeds 0 per cent. "MEADOW FESCUE (American).—A rem rkable seed, totally different in quality, and infinitely superior to the ordinary seed of this species; it is as heavy as a moderately heavy Rye-grass, and of a fine bright colour. It is quite ttue to kind, and free from any admixture with other seeds. It contains a very few, accidental seeds of Rye- grass, amounting, however, to 0 per cent. This is the first time I have seen American Fescue; but it is impossible not to recognise its superiority,aU once, "March 13th, 1882." The written report from the Botanist can be seen, and the Seeds from which samples were taken for testing, can be obtained at R. CATTERALLB WAREHOUSE, Moor-street, O rmskirk.
